When multiple firewall management utilities are active, the effective rule set becomes ambiguous and difficult to audit, and one utility can silently override the protective rules configured in another - weakening or negating the host firewall. Ensuring firewalld is the only active firewall manager keeps the enforced policy deterministic and auditable.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
For any conflicting firewall manager found in the Audit, migrate any required rules into firewalld first, then disable or remove it.
Stop, disable, and mask a standalone nftables.service:
# systemctl stop nftables.service
# systemctl --now disable nftables.service
# systemctl mask nftables.service
Remove the iptables-services package if installed:
# dnf remove iptables-services
Remove the ufw package if installed:
# dnf remove ufw
Reload firewalld to apply the firewalld-managed ruleset:
# firewall-cmd --reload

check.check-content:
Run the following checks to verify that no conflicting firewall manager is in use alongside firewalld.
1. Verify the standalone nftables.service is not enabled or active (firewalld programs the NFTables backend directly and does not use this service):
# systemctl is-enabled nftables.service
# systemctl is-active nftables.service
Neither command should return enabled or active ( disabled, masked, inactive, or a not-found result is expected).
2. Verify the legacy iptables-services package is not installed:
# rpm -q iptables-services
package iptables-services is not installed should be returned.
3. Verify ufw is not installed:
# rpm -q ufw
package ufw is not installed should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure firewalld logs denied packets
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The LogDenied option in /etc/firewalld/firewalld.conf controls logging of packets denied (dropped or rejected) by firewalld. Supported values are off (default), all, unicast, broadcast, and multicast. When enabled, firewalld adds kernel logging rules for denied packets immediately before the applicable reject/drop rules.

Rationale:
Logging denied packets provides visibility into blocked and attempted connections, supporting detection of firewall misconfigurations and malicious activity, and providing evidence for incident investigation.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to enable logging of denied packets (replace all with the value that meets local site policy):
# firewall-cmd --set-log-denied=all
Run the following command to reload firewalld:
# firewall-cmd --reload

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify firewalld is logging denied packets:
# firewall-cmd --get-log-denied
The value returned should be one of all, unicast, broadcast, or multicast (any value other than off), in accordance with local site policy.

Rule.title: Ensure firewalld blocks ICMP timestamp requests and replies
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>ICMP timestamp messages ( timestamp-request, ICMP type 13, and timestamp- reply, ICMP type 14) allow a remote host to query the system clock. firewalld can block these message types, per zone, so the host does not respond to timestamp requests.

Rationale:
Answering ICMP timestamp requests discloses the host's system clock, which can help an attacker fingerprint the host, correlate activity across hosts, or attack time-dependent protocols. Vulnerability scanners and several STIGs flag hosts that respond to ICMP timestamp requests. Blocking these ICMP types removes the disclosure.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Block the ICMP timestamp message types on each active zone that filters network traffic (target default). A zone whose target is ACCEPT (such as trusted) or DROP / %%REJECT%% already handles these messages and needs no change.
1. For each such zone, block both message types:
# firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=<ZONE> --add-icmp-block=timestamp-request
# firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=<ZONE> --add-icmp-block=timestamp-reply
2. Reload firewalld to apply the change:
# firewall-cmd --reload
Example (blocking on the public zone):
# firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-icmp-block=timestamp-request
# firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-icmp-block=timestamp-reply
# firewall-cmd --reload

check.check-content:
ICMP timestamp blocking applies to firewalld zones that filter network traffic. A zone whose target is ACCEPT (such as the built-in trusted zone) does not filter traffic and is not applicable; a zone whose target is DROP or %%REJECT%% already discards these messages. Only a zone whose target is default needs the explicit block.
1. Run the following command to list the active zones:
# firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
2. Run the following command to determine each active zone's target:
# firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=<ZONE> --get-target
3. For each active zone whose target is default, check the ICMP block inversion setting and list the zone's ICMP blocks:
# firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=<ZONE> --query-icmp-block-inversion
# firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=<ZONE> --list-icmp-blocks
If inversion is not enabled ( no), the icmp-block list is a block-list: timestamp-request and timestamp-reply should be listed. If inversion is enabled ( yes), the icmp-block list is an allow-list: timestamp-request and timestamp-reply should not be listed (any type not listed is blocked).
Example (target default, inversion disabled):
# firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --get-target
default
# firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --list-icmp-blocks
timestamp-reply timestamp-request

Rule.title: Ensure access to /etc/ssh/sshd_config is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The file /etc/ssh/sshd_config, and files ending in.conf in the /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d directory, contain configuration specifications for sshd.

Rationale:
Configuration specifications for sshd need to be protected from unauthorized access by non-privileged users.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following script to set ownership and permissions on /etc/ssh/sshd_config and files ending in.conf in the /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d directory:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
chmod u-x,og-rwx /etc/ssh/sshd_config
chown root:root /etc/ssh/sshd_config
while IFS= read -r -d $'\0' l_file; do
if [ -e "$l_file" ]; then
chmod u-x,og-rwx "$l_file"
chown root:root "$l_file"
fi
done < <(find /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d -type f -print0 2>/dev/null)
}
- IF - other locations are listed in an Include statement, *.conf files in these locations access should also be modified.

check.check-content:
Run the following commands to verify that /etc/ssh/sshd_config and the.conf files in the /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d directory are mode 0600 or more restrictive and are owned by the user and group root.
Verify the main configuration file. Nothing should be returned:
# find /etc/ssh/sshd_config -maxdepth 0 \( -perm /177 -o ! -user root -o ! -
group root \) 2>/dev/null
Verify the drop-in.conf files. Nothing should be returned:
# find /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ -type f -name '*.conf' \( -perm /177 -o ! -
user root -o ! -group root \) 2>/dev/null
Note: Mode 0600 or more restrictive means the file grants no group or other access and no execute permission for the owner. If other locations are listed in an Include statement, the.conf files in those locations should also be checked.

Rule.title: Ensure access to /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ directory is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>/etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ is the default drop-in configuration directory for the OpenSSH server daemon (sshd). The line Include /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf shipped in the default /etc/ssh/sshd_config causes every file in this directory ending in .conf to be processed as part of the effective server configuration, with first-occurrence-wins precedence over directives that follow the Include in the parent file.
This recommendation governs the directory itself: ownership of /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/, and the mode bits applied to the directory inode. It complements the recommendation that governs the parent /etc/ssh/sshd_config file and the .conf drop-in files inside this directory, which does not constrain the directory entry itself.
More information about the OpenSSH server configuration is available in the "Configure SSH Server" section overview.

Rationale:
A drop-in configuration directory at the default mode of 0755 root:root is world-readable and world-traversable. Any local user can therefore:
• Enumerate the per-host SSH server policy
• Read the contents of any .conf drop-in that itself is world-readable
• Reconnoitre for related artifacts: AllowGroups lists, ListenAddress restrictions, banner paths, alternative HostKey paths, and AuthorizedKeysFile overrides each reveal information useful to an attacker performing local reconnaissance prior to privilege escalation or lateral movement.
Configuration specifications for sshd — including the per-host overrides contained in this directory — need to be protected from unauthorized disclosure as well as unauthorized modification by non-privileged users. Restricting the directory to mode 0700 root:root ensures that only the root user can list, traverse, or modify the directory, matching the protection already required for the parent sshd_config file and the .conf files inside the directory.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following commands to set ownership and mode on /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/:
# chown root:root /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/
# chmod 0700 /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/
Note: If the SSH server reads drop-in files from an additional Include location, apply the same ownership and mode to each such directory.
No service reload is required — the directory mode does not affect the running sshd process, only future reads of the directory.

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify ownership and mode on /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ are configured:
# find /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ -maxdepth 0 \( ! -user root -o ! -group root -
o -perm /077 \)
Nothing should be returned.
Note: If the SSH server has been configured to read drop-in files from an Include location other than /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/, the additional directory or directories listed by that Include statement should also be checked against the same criteria.
Example identification of additional Include locations:
# sshd -T 2>/dev/null | awk '$1 == "include" {print $2}'
For each path returned, repeat the audit substituting the path for /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ and adjusting -maxdepth if the path is a glob or contains a wildcard.

Rule.title: Ensure access to SSH private host key files is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>An SSH private key is one of two files used in SSH public key authentication. In this authentication method, the possession of the private key is proof of identity. Only a private key that corresponds to a public key will be able to authenticate successfully.
The private keys need to be stored and handled carefully, and no copies of the private key should be distributed.

Rationale:
If an unauthorized user obtains the private SSH host key file, the host could be impersonated.</VulnDiscussion>

check.check-content:
Verify that each SSH private host key file is owned by user root and is either:
• group-owned by root with mode 0600 or more restrictive, or
• group-owned by ssh_keys with mode 0640 or more restrictive (the ssh_keys group is used only where the distribution provides it, for host-based authentication).
Run the following script to list any private host key file that does not meet the above.
Host key files are read from the running sshd configuration (so keys in non-default locations or with non-default names are included), and mode is tested with a permission bitmask (so more-restrictive modes also pass). Nothing should be returned:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
l_ssh_group=""
grep -Psiq -- '^\h*ID_LIKE="?([^#\n\r]+)?\bfedora\b' /etc/os-release
2>/dev/null && \
grep -Psq -- '^ssh_keys\b' /etc/group 2>/dev/null &&
l_ssh_group="ssh_keys"
while IFS= read -r l_file; do
ssh-keygen -lf "$l_file" &>/dev/null || continue
while IFS=: read -r l_mode l_owner l_group; do
[ "$l_group" = "$l_ssh_group" ] && l_mask="0137" || l_mask="0177"
if [ $(( l_mode & l_mask )) -gt 0 ] || [ "$l_owner" != "root" ] || \
{ [ "$l_group" != "$l_ssh_group" ] && [ "$l_group" != "root" ];
}; then
printf '%s\n' "\"$l_file\": mode $l_mode owner $l_owner group
$l_group"
fi
done < <(stat -Lc '%#a:%U:%G' "$l_file")
done < <(sshd -T 2>/dev/null | awk '$1=="hostkey"{print $2}')
}

Rule.title: Ensure access to SSH public host key files is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>An SSH public key is one of two files used in SSH public key authentication. In this authentication method, a public key is a key that can be used for verifying digital signatures generated using a corresponding private key. Only a public key that corresponds to a private key will be able to authenticate successfully.

Rationale:
If a public host key file is modified by an unauthorized user, the SSH service may be compromised.</VulnDiscussion>

check.check-content:
Verify that each SSH public host key file is owned by user root and group root, with mode 0644 or more restrictive.
Run the following script to list any public host key file that does not meet the above.
Public host key files are the ".pub" of each host key in the running sshd configuration, and mode is tested with a permission bitmask (so more-restrictive modes also pass).
Nothing should be returned:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
l_ssh_group=""
grep -Psiq -- '^\h*ID_LIKE="?([^#\n\r]+)?\bfedora\b' /etc/os-release
2>/dev/null && \
grep -Psq -- '^ssh_keys\b' /etc/group 2>/dev/null &&
l_ssh_group="ssh_keys"
while IFS= read -r l_key; do
l_file="${l_key}.pub"
ssh-keygen -lf "$l_file" &>/dev/null || continue
while IFS=: read -r l_mode l_owner l_group; do
if [ $(( l_mode & 0133 )) -gt 0 ] || [ "$l_owner" != "root" ] || \
{ [ "$l_group" != "$l_ssh_group" ] && [ "$l_group" != "root" ];
}; then
printf '%s\n' "\"$l_file\": mode $l_mode owner $l_owner group
$l_group"
fi
done < <(stat -Lc '%#a:%U:%G' "$l_file")
done < <(sshd -T 2>/dev/null | awk '$1=="hostkey"{print $2}')
}

Rule.title: Ensure sshd Ciphers are configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Secure Shell (SSH) ciphers are encryption algorithms used by the SSH protocol to secure data transmitted between a client and a server. They protect the privacy and integrity of the connection, using symmetric encryption to encrypt data after a secure session is established. During connection setup, the client and server negotiate to select the strongest available cipher that both support, ensuring the connection is as secure as possible More information about the openSSH server configuration is available in the "Configure SSH Server" section overview.

Rationale:
Weak ciphers that are used for authentication to the cryptographic module cannot be relied upon to provide confidentiality or integrity, and system data may be compromised.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
The ciphers available to the SSH server are governed by the system-wide crypto policy.
Disable the weak ciphers by configuring the system-wide crypto policy as described in the "Configure system wide crypto policy" section.
- IF - CVE-2023-48795 (Terrapin) has not been reviewed and addressed, chacha20- poly1305 should also be disabled through the system-wide crypto policy.
Once the crypto policy has been updated, reload the SSH daemon:
# systemctl reload-or-restart sshd

check.check-content:
Run the following script to list any weak ciphers that are enabled. Nothing should be returned:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
a_weak=(3des-cbc blowfish-cbc cast128-cbc aes128-cbc aes192-cbc aes256-cbc
arcfour arcfour128 arcfour256 rijndael-cbc@lysator.liu.se)
l_offered="$(sshd -T | awk '$1=="ciphers"{print $2}' | tr ',' '\n')"
for l_alg in "${a_weak[@]}"; do
grep -Fxq -- "$l_alg" <<< "$l_offered" && printf '%s\n' "$l_alg"
done
}
Note: (advisory - chacha20-poly1305 / CVE-2023-48795): The following command is an advisory check only and is not part of the pass/fail assessment above. It reports whether the chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com cipher is offered:
# sshd -T 2>&1 | awk '($1=="ciphers" && $2~/chacha20- poly1305@openssh\.com/){print}' On OpenSSH 9.6 and later the Terrapin attack (CVE-2023-48795) is mitigated by default through strict key exchange, so a returned line does not by itself indicate a weakness. On earlier OpenSSH releases, if a line is returned, review CVE-2023-48795 and verify the system has been patched, and consider excluding chacha20-poly1305 through the system-wide crypto policy.

Rule.title: Ensure sshd KexAlgorithms is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Key exchange is any method in cryptography by which cryptographic keys are exchanged between two parties, allowing use of a cryptographic algorithm. If the sender and receiver wish to exchange encrypted messages, each must be equipped to encrypt messages to be sent and decrypt messages received Notes:
• Kex algorithms have a higher preference the earlier they appear in the list
• Some organizations may have stricter requirements for approved Key exchange algorithms
• Ensure that Key exchange algorithms used are in compliance with site policy
• The only Key Exchange Algorithms currently FIPS 140 approved are:
o ecdh-sha2-nistp256
o ecdh-sha2-nistp384
o ecdh-sha2-nistp521
o diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256
o diffie-hellman-group16-sha512
o diffie-hellman-group18-sha512
o diffie-hellman-group14-sha256

Rationale:
Key exchange methods that are considered weak should be removed. A key exchange method may be weak because too few bits are used, or the hashing algorithm is considered too weak. Using weak algorithms could expose connections to man-in-the- middle attacks</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
The key exchange algorithms available to the SSH server are governed by the system- wide crypto policy. The weak key exchange algorithms in scope are SHA1-based;
disable them by disabling SHA1 hash and signature support in the system-wide crypto policy as described in the "Configure system wide crypto policy" section.
Once the crypto policy has been updated, reload the SSH daemon:
# systemctl reload-or-restart sshd

check.check-content:
Run the following script to list any weak key exchange algorithms that are enabled.
Nothing should be returned:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
a_weak=(diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 diffie-hellman-group14-sha1 diffie-
hellman-group-exchange-sha1)
l_offered="$(sshd -T | awk '$1=="kexalgorithms"{print $2}' | tr ',' '\n')"
for l_alg in "${a_weak[@]}"; do
grep -Fxq -- "$l_alg" <<< "$l_offered" && printf '%s\n' "$l_alg"
done
}
The following are considered "weak" Key Exchange Algorithms, and should not be used:
diffie-hellman-group1-sha1
diffie-hellman-group14-sha1
diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1

Rule.title: Ensure sshd MACs are configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>This variable limits the types of MAC algorithms that SSH can use during communication.
Notes:
• Some organizations may have stricter requirements for approved MACs.
• Ensure that MACs used are in compliance with site policy.
• The only "strong" MACs currently FIPS 140 approved are:
o HMAC-SHA1
o HMAC-SHA2-256
o HMAC-SHA2-384
o HMAC-SHA2-512

Rationale:
MD5-based, RIPEMD-160, 96-bit-truncated, and 64-bit (UMAC-64) MAC algorithms are considered weak and have been shown to increase exploitability in SSH downgrade attacks. Weak algorithms continue to have a great deal of attention as a weak spot that can be exploited with expanded computing power. An attacker that breaks the algorithm could take advantage of a MiTM position to decrypt the SSH tunnel and capture credentials and information.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
The MAC algorithms available to the SSH server are governed by the system-wide crypto policy. Disable the weak MACs by configuring the system-wide crypto policy as described in the "Configure system wide crypto policy" section.
- IF - CVE-2023-48795 (Terrapin) has not been reviewed and addressed, the Encrypt- then-MAC (EtM) MACs should also be disabled through the system-wide crypto policy.
Once the crypto policy has been updated, reload the SSH daemon:
# systemctl reload-or-restart sshd

check.check-content:
Run the following script to list any weak MACs that are enabled. Nothing should be returned:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
a_weak=(hmac-md5 hmac-md5-96 hmac-ripemd160 hmac-sha1-96 umac-
64@openssh.com hmac-md5-etm@openssh.com hmac-md5-96-etm@openssh.com hmac-
ripemd160-etm@openssh.com hmac-sha1-96-etm@openssh.com umac-64-
etm@openssh.com)
l_offered="$(sshd -T | awk '$1=="macs"{print $2}' | tr ',' '\n')"
for l_alg in "${a_weak[@]}"; do
grep -Fxq -- "$l_alg" <<< "$l_offered" && printf '%s\n' "$l_alg"
done
}
Note: Review CVE-2023-48795 and verify the system has been patched. If the system has not been patched, review the use of the Encrypt Then Mac (etm) MACs.
The following are considered "weak" MACs, and should not be used:
hmac-md5
hmac-md5-96
hmac-ripemd160
hmac-sha1-96
umac-64@openssh.com
hmac-md5-etm@openssh.com
hmac-md5-96-etm@openssh.com
hmac-ripemd160-etm@openssh.com
hmac-sha1-96-etm@openssh.com
umac-64-etm@openssh.com

Rule.title: Ensure sshd access is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>There are several options available to limit which users and group can access the system via SSH. It is recommended that at least one of the following options be leveraged:
• AllowUsers:
o The AllowUsers variable gives the system administrator the option of allowing specific users to ssh into the system. The list consists of space separated user names. Numeric user IDs are not recognized with this variable. If a system administrator wants to restrict user access further by only allowing the allowed users to log in from a particular host, the entry can be specified in the form of user@host.
• AllowGroups:
o The AllowGroups variable gives the system administrator the option of allowing specific groups of users to ssh into the system. The list consists of space separated group names. Numeric group IDs are not recognized with this variable.
• DenyUsers:
o The DenyUsers variable gives the system administrator the option of denying specific users to ssh into the system. The list consists of space separated user names. Numeric user IDs are not recognized with this variable. If a system administrator wants to restrict user access further by specifically denying a user's access from a particular host, the entry can be specified in the form of user@host.
• DenyGroups:
o The DenyGroups variable gives the system administrator the option of denying specific groups of users to ssh into the system. The list consists of space separated group names. Numeric group IDs are not recognized with this variable.

Rationale:
Restricting which users can remotely access the system via SSH will help ensure that only authorized users access the system.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to set one or more of the parameters above any Include and Match set statements as follows:
AllowUsers <userlist>
- AND/OR -
AllowGroups <grouplist>
Note:
• Be advised that these options are "ANDed" together. If both AllowUsers and AllowGroups are set, connections will be limited to the list of users that are also a member of an allowed group. It is recommended that only one be set for clarity and ease of administration.
• It is easier to manage an allow list than a deny list. In a deny list, you could potentially add a user or group and forget to add it to the deny list.

check.check-content:
Run the following command and verify the output:
# sshd -T | grep -Pi -- '^\h*(allow|deny)(users|groups)\h+\H+'
Verify that the output matches at least one of the following lines:
allowusers <userlist>
-OR-
allowgroups <grouplist>
-OR-
denyusers <userlist>
-OR-
denygroups <grouplist>
Review the list(s) to ensure included users and/or groups follow local site policy Note: This setting can be overridden within a Match block. If Match blocks are configured, also verify the effective value for the relevant contexts as described in the section overview.

Rule.title: Ensure sshd Banner is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The Banner parameter specifies a file whose contents must be sent to the remote user before authentication is permitted. By default, no banner is displayed.

Rationale:
Banners are used to warn connecting users of the particular site's policy regarding connection. Presenting a warning message prior to the normal user login may assist the prosecution of trespassers on the computer system.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to set the Banner parameter above any Include and Match entries as follows:
Banner /etc/issue.net
Edit the file being called by the Banner argument with the appropriate contents according to your site policy, remove any instances of \m, \r, \s, \v or references to the OS platform Example:
# printf '%s\n' "Authorized users only. All activity may be monitored and
reported." > "$(sshd -T | awk '$1 == "banner" {print $2}')"

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify Banner is set:
# sshd -T | grep -Pi -- '^banner\h+\/\H+'
Example:
banner /etc/issue.net
Run the following command and verify that the contents or the file being called by the Banner argument match site policy:
# [ -e "$(sshd -T | awk '$1 == "banner" {print $2}')" ] && cat "$(sshd -T |
awk '$1 == "banner" {print $2}')"
Run the following command and verify no results are returned:
# grep -Psi -- "(\\\v|\\\r|\\\m|\\\s|\b$(grep '^ID=' /etc/os-release | cut -
d= -f2 | sed -e 's/"//g')\b)" "$(sshd -T | awk '$1 == "banner" {print $2}')"
Note: This setting can be overridden within a Match block. If Match blocks are configured, also verify the effective value for the relevant contexts as described in the section overview.

Rule.title: Ensure sshd ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax are configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Note: To clarify, the two settings described below are only meant for idle connections from a protocol perspective and are not meant to check if the user is active or not. An idle user does not mean an idle connection. SSH does not and never had, intentionally, the capability to drop idle users. In SSH versions before 8.2p1 there was a bug that caused these values to behave in such a manner that they were abused to disconnect idle users. This bug has been resolved in 8.2p1 and thus it can no longer be abused disconnect idle users.
The two options ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax control the timeout of SSH sessions. Taken directly from man 5 sshd_config:
• ClientAliveInterval Sets a timeout interval in seconds after which if no data has been received from the client, sshd(8) will send a message through the encrypted channel to request a response from the client. The default is 0, indicating that these messages will not be sent to the client.
• ClientAliveCountMax Sets the number of client alive messages which may be sent without sshd(8) receiving any messages back from the client. If this threshold is reached while client alive messages are being sent, sshd will disconnect the client, terminating the session. It is important to note that the use of client alive messages is very different from TCPKeepAlive. The client alive messages are sent through the encrypted channel and therefore will not be spoofable. The TCP keepalive option en ‐ abled by TCPKeepAlive is spoofable.
The client alive mechanism is valuable when the client or server depend on knowing when a connection has become unresponsive.
The default value is 3. If ClientAliveInterval is set to 15, and ClientAliveCountMax is left at the default, unresponsive SSH clients will be disconnected after approximately 45 seconds. Setting a zero ClientAliveCountMax disables connection termination.

Rationale:
In order to prevent resource exhaustion, appropriate values should be set for both ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax. Specifically, looking at the source code, ClientAliveCountMax must be greater than zero in order to utilize the ability of SSH to drop idle connections. If connections are allowed to stay open indefinitely, this can potentially be used as a DDOS attack or simple resource exhaustion could occur over unreliable networks.
The example set here is a 45 second timeout. Consult your site policy for network timeouts and apply as appropriate.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to set the ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax parameters above any Include and Match entries according to site policy.
Example:
ClientAliveInterval 15
ClientAliveCountMax 3

check.check-content:
Run the following command and verify ClientAliveInterval and ClientAliveCountMax are greater than zero:
# sshd -T | grep -Pi -- '(clientaliveinterval|clientalivecountmax)'
Example Output:
clientaliveinterval 15
clientalivecountmax 3
Note: This setting can be overridden within a Match block. If Match blocks are configured, also verify the effective value for the relevant contexts as described in the section overview.

Rule.title: Ensure sshd DisableForwarding is enabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The DisableForwarding parameter disables all forwarding features, including X11, ssh-agent(1), TCP and StreamLocal. This option overrides all other forwarding-related options and may simplify restricted configurations.
• X11Forwarding provides the ability to tunnel X11 traffic through the connection to enable remote graphic connections.
• ssh-agent is a program to hold private keys used for public key authentication.
Through use of environment variables the agent can be located and automatically used for authentication when logging in to other machines using ssh.
• SSH port forwarding is a mechanism in SSH for tunneling application ports from the client to the server, or servers to clients. It can be used for adding encryption to legacy applications, going through firewalls, and some system administrators and IT professionals use it for opening backdoors into the internal network from their home machines.

Rationale:
Disable X11 forwarding unless there is an operational requirement to use X11 applications directly. There is a small risk that the remote X11 servers of users who are logged in via SSH with X11 forwarding could be compromised by other users on the X11 server. Note that even if X11 forwarding is disabled, users can always install their own forwarders.
Anyone with root privilege on the intermediate server can make free use of ssh-agent to authenticate as the user to other servers.
Leaving port forwarding enabled can expose the organization to security risks and backdoors. SSH connections are protected with strong encryption. This makes their contents invisible to most deployed network monitoring and traffic filtering solutions.
This invisibility carries considerable risk potential if it is used for malicious purposes such as data exfiltration. Cybercriminals or malware could exploit SSH to hide their unauthorized communications, or to exfiltrate stolen data from the target network.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to set the DisableForwarding parameter to yes above any Include entry as follows:
DisableForwarding yes

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify DisableForwarding is set to yes:
# sshd -T | grep -i disableforwarding
disableforwarding yes
Note: This setting can be overridden within a Match block. If Match blocks are configured, also verify the effective value for the relevant contexts as described in the section overview.

Rule.title: Ensure sshd GSSAPIAuthentication is disabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The GSSAPIAuthentication parameter specifies whether user authentication based on GSSAPI is allowed

Rationale:
Allowing GSSAPI authentication through SSH exposes the system's GSSAPI to remote hosts, and should be disabled to reduce the attack surface of the system</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to set the GSSAPIAuthentication parameter to no above any Include and Match entries as follows:
GSSAPIAuthentication no

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify GSSAPIAuthentication is set to no:
# sshd -T | grep gssapiauthentication
gssapiauthentication no
Note: This setting can be overridden within a Match block. If Match blocks are configured, also verify the effective value for the relevant contexts as described in the section overview.

Rule.title: Ensure sshd HostbasedAuthentication is disabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The HostbasedAuthentication parameter specifies if authentication is allowed through trusted hosts via the user of.rhosts, or /etc/hosts.equiv, along with successful public key client host authentication.

Rationale:
Even though the.rhosts files are ineffective if support is disabled in /etc/pam.conf, disabling the ability to use.rhosts files in SSH provides an additional layer of protection.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to set the HostbasedAuthentication parameter to no above any Include and Match entries as follows:
HostbasedAuthentication no

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify HostbasedAuthentication is set to no:
# sshd -T | grep hostbasedauthentication
hostbasedauthentication no
Note: This setting can be overridden within a Match block. If Match blocks are configured, also verify the effective value for the relevant contexts as described in the section overview.

Rule.title: Ensure sshd IgnoreRhosts is enabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The IgnoreRhosts parameter specifies that.rhosts and.shosts files will not be used in RhostsRSAAuthentication or HostbasedAuthentication.

Rationale:
Setting this parameter forces users to enter a password when authenticating with SSH.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to set the IgnoreRhosts parameter to yes above any Include entry as follows:
IgnoreRhosts yes

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify IgnoreRhosts is set to yes:
# sshd -T | grep ignorerhosts
ignorerhosts yes
Note: This setting can be overridden within a Match block. If Match blocks are configured, also verify the effective value for the relevant contexts as described in the section overview.

Rule.title: Ensure sshd LoginGraceTime is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The LoginGraceTime parameter specifies the time allowed for successful authentication to the SSH server. The longer the Grace period is the more open unauthenticated connections can exist. Like other session controls in this section the Grace Period should be limited to appropriate organizational limits to ensure the service is available for needed access.

Rationale:
Setting the LoginGraceTime parameter to a low number will minimize the risk of successful brute force attacks to the SSH server. It will also limit the number of concurrent unauthenticated connections. While the recommended setting is 60 seconds (1 minute), set the number based on site policy.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to set the LoginGraceTime parameter to 60 seconds or less above any Include entry as follows:
LoginGraceTime 60

check.check-content:
Run the following command and verify that output LoginGraceTime is between 1 and 60 seconds:
# sshd -T | grep logingracetime
logingracetime 60

Rule.title: Ensure sshd LogLevel is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>SSH provides several logging levels with varying amounts of verbosity. The DEBUG options are specifically not recommended other than strictly for debugging SSH communications. These levels provide so much data that it is difficult to identify important security information, and may violate the privacy of users.

Rationale:
The INFO level is the basic level that only records login activity of SSH users. In many situations, such as Incident Response, it is important to determine when a particular user was active on a system. The logout record can eliminate those users who disconnected, which helps narrow the field.
The VERBOSE level specifies that login and logout activity as well as the key fingerprint for any SSH key used for login will be logged. This information is important for SSH key management, especially in legacy environments.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to set the LogLevel parameter to VERBOSE or INFO above any Include and Match entries as follows:
LogLevel VERBOSE
- OR -
LogLevel INFO

check.check-content:
Run the following command and verify that output matches loglevel VERBOSE or loglevel INFO:
# sshd -T | grep loglevel
loglevel VERBOSE
- OR -
loglevel INFO
Note: This setting can be overridden within a Match block. If Match blocks are configured, also verify the effective value for the relevant contexts as described in the section overview.

Rule.title: Ensure sshd MaxAuthTries is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The MaxAuthTries parameter specifies the maximum number of authentication attempts permitted per connection. When the login failure count reaches half the number, error messages will be written to the syslog file detailing the login failure.

Rationale:
Setting the MaxAuthTries parameter to a low number will minimize the risk of successful brute force attacks to the SSH server. While the recommended setting is 4, set the number based on site policy.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to set the MaxAuthTries parameter to 4 or less above any Include and Match entries as follows:
MaxAuthTries 4

check.check-content:
Run the following command and verify that MaxAuthTries is 4 or less:
# sshd -T | grep maxauthtries
maxauthtries 4
Note: This setting can be overridden within a Match block. If Match blocks are configured, also verify the effective value for the relevant contexts as described in the section overview.

Rule.title: Ensure sshd MaxStartups is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The MaxStartups parameter specifies the maximum number of concurrent unauthenticated connections to the SSH daemon.

Rationale:
To protect a system from denial of service due to a large number of pending authentication connection attempts, use the rate limiting function of MaxStartups to protect availability of sshd logins and prevent overwhelming the daemon.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to set the MaxStartups parameter to 10:30:60 or more restrictive above any Include entries as follows:
MaxStartups 10:30:60

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify MaxStartups is 10:30:60 or more restrictive:
# sshd -T | awk '$1 ~ /^\s*maxstartups/{split($2, a, ":");{if(a[1] > 10 ||
a[2] > 30 || a[3] > 60) print $0}}'
Nothing should be returned

Rule.title: Ensure sshd MaxSessions is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The MaxSessions parameter specifies the maximum number of open sessions permitted from a given connection.

Rationale:
To protect a system from denial of service due to a large number of concurrent sessions, use the rate limiting function of MaxSessions to protect availability of sshd logins and prevent overwhelming the daemon.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to set the MaxSessions parameter to 10 or less above any Include and Match entries as follows:
MaxSessions 10

check.check-content:
Run the following command and verify that MaxSessions is 10 or less:
# sshd -T | grep -i maxsessions
maxsessions 10
Run the following command and verify the output:
grep -Psi -- '^\h*MaxSessions\h+\"?(1[1-9]|[2-9][0-9]|[1-9][0-9][0-9]+)\b'
/etc/ssh/sshd_config /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/*.conf
Nothing should be returned
Note: This setting can be overridden within a Match block. If Match blocks are configured, also verify the effective value for the relevant contexts as described in the section overview.

Rule.title: Ensure sshd PermitEmptyPasswords is disabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The PermitEmptyPasswords parameter specifies if the SSH server allows login to accounts with empty password strings.

Rationale:
Disallowing remote shell access to accounts that have an empty password reduces the probability of unauthorized access to the system.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit /etc/ssh/sshd_config and set the PermitEmptyPasswords parameter to no above any Include and Match entries as follows:
PermitEmptyPasswords no
The SSH daemon must be restarted for the changes to take effect. To restart the SSH daemon, run the following command:
# systemctl reload-or-restart sshd.service

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify PermitEmptyPasswords is set to no:
# sshd -T | grep permitemptypasswords
permitemptypasswords no
Note: This setting can be overridden within a Match block. If Match blocks are configured, also verify the effective value for the relevant contexts as described in the section overview.

Rule.title: Ensure sshd PermitRootLogin is disabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The PermitRootLogin parameter specifies if the root user can log in using SSH. The default is prohibit-password.

Rationale:
Disallowing root logins over SSH requires system admins to authenticate using their own individual account, then escalating to root. This limits opportunity for non- repudiation and provides a clear audit trail in the event of a security incident.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to set the PermitRootLogin parameter to no above any Include and Match entries as follows:
PermitRootLogin no

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify PermitRootLogin is set to no:
# sshd -T | grep permitrootlogin
permitrootlogin no
Note: This setting can be overridden within a Match block. If Match blocks are configured, also verify the effective value for the relevant contexts as described in the section overview.

Rule.title: Ensure sshd PermitUserEnvironment is disabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The PermitUserEnvironment option allows users to present environment options to the SSH daemon.

Rationale:
Permitting users the ability to set environment variables through the SSH daemon could potentially allow users to bypass security controls (e.g. setting an execution path that has SSH executing trojan'd programs)</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to set the PermitUserEnvironment parameter to no above any Include entries as follows:
PermitUserEnvironment no

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify PermitUserEnvironment is set to no:
# sshd -T | grep permituserenvironment
permituserenvironment no

Rule.title: Ensure sshd UsePAM is enabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The UsePAM directive enables the Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) interface. If set to yes this will enable PAM authentication using ChallengeResponseAuthentication and PasswordAuthentication directives in addition to PAM account and session module processing for all authentication types.

Rationale:
When UsePAM is set to yes, PAM runs through account and session types properly. This is important if you want to restrict access to services based off of IP, time or other factors of the account. Additionally, you can make sure users inherit certain environment variables on login or disallow access to the server</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file to set the UsePAM parameter to yes above any Include entries as follows:
UsePAM yes

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify UsePAM is set to yes:
# sshd -T | grep -i usepam
usepam yes

Rule.title: Ensure sudo is installed
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>sudo allows a permitted user to execute a command as the superuser or another user, as specified by the security policy. The invoking user's real (not effective) user ID is used to determine the user name with which to query the security policy.

Rationale:
sudo supports a plug-in architecture for security policies and input/output logging. Third parties can develop and distribute their own policy and I/O logging plug-ins to work seamlessly with the sudo front end. The default security policy is sudoers, which is configured via the file /etc/sudoers and any entries in /etc/sudoers.d.
The security policy determines what privileges, if any, a user has to run sudo. The policy may require that users authenticate themselves with a password or another authentication mechanism. If authentication is required, sudo will exit if the user's password is not entered within a configurable time limit. This limit is policy-specific.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to install sudo
# dnf install sudo

check.check-content:
Verify that the sudo package is installed. Run the following command:
# rpm -q sudo
The output should list the installed package, for example:
sudo-<version>

Rule.title: Ensure access on sudoers configuration files is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The sudo configuration is defined in /etc/sudoers and in any files included from /etc/sudoers.d/. These files determine which users may escalate privileges and under what conditions.

Rationale:
If a sudoers file is writable by a user other than root, that user could grant unauthorized privilege escalation; if it is readable beyond root, the escalation policy is disclosed.
Restricting each sudoers file to mode 0440 or more restrictive, owned by root and group root, ensures only root can read or modify the escalation policy. sudo refuses to run if these files are group- or world-writable.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Set the owner, group, and permissions on the sudoers files so that only root can read or modify them:
# chown root:root /etc/sudoers
# chmod u-wx,g-wx,o-rwx /etc/sudoers
# find /etc/sudoers.d/ -type f -exec chown root:root {} +
# find /etc/sudoers.d/ -type f -exec chmod u-wx,g-wx,o-rwx {} +
Modify sudoers content only with visudo.

check.check-content:
Verify that /etc/sudoers and every file in /etc/sudoers.d/ is mode 0440 or more restrictive and is owned by user root and group root. Run the following command to list any file that does not meet these requirements:
# find /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/ -type f \( -perm /0337 -o ! -user root -o
! -group root \)
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure access on the /etc/sudoers.d directory is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>/etc/sudoers.d/ is the drop-in directory sudo includes via the #includedir directive in /etc/sudoers. Files placed there become part of the effective sudo policy.

Rationale:
If /etc/sudoers.d/ is writable by a user other than root, that user could add a drop-in file granting unauthorized privilege escalation; if it is world-accessible, the presence and names of its policy files are exposed. Restricting the directory to mode 0750 or more restrictive, owned by root and group root, ensures only root can add, remove, or list drop-in policy files.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Set the owner, group, and permissions on the directory so that only root can add, remove, or list drop-in policy files:
# chown root:root /etc/sudoers.d
# chmod g-w,o-rwx /etc/sudoers.d

check.check-content:
Verify that the /etc/sudoers.d/ directory is mode 0750 or more restrictive and is owned by user root and group root. Run the following command:
# find /etc/sudoers.d -maxdepth 0 -type d \( -perm /0027 -o ! -user root -o !
-group root \)
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure sudo commands use pty
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>sudo can be configured to run only from a pseudo terminal ( pseudo-pty).

Rationale:
Attackers can run a malicious program using sudo which would fork a background process that remains even when the main program has finished executing.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit the file /etc/sudoers with visudo or a file in /etc/sudoers.d/ with visudo -f <PATH TO FILE> and add the following line:
Defaults use_pty
Edit the file /etc/sudoers with visudo and any files in /etc/sudoers.d/ with visudo -f <PATH TO FILE> and remove any occurrence of!use_pty Because sudo applies the last matching Defaults definition, place this setting so that no later-parsed file in /etc/sudoers.d overrides it; see this section's overview for how the sudoers files combine.
Note:
• sudo will read each file in /etc/sudoers.d, skipping file names that end in ~ or contain a. character to avoid causing problems with package manager or editor temporary/backup files.
• Files are parsed in sorted lexical order. That is, /etc/sudoers.d/01_first will be parsed before /etc/sudoers.d/10_second.
• Be aware that because the sorting is lexical, not numeric, /etc/sudoers.d/1_whoops would be loaded after /etc/sudoers.d/10_second.
• Using a consistent number of leading zeroes in the file names can be used to avoid such problems.

check.check-content:
Verify that sudo can only run other commands from a pseudo terminal.
Run the following command to verify Defaults use_pty is set:
# grep -rPi -- '^\h*Defaults\h+([^#\n\r]+,\h*)?use_pty\b' /etc/sudoers
/etc/sudoers.d/
Verify the output matches:
/etc/sudoers:Defaults use_pty
Run the following command to verify Defaults !use_pty is not set:
# grep -rPi -- '^\h*Defaults\h+([^#\n\r]+,\h*)?!use_pty\b' /etc/sudoers
/etc/sudoers.d/
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure sudo log file exists
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The Defaults logfile entry sets the path to the sudo log file. Setting a path turns on logging to a file; negating this option turns it off. By default, sudo logs via syslog.

Rationale:
Defining a dedicated log file for sudo simplifies auditing of sudo commands and creation of auditd rules for sudo.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit the file /etc/sudoers or a file in /etc/sudoers.d/ with visudo -f <PATH TO FILE> and add the following line:
Defaults logfile="<PATH TO CUSTOM LOG FILE>"
Example:
Defaults logfile="/var/log/sudo.log"
Because sudo applies the last matching Defaults definition, place this setting so that no later-parsed file in /etc/sudoers.d overrides it; see this section's overview for how the sudoers files combine.
Notes:
• sudo will read each file in /etc/sudoers.d, skipping file names that end in ~ or contain a. character to avoid causing problems with package manager or editor temporary/backup files.
• Files are parsed in sorted lexical order. That is, /etc/sudoers.d/01_first will be parsed before /etc/sudoers.d/10_second.
• Be aware that because the sorting is lexical, not numeric, /etc/sudoers.d/1_whoops would be loaded after /etc/sudoers.d/10_second.
• Using a consistent number of leading zeroes in the file names can be used to avoid such problems.

check.check-content:
Verify that sudo is configured to write to a custom log file. Run the following command:
# grep -rPsi
"^\h*Defaults\h+([^#]+,\h*)?logfile\h*=\h*(\"|\')?\H+(\"|\')?(,\h*\H+\h*)*\h*
(#.*)?$" /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/
The output should show a logfile entry, for example:
Defaults logfile="/var/log/sudo.log"

Rule.title: Ensure users must provide password for escalation
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>sudo can be configured to require users to authenticate before running commands with elevated privileges. The NOPASSWD tag, where present in the sudoers configuration, lets a user run sudo commands without entering a password; without it, sudo prompts for the user's password before escalating privileges.

Rationale:
The NOPASSWD tag allows a user to run commands via sudo without re-entering a password. Requiring a password for privilege escalation verifies the invoking user's identity before elevated commands run, and limits an attacker with access to an unlocked session or a compromised account from escalating privileges without knowing the account password.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Based on the outcome of the audit procedure, use visudo -f <PATH TO FILE> to edit the relevant sudoers file.
Remove any line with occurrences of NOPASSWD tags in the file.
Because sudo applies the last matching Defaults (and per-rule) definition, ensure no later-parsed file in /etc/sudoers.d re-introduces a NOPASSWD tag; see this section's overview for how the sudoers files combine.

check.check-content:
Verify that users must supply a password for privilege escalation - that is, no sudoers entry uses the NOPASSWD tag.
Note: If passwords are not being used for authentication, this is not applicable.
Run the following command to check /etc/sudoers and the files in /etc/sudoers.d/:
# grep -r "^[^#].*NOPASSWD" /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/
Nothing should be returned. A returned line indicates a NOPASSWD tag is in use; refer to the remediation procedure.

Rule.title: Ensure re-authentication for privilege escalation is not disabled globally
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>By default sudo re-authenticates the invoking user before escalating privileges. The !authenticate tag, where present in the sudoers configuration, disables that re- authentication; without it, sudo prompts the user to confirm their identity before running elevated commands.

Rationale:
Without re-authentication, users may access resources or perform tasks for which they do not have authorization.
When operating systems provide the capability to escalate a functional capability, it is critical the user re-authenticate.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Configure the operating system to require users to reauthenticate for privilege escalation.
Based on the outcome of the audit procedure, use visudo -f <PATH TO FILE> to edit the relevant sudoers file.
Remove any occurrences of!authenticate tags in the file(s).
Because sudo applies the last matching definition, ensure no later-parsed file in /etc/sudoers.d re-introduces an!authenticate tag; see this section's overview for how the sudoers files combine.

check.check-content:
Verify that re-authentication for privilege escalation is not disabled - that is, no sudoers entry uses the!authenticate tag.
Run the following command to check /etc/sudoers and the files in /etc/sudoers.d/:
# grep -r '^[^#].*!authenticate' /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/
Nothing should be returned. A returned line with a!authenticate tag indicates re- authentication has been disabled; refer to the remediation procedure.

Rule.title: Ensure sudo pwfeedback is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The pwfeedback option provides visual feedback (for example, an asterisk) for each character as the sudo password is typed. When not enabled (the default), no feedback is displayed.

Rationale:
Visual feedback discloses the exact length of the password to anyone able to observe the terminal or a session recording, weakening it against shoulder-surfing and offline analysis. The option has also been associated with input-handling defects in older versions of sudo. Leaving pwfeedback disabled removes the length side-channel and keeps sudo on its hardened default.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Ensure sudo does not display feedback while the password is typed. Edit the appropriate sudoers file with visudo and remove any line that enables pwfeedback, or explicitly disable it:
# visudo
Add or correct the line:
Defaults !pwfeedback

check.check-content:
Verify that the sudo pwfeedback option is not enabled (this is the secure default). Run the following command to review the sudoers configuration:
# grep -rPi -- '^\h*Defaults\h+([^#]+,\h*)?pwfeedback\b' /etc/sudoers
/etc/sudoers.d/
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure sudo visiblepw is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The visiblepw sudo option controls whether sudo will prompt for a password on a terminal that cannot disable local echo. When not enabled (the default), sudo refuses to run rather than prompt for a password that would be displayed as it is typed.

Rationale:
If visiblepw is enabled, sudo prompts for a password even when the terminal cannot suppress echo (for example, a command run over SSH without a pseudo-terminal). The password is then entered in cleartext where it can be observed, captured in a screen or session recording, or written to logs. Leaving visiblepw disabled ensures a password is only requested when it can be entered without being displayed.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Ensure sudo will not prompt for a password on a terminal where it would be displayed.
Edit the appropriate sudoers file with visudo and remove any line that enables visiblepw, or explicitly disable it:
# visudo
Add or correct the line:
Defaults !visiblepw

check.check-content:
Verify that the sudo visiblepw option is not enabled (this is the secure default). Run the following command to review the sudoers configuration:
# grep -rPi -- '^\h*Defaults\h+([^#]+,\h*)?visiblepw\b' /etc/sudoers
/etc/sudoers.d/
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure sudo timestamp_timeout is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>sudo timestamp_timeout controls how long a user's sudo privileges remain active after the initial password entry.

Rationale:
A timeout value reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized privileged sudo access.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit the file listed in the audit section with visudo -f <PATH TO FILE> and modify the entry timestamp_timeout= to 15 minutes or less as per your site policy. The value is in minutes. This particular entry may appear on its own, or on the same line as env_reset. See the following two examples:
Example 1:
Defaults env_reset, timestamp_timeout=15
Example 2:
Defaults timestamp_timeout=15
Defaults env_reset
Because sudo applies the last matching Defaults definition, place this setting so that no later-parsed file in /etc/sudoers.d overrides it with a larger value; see this section's overview for how the sudoers files combine.

check.check-content:
Verify that timestamp_timeout is not disabled and is not set greater than 15 minutes.
Run the following command to list any configured value:
# grep -roP "timestamp_timeout=\K[0-9]*" /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/
If no timestamp_timeout is configured in these files, sudo's compiled default of 5 minutes applies, which is within the required maximum of 15 minutes.

Rule.title: Ensure sudo timestamp_type is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>After a successful authentication, sudo caches the credential for a short period. The timestamp_type option controls the scope of that cached credential: tty (per terminal, the default), ppid (per parent process), kernel, or global (one record shared by all of the user's processes and sessions).

Rationale:
With timestamp_type=global, one successful sudo authentication is honored by every concurrent process and session belonging to that user, widening the window in which an unattended or hijacked session can escalate privileges without re-authenticating.
Scoping the timestamp to the terminal (the default, tty) limits credential reuse to the session in which the user actually authenticated.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Ensure the sudo authentication timestamp is scoped to the terminal rather than shared globally. Edit the appropriate sudoers file with visudo and remove any Defaults timestamp_type=global, or set a non-global value:
# visudo
Defaults timestamp_type=tty

check.check-content:
Verify that sudo's authentication timestamp is not shared across all of a user's sessions
- that is, timestamp_type is not set to global (the default tty scope, or any non-global value, is compliant). Run the following command:
# grep -rPi -- 'timestamp_type\h*=\h*global' /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure access to the su command is restricted
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The su command allows a user to run a command or shell as another user. The program has been superseded by sudo, which allows for more granular control over privileged access. Normally, the su command can be executed by any user. By uncommenting the pam_wheel.so statement in /etc/pam.d/su, the su command will only allow users in a specific group to execute su. This group should be empty to reinforce the use of sudo for privileged access.

Rationale:
Restricting the use of su, and using sudo in its place, provides system administrators better control of the escalation of user privileges to execute privileged commands. The sudo utility also provides a better logging and audit mechanism, as it can log each command executed via sudo, whereas su can only record that a user executed the su program.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Create an empty group that will be specified for use of the su command. The group should be named according to site policy.
Example:
# groupadd sugroup
Add the following line to the /etc/pam.d/su file, specifying the empty group:
auth required pam_wheel.so use_uid group=sugroup

check.check-content:
Verify that access to the su command is restricted to an empty group via pam_wheel.so.
Run the following command:
# grep -Pi
'^\h*auth\h+(?:required|requisite)\h+pam_wheel\.so\h+(?:[^#\n\r]+\h+)?((?!\2)
(use_uid\b|group=\H+\b))\h+(?:[^#\n\r]+\h+)?((?!\1)(use_uid\b|group=\H+\b))(\
h+.*)?$' /etc/pam.d/su
Verify the output matches:
auth required pam_wheel.so use_uid group=<group_name>
Run the following command and verify that the group specified in <group_name> contains no users:
# grep <group_name> /etc/group
Verify the output does not contain any users in the relevant group:
<group_name>:x:<GID>:
Note: The automated assessment confirms the pam_wheel.so configuration line only.
Confirming that the specified group contains no users is a manual verification step.

Rule.title: Ensure latest version of pam is installed
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The pam package provides the Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) framework and the core modules used by the system's authentication, login, and password-change services.

Rationale:
To ensure the system has access to the PAM module functionality used by this Benchmark, the installed version of pam should be 1.5.1-14 or later.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to install or update pam to the latest version:
# dnf install pam

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that pam version 1.5.1-14 or later is installed:
# rpm -q pam
The version returned should be 1.5.1-14 or later.
Example output:
pam-1.5.1-14.el9.x86_64

Rule.title: Ensure latest version of authselect is installed
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Authselect is a utility that simplifies the configuration of user authentication. Authselect offers ready-made profiles that can be universally used with all modern identity management systems.
You can create and deploy a custom profile by customizing one of the default profiles:
the sssd, winbind, or the nis profile. This is particularly useful if modifying a ready-made authselect profile is not enough for your needs. When you deploy a custom profile, the profile is applied to every user logging into the given host. This is the recommended method, so that the existing profiles can remain unmodified.
Authselect only modifies files in the following locations:
/etc/nsswitch.conf /etc/pam.d/* /etc/dconf/db/distro.d/*

Rationale:
To ensure the system has access to the authselect functionality used by this Benchmark, the installed version of authselect should be 1.2.6-1 or later.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to install or update authselect to the latest version:
# dnf install authselect

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that authselect version 1.2.6-1 or later is installed:
# rpm -q authselect
The version returned should be 1.2.6-1 or later.
Example output:
authselect-1.2.6-1.el9.x86_64

Rule.title: Ensure latest version of libpwquality is installed
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>libpwquality provides common functions for password quality checking and scoring them based on their apparent randomness. The library also provides a function for generating random passwords with good pronounceability.
This module can be plugged into the password stack of a given service to provide some plug-in strength-checking for passwords. The code was originally based on pam_cracklib module and the module is backwards compatible with its options.

Rationale:
Strong password requirements reduce the risk of successful password guessing and brute-force attacks. Ensuring a current version of libpwquality is installed makes the password-quality checking features used by this Benchmark available.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to install or update libpwquality to the latest version:
# dnf install libpwquality

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that libpwquality version 1.4.4-8 or later is installed:
# rpm -q libpwquality
The version returned should be 1.4.4-8 or later.
Example output:
libpwquality-1.4.4-8.el9.x86_64

Rule.title: Ensure PAM is managed by an active authselect profile
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>authselect renders and manages the system's PAM configuration from a single active profile. When PAM is managed by authselect, the effective /etc/pam.d/system-auth and /etc/pam.d/password-auth files are generated from that profile and their consistency can be verified, providing one supported, reproducible source of truth for authentication configuration.

Rationale:
A custom profile is required to customize many of the pam options.
Modifications made to a default profile may be overwritten during an update.
When you deploy a profile, the profile is applied to every user logging into the given host</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Configure the system to manage PAM through an authselect profile.
Select an authselect profile (a default profile such as sssd, or a custom profile) and apply it:
# authselect select sssd
# authselect apply-changes
Use # authselect select <profile> --force if existing files must be overwritten (for example, on a system not previously managed by authselect).
If authselect check reports the configuration is not valid, restore a valid configuration as described in the section overview.

check.check-content:
Verify PAM is managed by an active authselect profile and the configuration is consistent with it.
Run the following command to verify an authselect profile is active:
# authselect current
Example output:
Profile ID: sssd
Enabled features:
- with-sudo
A returned Profile ID indicates an authselect profile is active.
Run the following command to verify the configuration is consistent with the active profile:
# authselect check
Example output:
Current configuration is valid.
A valid result indicates PAM is managed by authselect and has not been modified outside it.
Note: The /etc/pam.d/system-auth and /etc/pam.d/password-auth files are generated by authselect and are the configuration enforced at runtime. If authselect check reports the configuration is not valid, PAM has been modified outside authselect.

Rule.title: Ensure pam_faillock module is enabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The pam_faillock.so module maintains a list of failed authentication attempts per user during a specified interval and locks the account in case there were more than the configured number of consecutive failed authentications (this is defined by the deny parameter in the faillock configuration). It stores the failure records into per-user files in the tally directory.

Rationale:
Locking out user IDs after n unsuccessful consecutive login attempts mitigates brute force password attacks against your systems.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
On a system already managed by an authselect profile, run the following commands to enable the faillock feature and apply the changes:
# authselect enable-feature with-faillock
# authselect apply-changes
authselect regenerates /etc/pam.d/system-auth and /etc/pam.d/password-auth with the pam_faillock.so lines.
If the system is not yet managed by authselect, or authselect check reports the configuration is not valid, first establish or restore the profile as described in the section overview, then run the commands above.

check.check-content:
Verify the pam_faillock module is enabled in the effective PAM configuration on an authselect-managed system.
1. Run the following command to verify the configuration is managed by authselect and is consistent with the active profile:
# authselect check
Example output:
Current configuration is valid.
2. Run the following command to verify the pam_faillock.so lines are present in the effective files PAM reads at runtime:
# grep -P -- '\bpam_faillock\.so\b' /etc/pam.d/system-auth
/etc/pam.d/password-auth
An auth preauth line, an auth authfail line, and an account line for pam_faillock.so in both files indicate the module is enabled.
Example output:
/etc/pam.d/system-auth:auth required pam_faillock.so preauth
/etc/pam.d/system-auth:auth required pam_faillock.so authfail
/etc/pam.d/system-auth:account required pam_faillock.so
/etc/pam.d/password-auth:auth required pam_faillock.so preauth
/etc/pam.d/password-auth:auth required pam_faillock.so authfail
/etc/pam.d/password-auth:account required pam_faillock.so
Note: /etc/pam.d/system-auth and /etc/pam.d/password-auth are generated by authselect and are the configuration enforced at runtime. If authselect check reports the configuration is not valid, PAM has been modified outside authselect and these files are not authoritative.

Rule.title: Ensure pam_pwquality module is enabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The pam_pwquality.so module performs password quality checking. This module can be plugged into the password stack of a given service to provide strength-checking for passwords. The code was originally based on pam_cracklib module and the module is backwards compatible with its options.
The action of this module is to prompt the user for a password and check its strength against a system dictionary and a set of rules for identifying poor choices.
The first action is to prompt for a single password, check its strength and then, if it is considered strong, prompt for the password a second time (to verify that it was typed correctly on the first occasion). All being well, the password is passed on to subsequent modules to be installed as the new authentication token.

Rationale:
Use of a unique, complex passwords helps to increase the time and resources required to compromise the password.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
pam_pwquality is part of the default authselect profiles, so a system using a default profile already provides it.
On a system already managed by an authselect profile, ensure the active profile includes pam_pwquality:
• The default profiles include it; no change is required.
• If a custom profile has removed it, add the following line to the custom profile's system-auth and password-auth templates in /etc/authselect/custom/<profile>/:
password requisite pam_pwquality.so
Then apply the configuration:
# authselect apply-changes
If the system is not yet managed by authselect, or authselect check reports the configuration is not valid, first establish or restore the profile as described in the section overview.
Note: pam_pwquality is a base-profile module - there is no with-pwquality feature to enable (unlike with-faillock and with-pwhistory).

check.check-content:
Verify the pam_pwquality module is enabled in the effective PAM configuration on an authselect-managed system.
1. Run the following command to verify the configuration is managed by authselect and is consistent with the active profile:
# authselect check
Example output:
Current configuration is valid.
2. Run the following command to verify the pam_pwquality.so line is present in the effective files PAM reads at runtime:
# grep -P -- '\bpam_pwquality\.so\b' /etc/pam.d/system-auth
/etc/pam.d/password-auth
A password ( requisite or required) line for pam_pwquality.so in both files indicates the module is enabled.
Example output:
/etc/pam.d/system-auth:password requisite pam_pwquality.so
local_users_only
/etc/pam.d/password-auth:password requisite pam_pwquality.so
local_users_only
Note: /etc/pam.d/system-auth and /etc/pam.d/password-auth are generated by authselect and are the configuration enforced at runtime. If authselect check reports the configuration is not valid, PAM has been modified outside authselect and these files are not authoritative.

Rule.title: Ensure pam_pwhistory module is enabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The pam_pwhistory.so module saves the last passwords for each user in order to force password change history and keep the user from alternating between the same password too frequently.

Rationale:
Requiring users not to reuse their passwords make it less likely that an attacker will be able to guess the password or use a compromised password.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
On a system already managed by an authselect profile, run the following commands to enable the pwhistory feature and apply the changes:
# authselect enable-feature with-pwhistory
# authselect apply-changes
authselect regenerates /etc/pam.d/system-auth and /etc/pam.d/password-auth with the pam_pwhistory.so lines.
If the system is not yet managed by authselect, or authselect check reports the configuration is not valid, first establish or restore the profile as described in the section overview, then run the commands above.

check.check-content:
Verify the pam_pwhistory module is enabled in the effective PAM configuration on an authselect-managed system.
1. Run the following command to verify the configuration is managed by authselect and is consistent with the active profile:
# authselect check
Example output:
Current configuration is valid.
2. Run the following command to verify the pam_pwhistory.so line is present in the effective files PAM reads at runtime:
# grep -P -- '\bpam_pwhistory\.so\b' /etc/pam.d/system-auth
/etc/pam.d/password-auth
A password ( requisite or required) line for pam_pwhistory.so in both files indicates the module is enabled.
Example output:
/etc/pam.d/system-auth:password requisite pam_pwhistory.so use_authtok
/etc/pam.d/password-auth:password requisite pam_pwhistory.so use_authtok
Note: /etc/pam.d/system-auth and /etc/pam.d/password-auth are generated by authselect and are the configuration enforced at runtime. If authselect check reports the configuration is not valid, PAM has been modified outside authselect and these files are not authoritative.

Rule.title: Ensure pam_unix module is enabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The pam_unix.so module is the standard Unix authentication module. It uses standard calls from the system's libraries to retrieve and set account information as well as authentication. Usually this is obtained from the /etc/passwd and the /etc/shadow file as well if shadow is enabled.

Rationale:
Requiring users to use authentication make it less likely that an attacker will be able to access the system.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
pam_unix is part of the default authselect profiles, so a system using a default profile already provides it.
On a system already managed by an authselect profile, ensure the active profile includes pam_unix:
• The default profiles include it; no change is required.
• If a custom profile has removed it, restore its auth, account, password, and session pam_unix.so entries to the custom profile's system-auth and password-auth templates in /etc/authselect/custom/<profile>/ (copy them from the corresponding default profile under /usr/share/authselect/default/<profile>/).
Then apply the configuration:
# authselect apply-changes
If the system is not yet managed by authselect, or authselect check reports the configuration is not valid, first establish or restore the profile as described in the section overview.
Note: pam_unix is a base-profile module - there is no with-unix feature to enable (unlike with-faillock and with-pwhistory).

check.check-content:
Verify the pam_unix module is enabled in the effective PAM configuration on an authselect-managed system.
1. Run the following command to verify the configuration is managed by authselect and is consistent with the active profile:
# authselect check
Example output:
Current configuration is valid.
2. Run the following command to verify the pam_unix.so lines are present in the effective files PAM reads at runtime:
# grep -P -- '\bpam_unix\.so\b' /etc/pam.d/system-auth /etc/pam.d/password-
auth
An auth line, an account line, a password line, and a session line for pam_unix.so in both files indicate the module is enabled.
Example output:
/etc/pam.d/system-auth:auth sufficient pam_unix.so
/etc/pam.d/system-auth:account required pam_unix.so
/etc/pam.d/system-auth:password sufficient pam_unix.so
/etc/pam.d/system-auth:session required pam_unix.so
/etc/pam.d/password-auth:auth sufficient pam_unix.so
/etc/pam.d/password-auth:account required pam_unix.so
/etc/pam.d/password-auth:password sufficient pam_unix.so
/etc/pam.d/password-auth:session required pam_unix.so
Note: /etc/pam.d/system-auth and /etc/pam.d/password-auth are generated by authselect and are the configuration enforced at runtime. If authselect check reports the configuration is not valid, PAM has been modified outside authselect and these files are not authoritative.

Rule.title: Ensure password failed attempts lockout is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The pam_faillock module locks an account after a number of consecutive failed authentication attempts. The deny option, set in /etc/security/faillock.conf, defines that threshold: the number of consecutive failed authentication attempts after which the account is locked. A value of 0 disables the lockout.

Rationale:
Locking an account after a defined number of consecutive failed authentication attempts limits the number of password guesses an attacker can make in a short period, mitigating brute force and password-spraying attacks. Setting deny to a low, non-zero value ensures an account is locked before an attacker can attempt a large number of credentials.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Create or edit the following line in /etc/security/faillock.conf setting the deny option to 5 or less:
deny = 5
Run the following script to remove the deny argument from the pam_faillock.so module in the PAM files:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
for l_pam_file in system-auth password-auth; do
l_authselect_file="/etc/authselect/$(head -1
/etc/authselect/authselect.conf | grep 'custom/')/$l_pam_file"
sed -ri
's/(^\s*auth\s+(requisite|required|sufficient)\s+pam_faillock\.so.*)(\s+deny\
s*=\s*\S+)(.*$)/\1\4/' "$l_authselect_file"
done
authselect apply-changes
}

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that the number of failed authentication attempts before the account is locked is no greater than 5 and meets local site policy:
# grep -Pi -- '^\h*deny\h*=\h*[1-5]\b' /etc/security/faillock.conf
Example output:
deny = 5
Run the following command to verify that the deny argument has not been set, or is set to 5 or less and meets local site policy:
# grep -Pi --
'^\h*auth\h+(requisite|required|sufficient)\h+pam_faillock\.so\h+([^#\n\r]+\h
+)?deny\h*=\h*(0|[6-9]|[1-9][0-9]+)\b' /etc/pam.d/system-auth
/etc/pam.d/password-auth
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure password unlock time is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The unlock_time option, set in /etc/security/faillock.conf, controls how long a locked account remains locked before access is automatically re-enabled. Access is restored unlock_time seconds after the account is locked. A value of 0 means the account is never automatically unlocked and access can only be restored by resetting the faillock entries with the faillock(8) command.

Rationale:
