A nonzero unlock_time automatically restores access after the configured interval, balancing protection against brute force attacks with the operational cost of locked-out accounts and reducing administrative overhead. Setting unlock_time to 0 maximizes protection by keeping an account locked until an administrator resets it, at the cost of requiring manual recovery.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Set password unlock time to conform to site policy. unlock_time should be 0 (never), or 900 seconds or greater.
Edit /etc/security/faillock.conf and update or add the following line:
unlock_time = 900
Run the following script to remove the unlock_time argument from the pam_faillock.so module in the PAM files:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
for l_pam_file in system-auth password-auth; do
l_authselect_file="/etc/authselect/$(head -1
/etc/authselect/authselect.conf | grep 'custom/')/$l_pam_file"
sed -ri
's/(^\s*auth\s+(requisite|required|sufficient)\s+pam_faillock\.so.*)(\s+unloc
k_time\s*=\s*\S+)(.*$)/\1\4/' "$l_authselect_file"
done
authselect apply-changes
}

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that the time in seconds before the account is unlocked is either 0 (never) or 900 (15 minutes) or more and meets local site policy:
# grep -Pi -- '^\h*unlock_time\h*=\h*(0|9[0-9][0-9]|[1-9][0-9]{3,})\b'
/etc/security/faillock.conf
Example output:
unlock_time = 900
Run the following command to verify that the unlock_time argument has not been set, or is either 0 (never) or 900 (15 minutes) or more and meets local site policy:
# grep -Pi --
'^\h*auth\h+(requisite|required|sufficient)\h+pam_faillock\.so\h+([^#\n\r]+\h

Rule.title: Ensure password failed attempts lockout includes root account
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>even_deny_root - Root account can become locked as well as regular accounts root_unlock_time=n - This option implies even_deny_root option. Allow access after n seconds to root account after the account is locked. In case the option is not specified the value is the same as of the unlock_time option.

Rationale:
By default the root account is exempt from pam_faillock lockout, leaving it able to be subjected to unlimited password-guessing attempts. Because root is a high-value target, including it in the lockout with even_deny_root applies the same brute force protection to the most privileged account. A finite root_unlock_time can be used to balance this protection against the need to recover the root account.</VulnDiscussion>

Edit /etc/security/faillock.conf:
• Remove or update any line containing root_unlock_time, - OR - set it to a value of 60 or more
• Update or add the following line:
even_deny_root

{

sed -ri
's/(^\s*auth\s+(.*)\s+pam_faillock\.so.*)(\s+even_deny_root)(.*$)/\1\4/'
"$l_authselect_file"
sed -ri
's/(^\s*auth\s+(.*)\s+pam_faillock\.so.*)(\s+root_unlock_time\s*=\s*\S+)(.*$)
/\1\4/' "$l_authselect_file"
done
authselect apply-changes

Rule.title: Ensure password number of changed characters is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The pwquality difok option sets the number of characters in a password that must not be present in the old password.

A new password that differs from the previous password in only a few characters can be trivially derived from a known, compromised, or expired password. Requiring that a minimum number of characters differ from the old password prevents users from making minor, predictable variations of a prior password when it is changed.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure password length is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The minlen option sets the minimum acceptable length for a new password. When character-class credits are enabled (the default), each credited class can count as one additional character toward satisfying this minimum. The value cannot be set lower than 6.

Rationale:
The effort required to guess or crack a password, particularly through offline brute-force attacks, grows rapidly as the password lengthens. Enforcing a minimum password length raises the work factor an attacker must expend and reduces the effectiveness of exhaustive guessing.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure password complexity is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Password complexity can be set through:
• minclass - The minimum number of classes of characters required in a new password. (digits, uppercase, lowercase, others). e.g. minclass = 4 requires digits, uppercase, lower case, and special characters.
• dcredit - The maximum credit for having digits in the new password. If less than 0 it is the minimum number of digits in the new password. e.g. dcredit = -1 requires at least one digit
• ucredit - The maximum credit for having uppercase characters in the new password. If less than 0 it is the minimum number of uppercase characters in the new password. e.g. ucredit = -1 requires at least one uppercase character
• ocredit - The maximum credit for having other characters in the new password.
If less than 0 it is the minimum number of other characters in the new password.
e.g. ocredit = -1 requires at least one special character
• lcredit - The maximum credit for having lowercase characters in the new password. If less than 0 it is the minimum number of lowercase characters in the new password. e.g. lcredit = -1 requires at least one lowercase character

Rationale:
Requiring a password to draw from multiple classes of characters - digits, uppercase letters, lowercase letters, and other characters - enlarges the pool of possible passwords an attacker must search. A larger keyspace increases the password's resistance to guessing and brute-force attacks.</VulnDiscussion>

• ucredit = -_N_
• ocredit = -_N_

pwcomplexity.conf

1" > /etc/security/pwquality.conf.d/50-pwcomplexity.conf

Rule.title: Ensure password quality is enforced for the root user
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>If the pwquality enforce_for_root option is enabled, the module will return error on failed check even if the user changing the password is root.

Rationale:
By default the pam_pwquality checks are not enforced when the root user sets a password: a failed quality check produces only a warning and the password is still accepted. Because the root account is the highest-value target on the system, allowing its password to be set without meeting the quality requirements applied to every other account leaves a significant gap. Enforcing password quality for root closes that gap.</VulnDiscussion>

Remembering a number of previously used passwords and checking new passwords against them prevents users from cycling back to a recently used - and possibly compromised or expired - password. This defeats password reuse and makes it less likely that an attacker can reuse or guess a password the account has used before.</VulnDiscussion>

}

check.check-content:
Run the following command and verify that the remember option is set to 24 or more and meets local site policy in /etc/security/pwhistory.conf:
# grep -Pi -- '^\h*remember\h*=\h*(2[4-9]|[3-9][0-9]|[1-9][0-9]{2,})\b'
/etc/security/pwhistory.conf
Example output:
remember = 24
Run the following command to verify that the remember option is not set to less than 24 on the pam_pwhistory.so module in /etc/pam.d/password-auth and /etc/pam.d/system-auth:
# grep -Pi --
'^\h*password\h+(requisite|required|sufficient)\h+pam_pwhistory\.so\h+([^#\n\
r]+\h+)?remember=(2[0-3]|1[0-9]|[0-9])\b' /etc/pam.d/system-auth
/etc/pam.d/password-auth
Nothing should be returned.
Note: The remember value must be set in /etc/security/pwhistory.conf to be durable. A value set only on the pam_pwhistory.so module line is not a passing configuration: authselect apply-changes regenerates the PAM files and removes inline arguments, so an inline-only value would not persist.

Rule.title: Ensure password history is enforced for the root user
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>If the pwhistory enforce_for_root option is enabled, the module will enforce password history for the root user as well

Rationale:
By default the password-history check does not apply to the root account, so root can be changed back to a recently used password even when history enforcement is configured for other users. Enabling enforce_for_root subjects root's password changes to the same history check. Because the root account is a high-value target, preventing reuse of a recent - and possibly compromised - root password closes that gap.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit or add the following line in /etc/security/pwhistory.conf:
enforce_for_root

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that the enforce_for_root option is enabled in /etc/security/pwhistory.conf:
# grep -Pi -- '^\h*enforce_for_root\b' /etc/security/pwhistory.conf
Example output:
enforce_for_root

Rule.title: Ensure pam_pwhistory includes use_authtok
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>use_authtok - When password changing enforce the module to set the new password to the one provided by a previously stacked password module

Rationale:
use_authtok directs pam_pwhistory to use the new password token already supplied by an earlier module in the password stack instead of prompting for it again. This ensures the password actually being set is the one checked against the password history. Without it, the history check may be applied to a different value or skipped, weakening enforcement and allowing a reused password to slip through.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
On an authselect-managed system, use_authtok is a module-line argument and must be present on the pam_pwhistory.so line in the active profile's password stack. Set it in the active custom profile's templates so that it persists across authselect apply- changes.
Edit the active custom profile's system-auth and password-auth templates under /etc/authselect/custom/<profile>/ so that the pam_pwhistory.so line in the password stack includes use_authtok:
password requisite pam_pwhistory.so use_authtok
Apply the changes to regenerate the PAM configuration:
# authselect apply-changes
Note: If the system is not yet using a custom authselect profile, first create one from the active base profile and select it, then edit its templates as above and apply:
# authselect create-profile <profile> -b <current-base>
# authselect select custom/<profile> <features>
See the section overview for the authselect profile mechanics.

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that use_authtok is set on the pam_pwhistory.so module lines in the password stack:
# grep -P --
'^\h*password\h+([^#\n\r]+)\h+pam_pwhistory\.so\h+([^#\n\r]+\h+)?use_authtok\
b' /etc/pam.d/{password,system}-auth
Output should be similar to:
/etc/pam.d/password-auth:password required pam_pwhistory.so use_authtok
/etc/pam.d/system-auth:password required pam_pwhistory.so use_authtok
Verify that the lines include use_authtok

Rule.title: Ensure pam_unix does not include nullok
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The nullok argument overrides the default action of pam_unix.so to not permit the user access to a service if their official password is blank.

Rationale:
The nullok argument permits authentication for a local account that has a blank or empty password, allowing access to a pam_unix backed service with no password.
Removing nullok ensures every account must present a real password to authenticate.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
without-nullok is provided as an authselect feature, so it is enabled on the active profile directly and does not require a custom profile (see the section overview for the authselect profile model).
Enable the feature on the active profile:
# authselect enable-feature without-nullok
Apply the change so that /etc/pam.d/system-auth and /etc/pam.d/password-auth are regenerated without the nullok argument:
# authselect apply-changes

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify the nullok argument is not present on any pam_unix.so line in the effective PAM configuration:
# grep -Pi --
'^\h*(auth|account|password|session)\h+(requisite|required|sufficient)\h+pam_
unix\.so\h+([^#\n\r]+\h+)?nullok\b' /etc/pam.d/system-auth
/etc/pam.d/password-auth
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure pam_unix does not include remember
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The remember=n argument saves the last n passwords for each user in /etc/security/opasswd in order to force password change history and keep the user from alternating between the same password too frequently. The MD5 password hash algorithm is used for storing the old passwords. Instead of this option the pam_pwhistory module should be used. The pam_pwhistory module saves the last n passwords for each user in /etc/security/opasswd using the password hash algorithm set on the pam_unix module. This allows for the sha512 hash algorithm to be used.

Rationale:
Password history is enforced through the pam_pwhistory module, which records prior passwords using the strong hash configured on pam_unix. The remember argument on pam_unix is the legacy mechanism: it stores prior passwords in /etc/security/opasswd using the weak MD5 hash. It should not be set on pam_unix so that password history relies on the stronger pam_pwhistory implementation.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
The pam_unix arguments are set on the pam_unix.so module lines in the active authselect profile; editing /etc/pam.d/system-auth or /etc/pam.d/password-auth directly is not durable, because authselect regenerates those files (see the section overview for the authselect profile model).
Remove the remember argument so password history is handled by pam_pwhistory rather than pam_unix:
1. Ensure the system is using a custom authselect profile. If it is still on a stock profile, create and select one first, as described in the section overview.
2. On the pam_unix.so lines in the active custom profile templates (/etc/authselect/custom/<profile>/system-auth and /etc/authselect/custom/<profile>/password-auth), remove any remember=N argument. A compliant line reads:
password sufficient pam_unix.so yescrypt shadow use_authtok
3. Apply the change so that /etc/pam.d/system-auth and /etc/pam.d/password-auth are regenerated without the remember argument:
# authselect apply-changes

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify the remember argument is not present on any pam_unix.so line in the effective PAM configuration:
# grep -Pi --
'^\h*password\h+([^#\n\r]+\h+)?pam_unix\.so\h+([^#\n\r]+\h+)?remember='
/etc/pam.d/system-auth /etc/pam.d/password-auth
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure pam_unix includes a strong password hashing algorithm
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>A cryptographic hash function converts an arbitrary-length input into a fixed length output. Password hashing performs a one-way transformation of a password, turning the password into another string, called the hashed password.

Rationale:
Weak or legacy password hashing algorithms such as md5 and DES are fast to compute, so an attacker who obtains the stored password hashes can crack them offline at high speed. A strong algorithm (yescrypt or SHA-512) is deliberately expensive to compute, greatly increasing the effort required to recover local user passwords from the stored hashes.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
The pam_unix arguments are configured through the active authselect profile so that the change is durable; editing /etc/pam.d/system-auth or /etc/pam.d/password-auth directly is not durable, because authselect regenerates those files (see the section overview for the authselect profile model).
Set yescrypt, the default and recommended algorithm on this platform:
1. Ensure the system is using a custom authselect profile. If it is still on a stock profile, create and select one first, as described in the section overview.
2. On the pam_unix.so line in the password stack of the active custom profile templates ( /etc/authselect/custom/<profile>/system-auth and /etc/authselect/custom/<profile>/password-auth), ensure the hashing algorithm is set to yescrypt and remove any other algorithm such as md5, sha256, bigcrypt, or blowfish. A compliant line reads:
password sufficient pam_unix.so yescrypt shadow use_authtok
3. Apply the change so that /etc/pam.d/system-auth and /etc/pam.d/password-auth are regenerated with the strong hashing algorithm:
# authselect apply-changes
Note: The hashing algorithm applies to passwords set after the change; existing password hashes remain in place until each account's password is next changed.
Systems with a FIPS 140 requirement:
yescrypt is not a FIPS-approved algorithm and must not be used where FIPS compliance is mandated. Use sha512 instead, which is also a strong algorithm, by specifying sha512 in place of yescrypt in step 2 and then applying the change. Such environments additionally enable system-wide FIPS mode, which aligns the system crypto policy with the FIPS-approved algorithm:
# fips-mode-setup --enable

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify a strong password hashing algorithm (sha512 or yescrypt) is set on the pam_unix.so password lines in the effective PAM configuration:
# grep -Pi --
'^\h*password\h+(requisite|required|sufficient)\h+pam_unix\.so(\h+[^#\n\r]+)?
\h+(sha512|yescrypt)\b' /etc/pam.d/system-auth /etc/pam.d/password-auth
A line should be returned for both files, each including either sha512 or yescrypt.
Example output:
/etc/pam.d/password-auth:password sufficient pam_unix.so yescrypt shadow
use_authtok
/etc/pam.d/system-auth:password sufficient pam_unix.so yescrypt shadow
use_authtok

Rule.title: Ensure pam_unix includes use_authtok
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The use_authtok argument tells pam_unix, during a password change, to use the new password token already supplied by an earlier module in the password stack rather than prompting for a new one.

Rationale:
With use_authtok, pam_unix commits the password that was already validated by earlier modules in the password stack, such as the quality and history checks, so the password that passed those checks is the one that is stored. Without use_authtok, pam_unix may prompt for and store a different password, bypassing the preceding validation.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
The pam_unix arguments are set on the pam_unix.so module lines in the active authselect profile; editing /etc/pam.d/system-auth or /etc/pam.d/password-auth directly is not durable, because authselect regenerates those files (see the section overview for the authselect profile model).
Add the use_authtok argument so pam_unix uses the password already validated by the preceding modules:
1. Ensure the system is using a custom authselect profile. If it is still on a stock profile, create and select one first, as described in the section overview.
2. On the pam_unix.so line in the password stack of the active custom profile templates (/etc/authselect/custom/<profile>/system-auth and /etc/authselect/custom/<profile>/password-auth), add use_authtok. A compliant line reads:
password sufficient pam_unix.so yescrypt shadow use_authtok
3. Apply the change so that /etc/pam.d/system-auth and /etc/pam.d/password-auth are regenerated with the use_authtok argument:
# authselect apply-changes

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that use_authtok is set on the pam_unix.so module lines in the password stack:
# grep -P --
'^\h*password\h+([^#\n\r]+)\h+pam_unix\.so\h+([^#\n\r]+\h+)?use_authtok\b'
/etc/pam.d/{password,system}-auth
Output should be similar to:
/etc/pam.d/password-auth:password sufficient pam_unix.so sha512 shadow
use_authtok
/etc/pam.d/system-auth:password sufficient pam_unix.so sha512 shadow
use_authtok
Verify that the lines include use_authtok

Rule.title: Ensure password expiration is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The PASS_MAX_DAYS parameter in /etc/login.defs allows an administrator to force passwords to expire once they reach a defined age.
PASS_MAX_DAYS <N> - The maximum number of days a password may be used. If the password is older than this, a password change will be forced. If not specified, -1 will be assumed (which disables the restriction).

Rationale:
The window of opportunity for an attacker to leverage compromised credentials or successfully compromise credentials via an online brute force attack is limited by the age of the password. Therefore, reducing the maximum age of a password also reduces an attacker's window of opportunity.
We recommend a yearly password change. This is primarily because for all their good intentions users will share credentials across accounts. Therefore, even if a breach is publicly identified, the user may not see this notification, or forget they have an account on that site. This could leave a shared credential vulnerable indefinitely. Having an organizational policy of a 1-year (annual) password expiration is a reasonable compromise to mitigate this with minimal user burden.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit /etc/login.defs and set PASS_MAX_DAYS to a value greater than 0 and no greater than 365 that follows local site policy:
Example:
PASS_MAX_DAYS 365
Run the following command to modify user parameters for all users with a password set to a maximum age no greater than 365 or less than 1 that follows local site policy:
# chage --maxdays <N> <user>
Example:
# awk -F: '($2~/^\$.+\$/) {if($5 > 365 || $5 < 1)system ("chage --maxdays 365
" $1)}' /etc/shadow
Warning: If a password has been set at system install or kickstart, the last change date field is not set, In this case, setting PASS_MAX_DAYS will immediately expire the password. One possible solution is to populate the last change date field through a command like: chage -d "$(date +%Y-%m-%d)" root

check.check-content:
Run the following command and verify PASS_MAX_DAYS is set to a value greater than 0, no greater than 365, and conforms to local site policy:
# grep -Pi -- '^\h*PASS_MAX_DAYS\h+\d+\b' /etc/login.defs
Example output:
PASS_MAX_DAYS 365
Run the following command to verify all /etc/shadow passwords PASS_MAX_DAYS:
• is greater than 0 days
• is less than or equal to 365 days
• conforms to local site policy
# awk -F: '($2~/^\$.+\$/) {if($5 > 365 || $5 < 1)print "User: " $1 "
PASS_MAX_DAYS: " $5}' /etc/shadow
Nothing should be returned

Rule.title: Ensure minimum password days is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>PASS_MIN_DAYS < N > - The minimum number of days allowed between password changes. Any password changes attempted sooner than this will be rejected. If not specified, 0 will be assumed (which disables the restriction).

Rationale:
Users may have favorite passwords that they like to use because they are easy to remember and they believe that their password choice is secure from compromise.
Unfortunately, passwords are compromised and if an attacker is targeting a specific individual user account, with foreknowledge of data about that user, reuse of old, potentially compromised passwords, may cause a security breach.
By restricting the frequency of password changes, an administrator can prevent users from repeatedly changing their password in an attempt to circumvent password reuse controls</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit /etc/login.defs and set PASS_MIN_DAYS to a value greater than 0 that follows local site policy:
Example:
PASS_MIN_DAYS 1
Run the following command to modify user parameters for all users with a password set to a minimum days greater than zero that follows local site policy:
# chage --mindays <N> <user>
Example:
# awk -F: '($2~/^\$.+\$/) {if($4 < 1)system ("chage --mindays 1 " $1)}'
/etc/shadow

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that PASS_MIN_DAYS is set to a value greater than 0 and follows local site policy:
# grep -Pi -- '^\h*PASS_MIN_DAYS\h+\d+\b' /etc/login.defs
Example output:
PASS_MIN_DAYS 1
Run the following command to verify all passwords have a PASS_MIN_DAYS greater than 0:
# awk -F: '($2~/^\$.+\$/) {if($4 < 1)print "User: " $1 " PASS_MIN_DAYS: "
$4}' /etc/shadow
Nothing should be returned

Rule.title: Ensure password expiration warning days is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The PASS_WARN_AGE parameter in /etc/login.defs allows an administrator to notify users that their password will expire in a defined number of days.
PASS_WARN_AGE <N> - The number of days warning given before a password expires. A zero means warning is given only upon the day of expiration, a negative value means no warning is given. If not specified, no warning will be provided.

Rationale:
Providing an advance warning that a password will be expiring gives users time to think of a secure password. Users caught unaware may choose a simple password or write it down where it may be discovered.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit /etc/login.defs and set PASS_WARN_AGE to a value of 7 or more that follows local site policy:
Example:
PASS_WARN_AGE 7
Run the following command to modify user parameters for all users with a password set to a minimum warning to 7 or more days that follows local site policy:
# chage --warndays <N> <user>
Example:
# awk -F: '($2~/^\$.+\$/) {if($6 < 7)system ("chage --warndays 7 " $1)}'
/etc/shadow

check.check-content:
Run the following command and verify PASS_WARN_AGE is 7 or more and follows local site policy:
# grep -Pi -- '^\h*PASS_WARN_AGE\h+\d+\b' /etc/login.defs
Example output:
PASS_WARN_AGE 7
Run the following command to verify all passwords have a PASS_WARN_AGE of 7 or more:
# awk -F: '($2~/^\$.+\$/) {if($6 < 7)print "User: " $1 " PASS_WARN_AGE: "
$6}' /etc/shadow
Nothing should be returned

Rule.title: Ensure strong password hashing algorithm is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>A cryptographic hash function converts an arbitrary-length input into a fixed length output. Password hashing performs a one-way transformation of a password, turning the password into another string, called the hashed password.
ENCRYPT_METHOD (string) - This defines the system default encryption algorithm for encrypting passwords (if no algorithm are specified on the command line). It can take one of these values:
• MD5 - MD5-based algorithm will be used for encrypting password
• SHA256 - SHA256-based algorithm will be used for encrypting password
• SHA512 - SHA512-based algorithm will be used for encrypting password
• BCRYPT - BCRYPT-based algorithm will be used for encrypting password
• YESCRYPT - YESCRYPT-based algorithm will be used for encrypting password
• DES - DES-based algorithm will be used for encrypting password (used only if ENCRYPT_METHOD is unset) Note: This parameter overrides the deprecated MD5_CRYPT_ENAB variable. This parameter will only affect the generation of group passwords. The generation of user passwords is done by PAM and subject to the PAM configuration. It is recommended to set this variable consistently with the PAM configuration.

Rationale:
The SHA-512 and yescrypt algorithms provide a stronger hash than other algorithms used by Linux for password hash generation. A stronger hash provides additional protection to the system by increasing the level of effort needed for an attacker to successfully determine local group passwords.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit /etc/login.defs and set the ENCRYPT_METHOD to SHA512 or YESCRYPT:
ENCRYPT_METHOD <HASHING_ALGORITHM>
Example:
ENCRYPT_METHOD SHA512
Note: This only effects local groups' passwords created after updating the file to use sha512 or yescrypt. If it is determined that the password algorithm being used is not sha512 or yescrypt, once it is changed, it is recommended that all group passwords be updated to use the stronger hashing algorithm. It is recommended that the chosen hashing algorithm is consistent across /etc/login.defs and the PAM configuration

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify the hashing algorithm is sha512 or yescrypt in /etc/login.defs:
# grep -Pi -- '^\h*ENCRYPT_METHOD\h+(SHA512|YESCRYPT)\b' /etc/login.defs
Example output:
ENCRYPT_METHOD SHA512
- OR -
ENCRYPT_METHOD YESCRYPT

Rule.title: Ensure inactive password lock is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>User accounts that have been inactive for over a given period of time can be automatically disabled.
INACTIVE - Defines the number of days after the password exceeded its maximum age where the user is expected to replace this password.
The value is stored in the shadow password file. An input of 0 will disable an expired password with no delay. An input of -1 will blank the respective field in the shadow password file.

Rationale:
Inactive accounts pose a threat to system security since the users are not logging in to notice failed login attempts or other anomalies.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to set the default password inactivity period to 45 days or less that meets local site policy:
# useradd -D -f <N>
Example:
# useradd -D -f 45
Run the following command to modify user parameters for all users with a password set to a inactive age of 45 days or less that follows local site policy:
# chage --inactive <N> <user>
Example:
# awk -F: '($2~/^\$.+\$/) {if($7 > 45 || $7 < 0)system ("chage --inactive 45
" $1)}' /etc/shadow

check.check-content:
Run the following command and verify INACTIVE conforms to site policy (no more than 45 days):
# useradd -D | grep INACTIVE
INACTIVE=45
Verify all users with a password have Password inactive no more than 45 days after password expires. Run the following command and review the list of users and INACTIVE to verify that all users' INACTIVE conforms to site policy (no more than 45 days):
# awk -F: '($2~/^\$.+\$/) {if($7 == "" || $7 > 45 || $7 < 0)print "User: " $1
" INACTIVE: " $7 "Days"}' /etc/shadow
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure all users last password change date is in the past
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>All users should have a password change date in the past.

Rationale:
If a user's recorded password change date is in the future, then they could bypass any set password expiration. The shadow password suite calculates password expiry relative to the last password change date, so an account with a far-future last-change date can permanently bypass password expiration policies: the password never expires regardless of PASS_MAX_DAYS.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Investigate any users with a password change date in the future and correct them.
Locking the account, expiring the password, or resetting the password manually may be appropriate.
Examples Reset last change date to today for a single user:
# chage -d "$(date +%Y-%m-%d)" <user>
Force password change on next login (recommended companion):
# chage -d 0 <user>

check.check-content:
Run the following script and verify nothing is returned:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
while IFS= read -r l_user; do
l_change_raw=$(chage --list "$l_user" | grep '^Last password change' | cut -
d: -f2 | tr -d ' ')
[ "$l_change_raw" = "never" ] && continue
l_change=$(date -u -d "$l_change_raw" +%s 2>/dev/null) || continue
if [[ "$l_change" -gt "$(date +%s)" ]]; then
echo "User: \"$l_user\" last password change was \"$l_change_raw\""
fi
done < <(awk -F: '$2~/^\$.+\$/{print $1}' /etc/shadow)
}

Group.title: 5.4.2 Configure root and system accounts and environment

Rule.title: Ensure root is the only UID 0 account
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>On a Linux system, the user ID (UID) 0 is the superuser identity: the kernel grants any account assigned UID 0 complete, unrestricted control of the host, regardless of the account's name. The root account holds UID 0 by default.

Rationale:
Limiting UID 0 to the single default root account ensures privileged access is accountable and cannot be silently obtained through a second, easily overlooked superuser identity. Administrative access should be performed through an unprivileged account using an approved escalation mechanism, as described in the recommendation covering restriction of the su command.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Run the following command to reassign any account other than root that has UID 0 to a new, unused UID (and update ownership of that account's files):
# usermod -u <NEW_UID> <username>
Example:
# usermod -u 1234 bsmith
2. If the root account's UID is not 0, run the following command to reset it:
# usermod -u 0 root

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that root is the only account with UID 0:
# awk -F: '($3 == 0) { print $1 }' /etc/passwd
Only root should be returned.

Group.title: 5.4.2 Configure root and system accounts and environment

Rule.title: Ensure root is the only GID 0 account
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>An account's primary group is identified by the group ID (GID) in its /etc/passwd entry.
GID 0 is the root group, which the root account uses as its primary group by default.

Rationale:
Using GID 0 for the root account helps prevent root -owned files from accidentally becoming accessible to non-privileged users.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to reassign any account other than root that has primary GID 0 to an appropriate group:
# usermod -g <NEW_GID> <username>
Example:
# usermod -g 100 bsmith
If the root account's primary GID is not 0, run the following command to reset it:
# usermod -g 0 root

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that only root and the default system accounts have primary GID 0:
# awk -F: '($4 == 0) { print $1 }' /etc/passwd
root should be returned; the default system accounts sync, shutdown, halt, and operator may also be returned.

Group.title: 5.4.2 Configure root and system accounts and environment

Rule.title: Ensure group root is the only GID 0 group
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Groups are defined in /etc/group, each identified by a group ID (GID). GID 0 is reserved for the root group, the privileged group associated with the superuser.

Rationale:
If a group other than root is assigned GID 0, it silently shares the privileges of the root group. Such a duplicate is easy to overlook and undermines accountability for access granted through the root group.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to reassign any group other than root that has GID 0 to an unused GID:
# groupmod -g <NEW_GID> <groupname>
Example:
# groupmod -g 200 legacyadmins
If the root group's GID is not 0, run the following command to reset it:
# groupmod -g 0 root

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that root is the only group with GID 0:
# awk -F: '($3 == 0) { print $1 }' /etc/group
Only root should be returned.

Group.title: 5.4.2 Configure root and system accounts and environment

Rule.title: Ensure root account access is controlled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>There are several ways to gain access to the root account directly: authenticating at the console or a login prompt, switching to it with the su command, or opening a root shell through sudo. Direct access to the root account is governed by its authentication state: whether a password is set and whether the account is locked.

Rationale:
If the root account has no password set and is not locked, any user who can reach a root login prompt or otherwise select the root account can gain access without authenticating, and thus gain control over the entire system. Ensuring that the root password is set, or that the root account is locked so that direct authentication is disabled in favor of an auditable escalation path such as sudo, prevents an unauthenticated user from taking control of the system.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to set a password for the root user:
# passwd root
- OR - Run the following command to lock the root user account:
# usermod -L root

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that either the root user's password is set or the root user's account is locked:
# passwd -S root | awk '$2 ~ /^(P|L)/ {print "User: \"" $1 "\" Password is
status: " $2}'
Verify the output is either:
User: "root" Password is status: PS
- OR -
User: "root" Password is status: LK
Note:
• PS - Password is set
• LK - Password is locked

Group.title: 5.4.2 Configure root and system accounts and environment

Rule.title: Ensure root path integrity
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The PATH variable for the root user determines the directories the shell searches for executables when root runs a command that is not given as an absolute path. Its integrity depends on the ownership, permissions, and composition of the directories it lists.

Rationale:
Including the current working directory (.) or other writable directory in root 's executable path makes it likely that an attacker can gain superuser access by forcing an administrator operating as root to execute a Trojan horse program.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
For each non-compliant item identified by the audit, correct root's PATH as follows.
Edit the shell initialization file that sets root's PATH (for example /root/.bash_profile, /root/.bashrc, or the relevant file under /etc/profile.d/) and remove any current-working- directory (.) entry, any empty entry (::), and any trailing colon (:).
For each directory in root's PATH that is not owned by root, run the following command to set its owner to root:
# chown root <directory>
For each directory in root's PATH that is writable by group or other, run the following command to remove those permissions so the mode is 0755 or more restrictive:
# chmod 0755 <directory>
For each PATH entry that does not exist on the system, either remove it from root's PATH or run the following command to create it with root ownership and an appropriate mode:
# mkdir -p <directory> && chown root <directory> && chmod 0755 <directory>
After making these changes, re-run the audit to confirm root's PATH contains only existing, root-owned directories that are not writable by group or other, with no empty, trailing, or . entries.

check.check-content:
Run the following script to review root's PATH; it reports any empty (::), trailing (:), or current-working-directory (.) entry, and any PATH directory that does not exist, is not owned by root, or is writable by group or other:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
l_pmask="0022"
l_root_path="$(su - root -c 'printf "%s" "$PATH"')"
grep -q -- "::" <<< "$l_root_path" && echo " - root's PATH contains an
empty directory (::)"
grep -Pq -- ":\h*$" <<< "$l_root_path" && echo " - root's PATH ends with a
trailing colon (:)"
grep -Pq -- '(^\h*|:)\.(:|\h*$)' <<< "$l_root_path" && echo " - root's
PATH contains the current working directory (.)"
IFS=":" read -ra a_path_loc <<< "$l_root_path"
for l_path in "${a_path_loc[@]}"; do
if [ -d "$l_path" ]; then
while IFS=: read -r l_fmode l_fown; do
[ "$l_fown" != "root" ] && echo " - Directory \"$l_path\" is
owned by \"$l_fown\" (should be owned by root)"
[ $(( l_fmode & l_pmask )) -gt 0 ] && echo " - Directory
\"$l_path\" is mode \"$l_fmode\" (should be 0755 or more restrictive)"
done <<< "$(stat -Lc '%#a:%U' "$l_path")"
else
echo " - \"$l_path\" is not an existing directory"
fi
done
}
Nothing should be returned.

Group.title: 5.4.2 Configure root and system accounts and environment

Rule.title: Ensure root user umask is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The user file-creation mode mask ( umask) determines the permissions applied to newly created files and directories. On Linux the default permissions are 0777 (rwxrwxrwx) for a new directory and 0666 (rw-rw-rw-) for a new file; the umask restricts (masks) these defaults bitwise - bits set in the umask are cleared in the resulting mode.
A umask can be expressed as an octal or a symbolic value:
• Octal (numeric) value - three or four digits, for example umask 0027 or umask 027. When four digits are given the leading digit is ignored; the remaining three set the masking for user, group, and other respectively.
• Symbolic value - a comma-separated list of the permissions to keep for user ( u), group ( g), and other ( o). For example, umask u=rwx,g=rx,o= is equivalent to the octal umask 027, producing a new directory of drwxr-x--- and a new file of rw-r-----.
root's effective umask is the value in force after every source that sets it (the system defaults and root's own shell initialization files) has been applied in order of precedence.

Rationale:
A permissive umask value could result in directories or files with excessive permissions that can be read and/or written to by unauthorized users.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit /root/.bash_profile and /root/.bashrc and set root's umask to 0027 or more restrictive by adding or modifying the umask line to read:
umask 027
After making the change, verify that root's effective login umask resolves to 0027 or more restrictive, since a umask set in a system-wide location (for example /etc/profile or a file under /etc/profile.d/) can override the value set in root's shell initialization files.
Note: The recommendation "Ensure default user umask is configured" includes guidance to set the default umask.

check.check-content:
Run the following command to display the root user's effective login umask - the value in force after the system defaults and root's shell initialization files have been applied:
# su - root -c 'umask'
The value returned should be 0027 (or the equivalent 027) or more restrictive - that is, every permission bit denied by 0027 is also denied by the effective umask. A returned value of 0027, 0077, or any value at least as restrictive is compliant; a less restrictive value such as 0022 is not.

Group.title: 5.4.2 Configure root and system accounts and environment

Rule.title: Ensure system accounts do not have a valid login shell
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>There are a number of accounts provided with most distributions that are used to manage applications and are not intended to provide an interactive shell. Furthermore, a user may add special accounts that are not intended to provide an interactive shell.

Rationale:
A system account that retains a valid login shell provides an interactive foothold for anyone who obtains its credentials. Removing the login shell from accounts that do not need interactive access eliminates that foothold.</VulnDiscussion>

Group.title: 5.4.2 Configure root and system accounts and environment

Rule.title: Ensure accounts without a valid login shell are locked
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>There are a number of accounts provided with most distributions that are used to manage applications. Additionally, an administrator may add special accounts that are not intended for interactive use.

Rationale:
An account without a valid login shell can still be used for authentication unless it is locked. Locking such accounts closes that residual authentication path.</VulnDiscussion>

Rule.title: Ensure nologin is not listed in /etc/shells
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>/etc/shells is a text file which contains the full pathnames of valid login shells. This file is consulted by chsh and available to be queried by other programs.
Be aware that there are programs which consult this file to find out if a user is a normal user; for example, FTP daemons traditionally disallow access to users with shells not included in this file.

Rationale:
A user can use chsh to change their configured shell.
If a user has a shell configured that isn't in /etc/shells, then the system assumes that they're somehow restricted. In the case of chsh it means that the user cannot change that value.
Other programs might query that list and apply similar restrictions.
By putting nologin in /etc/shells, any user that has nologin as its shell is considered a full, unrestricted user. This is not the expected behavior for nologin.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content: Edit /etc/shells and remove any lines that include nologin

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that nologin is not listed in the /etc/shells file:
# grep -Ps '^\h*([^#\n\r]+)?\/nologin\b' /etc/shells
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure default user shell timeout is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>TMOUT is a shell environment variable that sets an interactive shell's idle timeout, in seconds: after TMOUT seconds with no input, the shell exits. TMOUT=<n> sets the timeout to n seconds (a value of 0 disables it); marking the variable readonly prevents a user from overriding it during the session, and export ing it applies it to the user's shell environment.

Rationale:
Setting a timeout value reduces the window of opportunity for unauthorized user access to another user's shell session that has been left unattended. It also ends the inactive session and releases the resources associated with that session.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Configure TMOUT in a single file. Because best practice marks TMOUT readonly, a second assignment from a later-sourced file produces a "TMOUT: readonly variable" error at every login, so it must be set exactly once.
1. Run the following command to locate any existing TMOUT assignments in the shell initialization files:
# grep -PHrs -- '\bTMOUT\b' /etc/profile /etc/profile.d/ /etc/bashrc
/etc/*bashrc
2. In each file returned in step one, remove or comment out the TMOUT lines so TMOUT is no longer set in more than one location.
3. Create a single drop-in file in /etc/profile.d/ that sets, marks readonly, and exports TMOUT in one statement, using a value greater than 0 and no greater than 900 seconds in line with local site policy.
Example:
# printf '%s\n' "# Set a 900 second interactive shell timeout" "typeset -xr
TMOUT=900" > /etc/profile.d/50-tmout.sh

check.check-content:
Run the following script to verify that TMOUT is set to a value greater than 0 and no larger than 900 seconds, and is marked readonly and exported, in each shell initialization file that configures it:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
l_max=900
a_files=()
while IFS= read -r l_file; do a_files+=("$l_file"); done < <(grep -Pls --
'^([^#\n\r]+)?\bTMOUT\b' \
/etc/*bashrc /etc/profile /etc/profile.d/*.sh /etc/profile.d/sh.local \
/usr/etc/profile.d/*.sh /usr/etc/profile.d/sh.local 2>/dev/null)
l_set=0
for l_file in "${a_files[@]}"; do
l_val="$(grep -Po -- '^([^#\n\r]+)?\bTMOUT=\d+\b' "$l_file" | awk -F=
'{v=$2} END{if (NR>0) print v}')"
[ -z "$l_val" ] && continue
l_set=1
l_ro="$(grep -P -- '^\h*(typeset\h\-
xr\hTMOUT=\d+|([^#\n\r]+)?\breadonly\h+TMOUT\b)' "$l_file")"
l_exp="$(grep -P -- '^\h*(typeset\h\-
xr\hTMOUT=\d+|([^#\n\r]+)?\bexport\b([^#\n\r]+\b)?TMOUT\b)' "$l_file")"
[ "$l_val" -gt 0 ] && [ "$l_val" -le "$l_max" ] || echo "$l_file:
TMOUT=$l_val is out of range (must be >0 and <=$l_max)"
[ -n "$l_ro" ] || echo "$l_file: TMOUT is not marked readonly"
[ -n "$l_exp" ] || echo "$l_file: TMOUT is not exported"
done
[ "$l_set" -eq 0 ] && echo "TMOUT is not set in any shell initialization
file"
}
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure default user umask is configured in /etc/login.defs
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>/etc/login.defs sets system-wide account defaults. Its UMASK value is the umask baseline that pam_umask applies to a login session before any shell-initialization file runs, and that useradd uses when creating a home directory. It governs the umask for sessions that do not source the interactive shell-initialization files.

Rationale:
If the /etc/login.defs UMASK is missing or less restrictive than 0027, sessions that never run the shell-initialization files -- and files created during account setup -- receive permissions readable or writable by other users. A restrictive baseline here ensures a safe default even where shell-level umask settings do not apply.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit /etc/login.defs and set the UMASK line to 0027 or more restrictive:
UMASK 027

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify the UMASK value in /etc/login.defs is 0027 or more restrictive:
# grep -Pi -- '^\h*UMASK\h+\H+' /etc/login.defs
A UMASK value of 0027 (or 027) or more restrictive with UMASK being uppercase should be returned.
Example output:
UMASK 0027

Rule.title: Ensure default user umask is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The user file-creation mode mask ( umask) determines the permissions withheld from newly created files and directories. A user's effective umask is the value in force after login; the shell-initialization files /etc/profile, files under /etc/profile.d/, and /etc/bashrc can set it and can override the system baseline. This recommendation covers those shell-initialization sources; the baseline value in /etc/login.defs is covered by the separate recommendation Ensure default user umask is configured in /etc/login.defs.

Rationale:
A umask less restrictive than 0027 causes new files and directories to be readable or writable by users other than the owner. A shell-initialization file that sets a permissive umask overrides a restrictive baseline for every interactive login, extending those group- or other-accessible defaults to every file created in that session.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Identify any shell-initialization umask statement less restrictive than 0027, and tighten or remove it. When no shell-init source sets a umask, the /etc/login.defs baseline (a separate recommendation) governs the default.
1. Locate the umask statements in the shell-initialization files:
# grep -PHrsi -- '^\h*umask\b' /etc/profile /etc/profile.d/ /etc/bashrc
/etc/bash.bashrc
2. For each statement returned that is less restrictive than 0027, edit the file to set a compliant value:
umask 027
or remove the statement so the /etc/login.defs baseline governs the default.

check.check-content:
Run the following script to verify that none of the shell-initialization sources -- /etc/profile, the files ending in .sh under /etc/profile.d/, /etc/profile.d/sh.local, /etc/bashrc, and /etc/bash.bashrc -- set a umask less restrictive than 0027. Both octal and symbolic umask statements are evaluated:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
l_floor=$(( 8#0027 ))
# Convert a umask argument (octal "0027" or symbolic "u=rwx,g=rx,o=") to
its
# decimal deny-bits value; prints "INVALID" for a form that cannot be
# evaluated statically (relative +/- operators or unknown tokens).
f_umask_to_dec() {
local l_arg="$1" l_u=0 l_g=0 l_o=0 l_clause l_who l_perms l_bits l_deny
if [[ "$l_arg" =~ ^[0-7]{3,4}$ ]]; then
printf '%d' "$(( 8#$l_arg ))"; return 0
fi
local IFS=','
local -a a_clauses=( $l_arg )
for l_clause in "${a_clauses[@]}"; do
if [[ "$l_clause" =~ ^([augo]+)=([rwx]*)$ ]]; then
l_who="${BASH_REMATCH[1]}"; l_perms="${BASH_REMATCH[2]}";
l_bits=0
[[ "$l_perms" == *r* ]] && l_bits=$(( l_bits | 4 ))
[[ "$l_perms" == *w* ]] && l_bits=$(( l_bits | 2 ))
[[ "$l_perms" == *x* ]] && l_bits=$(( l_bits | 1 ))
l_deny=$(( 7 - l_bits ))
[[ "$l_who" == *a* ]] && { l_u=$l_deny; l_g=$l_deny; l_o=$l_deny;
}
[[ "$l_who" == *u* ]] && l_u=$l_deny
[[ "$l_who" == *g* ]] && l_g=$l_deny
[[ "$l_who" == *o* ]] && l_o=$l_deny
else
printf 'INVALID'; return 0
fi
done
printf '%d' "$(( l_u * 64 + l_g * 8 + l_o ))"
}
a_files=(/etc/profile /etc/bashrc /etc/bash.bashrc
/etc/profile.d/sh.local)
while IFS= read -r -d '' l_file; do
a_files+=("$l_file")
done < <(find /etc/profile.d/ -type f -name '*.sh' -print0 2>/dev/null)
for l_file in "${a_files[@]}"; do
[ -r "$l_file" ] || continue
grep -Psi -- '^\h*umask\h+\S' "$l_file" 2>/dev/null | while IFS= read -
r l_line; do
l_arg="$(printf '%s' "$l_line" | grep -Poi --
'^\h*umask\h+\K[^[:space:]#]+')"
[ -n "$l_arg" ] || continue
l_dec="$(f_umask_to_dec "$l_arg")"
{ [ "$l_dec" = "INVALID" ] || [ "$(( l_dec & l_floor ))" -ne
"$l_floor" ]; } && printf '%s: %s\n' "$l_file" "$l_line"
done
done
}
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure journald service is active
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>systemd-journald is the systemd journaling service that collects and stores system log data. It is a static, socket-activated unit that is always present as the initial collector of log events on a systemd-based system; it is started by systemd rather than enabled to start on boot.

Rationale:
systemd-journald must be running for the system to capture log events. If the service is not active, log events are not collected, removing the local record needed to detect, investigate, and respond to security-relevant activity.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following commands to unmask and start systemd-journald.service:
# systemctl unmask systemd-journald.service
# systemctl start systemd-journald.service

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify systemd-journald is active:
# systemctl is-active systemd-journald.service
active

Rule.title: Ensure systemd-journal-remote is not in use
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The systemd-journal-remote package provides the ability to receive journal log entries from remote hosts over the network, which makes the receiving host a log server. The same package supplies both the sending and the receiving functions; the receiving side is handled by two units, systemd-journal-remote.socket and systemd-journal- remote.service.

Rationale:
If a client is configured to also receive log data, thus turning it into a log server, the client system is acting outside its operational boundary. Disabling the systemd-journal- remote receiver is collector hygiene that applies regardless of whether rsyslog or journald is the primary log path.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following commands to stop and mask systemd-journal-remote.socket and systemd-journal-remote.service:
# systemctl stop systemd-journal-remote.socket systemd-journal-remote.service
# systemctl mask systemd-journal-remote.socket systemd-journal-remote.service

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify the systemd-journal-remote receiver is not in use.
It reports any of its units that are enabled (including enabled-runtime) or active:
# systemctl show -p Id -p UnitFileState -p ActiveState systemd-journal-
remote.socket systemd-journal-remote.service | awk -v RS='' '{ id=""; u=0;
for(i=1;i<=NF;i++){ if($i ~ /^Id=/) id=substr($i,4); if($i ~
/^UnitFileState=(enabled|enabled-runtime)$/) u=1; if($i ~
/^ActiveState=active$/) u=1 } if(u) print id " is in use" }'
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure journald is configured to send logs to rsyslog
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Data from systemd-journald may be stored in volatile memory or persisted locally on the server. Utilities exist to accept remote export of systemd-journald logs, however, use of the rsyslog service provides a consistent means of log collection and export.

Rationale:
systemd-journald is always present and acts as the initial collector of system log events.
Forwarding those events to rsyslog provides a single, consistent path for log processing and export, including reliable delivery to a centralized log server for retention and correlation. When forwarding is not enabled, events collected by journald are not passed to rsyslog for further processing.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Ensure ForwardToSyslog is set to yes and that no other entry overrides it.
1. Run the following command to locate every file that sets ForwardToSyslog:
# grep -PHrs -- '^\h*ForwardToSyslog\h*=' /etc/systemd/journald.conf
/etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/
2. In each file returned, remove or comment out the ForwardToSyslog line so the setting is defined in only one place.
3. Set ForwardToSyslog=yes in a drop-in file in /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/ ending in.conf.
Example:
# [ ! -d /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d ] && mkdir -p
/etc/systemd/journald.conf.d
# printf '%s\n' "[Journal]" "ForwardToSyslog=yes" >>
/etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/60-journald.conf
Run the following command to apply the change to the running service:
# systemctl reload-or-restart systemd-journald.service

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that ForwardToSyslog is effectively set to yes, using the highest-precedence active setting across the main configuration file and any drop-ins:
# systemd-analyze cat-config systemd/journald.conf | grep -Pi --
'^\h*ForwardToSyslog\h*=' | tail -n 1
Verify the output:
ForwardToSyslog=yes

Rule.title: Ensure journald log file rotation is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Journald includes the capability of rotating log files regularly to avoid filling up the system with logs or making the logs unmanageably large. Journal rotation is configured in /etc/systemd/journald.conf and in drop-in files under /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/.

Rationale:
By keeping the log files smaller and more manageable, a system administrator can easily archive these files to another system and spend less time looking through inordinately large log files.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Set the journal rotation parameters in a drop-in file in /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/ ending in .conf. Set the parameters in the [Journal] section, adjusting the values to site policy, and ensure no other file overrides them.
Example:
[Journal]
SystemMaxUse=1G
SystemKeepFree=500M
SystemMaxFileSize=100M
RuntimeMaxUse=200M
RuntimeKeepFree=50M
RuntimeMaxFileSize=50M
MaxFileSec=1month
Note: These parameters have specific edge cases and interactions; review journald.conf(5) for the exact semantics.

check.check-content:
Review /etc/systemd/journald.conf and the files ending in .conf under /etc/systemd/journald.conf.d/, and verify that journal rotation is configured according to site policy. The following command lists the effective (highest-precedence) rotation settings:
# systemd-analyze cat-config systemd/journald.conf | tac | grep -Psi --
'^\h*(SystemMaxUse|SystemKeepFree|SystemMaxFileSize|RuntimeMaxUse|RuntimeKeep
Free|RuntimeMaxFileSize|MaxFileSec)\h*='
One or more of the following should be set according to site policy:
SystemMaxUse=
SystemKeepFree=
SystemMaxFileSize=
RuntimeMaxUse=
RuntimeKeepFree=
RuntimeMaxFileSize=
MaxFileSec=

Rule.title: Ensure journald log file access is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Journald creates log files that do not already exist on the system. The permissions applied to these newly created files are governed by systemd-tmpfiles directives in /usr/lib/tmpfiles.d/systemd.conf, which an administrator may override in /etc/tmpfiles.d/systemd.conf.

Rationale:
Journal files can contain sensitive information such as usernames, IP addresses, and details of system and user activity. Restricting access to these files to their owner and group prevents unauthorized users from reading that information or tampering with the local log record.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Set the journald log file mode to 0640 (or a more restrictive value per site policy), then correct any existing files.
1. Run the following command to create a local override of the tmpfiles configuration, if it does not already exist, so the change survives package updates:
# [ -f /etc/tmpfiles.d/systemd.conf ] || cp /usr/lib/tmpfiles.d/systemd.conf
/etc/tmpfiles.d/systemd.conf
2. Edit /etc/tmpfiles.d/systemd.conf and set the mode field (the third column) of each journald log file directive to 0640 or more restrictive.
Run the following command to apply the updated tmpfiles configuration:
# systemd-tmpfiles --create
Run the following command to correct the mode of any existing journald log files that are looser than 0640 (this removes only the excess permission bits and does not loosen files that are already more restrictive):
# find /var/log/journal /run/log/journal -type f -name '*.journal*' -perm
/0137 -exec chmod u-x,g-wx,o-rwx {} +

check.check-content:
Journald applies the modes defined by systemd-tmpfiles directives in /usr/lib/tmpfiles.d/systemd.conf (or an override in /etc/tmpfiles.d/systemd.conf, which takes precedence) to the log files it creates. Existing files keep their current mode until recreated, so review both the directive and the files on disk.
1. Run the following command to review the mode field (the third column) of the journald log file directives:
# systemd-tmpfiles --cat-config | grep -P -- '/var/log/journal/.*\.journal'
Each returned mode should be 0640 or more restrictive 2. Run the following command to list any journald log files on disk with permissions less restrictive than 0640:
# find /var/log/journal /run/log/journal -type f -name '*.journal*' -perm
/0137
Nothing should be returned

Rule.title: Ensure rsyslog is installed
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>rsyslog is a reliable, feature-rich system logging service. The rsyslog package provides the rsyslogd daemon, which collects log messages from the kernel, system services, and applications (including those gathered by the systemd journal) and writes them to persistent on-disk log files under /var/log, and can filter, rate-limit, and forward them to a central log host.

Rationale:
Persistent, reliable logging is fundamental to security operations: it preserves the record of system and security events needed for accountability, threat detection, incident investigation, and forensic analysis. The systemd journal stores its logs in volatile memory by default, so without a persistent logging service those records can be lost across a reboot or under memory pressure. Installing rsyslog establishes durable on- disk log retention and the foundation for later centralization and protection of that log data.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to install rsyslog:
# dnf install rsyslog

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify the rsyslog package is installed:
# rpm -q rsyslog
Example output:
rsyslog-8.2402.0-1
A package name and version should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure rsyslog service is enabled and active
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The rsyslog service (rsyslogd) runs the logging daemon. It must be enabled so it starts automatically at boot and active so it is running in the current session; an enabled-and- active service ensures log collection begins at boot and continues without manual intervention.

Rationale:
If the rsyslog service is not running and enabled at boot, the system stops capturing and persisting log messages, leaving gaps in the record of system and security events that accountability, detection, and investigation depend on.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following commands to unmask, enable, and start rsyslog.service:
# systemctl unmask rsyslog.service
# systemctl enable rsyslog.service
# systemctl start rsyslog.service

check.check-content:
1. Run the following command to verify rsyslog.service is enabled:
# systemctl is-enabled rsyslog.service
Example output:
enabled
2. Run the following command to verify rsyslog.service is active:
# systemctl is-active rsyslog.service
Example output:
active

Rule.title: Ensure rsyslog log file creation mode is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>rsyslog sets the permissions on the log files it creates. The file creation mode is controlled by the fileCreateMode parameter - the modern global(fileCreateMode="...") / omfile-action form or the legacy $FileCreateMode directive - and is further constrained by rsyslog's umask ( global(umask=...) or the legacy $umask). The value is a four-digit octal mode; if no creation mode is set, rsyslog defaults to 0644. This recommendation governs that creation mode so newly created log files are not world-readable.

Rationale:
Log files routinely contain sensitive event data - usernames, source addresses, service and command detail, and occasionally secrets logged in error. If rsyslog creates log files readable by group or other, any local user can read that data. Constraining the creation mode to 0640 or more restrictive ensures newly created logs are readable only by root (and the log group).</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Run the following command to list any existing file-creation-mode directives:
# grep -PHrs -- '^\h*(\$FileCreateMode\b|[^#]*\bfileCreateMode\h*=)'
/etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/
Remove or correct any $FileCreateMode / fileCreateMode= line more permissive than 0640 so the mode is defined once 2. Create a drop-in file (for example /etc/rsyslog.d/20-file-create- mode.conf) with the following content, setting the mode to 0640 or more restrictive:
global(fileCreateMode="0640")
3. Run the following command to restart rsyslog:
# systemctl restart rsyslog
The legacy directive $FileCreateMode 0640 is equivalent and remains supported where the modern syntax is not used.

check.check-content:
Run the following script to assemble the effective rsyslog configuration and verify the log file creation mode is 0640 or more restrictive. The check matches both the modern advanced fileCreateMode= parameter (for example global(fileCreateMode="0640")) and the legacy $FileCreateMode directive; a match on either satisfies this recommendation, though the legacy $ -directive form is deprecated and should be migrated to the advanced format:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
a_conf=(/etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf)
while IFS= read -r l_inc; do
for l_f in $l_inc; do
[ -d "$l_f" ] && a_conf+=("$l_f"/*.conf) || a_conf+=("$l_f")
done
done < <(grep -Psoih --
'^\h*(?:\$IncludeConfig\h+|include\h*\(\h*file\h*=\h*"?)\K[^")\h]+'
"${a_conf[@]}" 2>/dev/null)
grep -Psi -- '^\h*(\$FileCreateMode\h+|.*\bfileCreateMode\h*=\h*"?)0[0-
7]{3}' "${a_conf[@]}" 2>/dev/null
}
Example output (the first line is the modern advanced form, the second the equivalent legacy directive; either satisfies):
global(fileCreateMode="0640")
$FileCreateMode 0640
A value of 0640 or more restrictive (for example 0640, 0600, 0400) should be configured. Where site policy dictates a different mode, follow that policy.
Note: A umask setting ( $umask or global(umask=)) is a separate, coarser control that masks permission bits and does not by itself satisfy this recommendation; the file creation mode must be set via fileCreateMode or $FileCreateMode.

Rule.title: Ensure access to rsyslog configuration files is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The main rsyslog configuration file /etc/rsyslog.conf and the drop-in configuration files ending in .conf under /etc/rsyslog.d/ control how rsyslog collects, filters, stores, and forwards system log data. These files should be owned by root, group-owned by root, and no more permissive than mode 0640, so that they can be modified only by root and are not readable by any account other than root.

Rationale:
The rsyslog configuration governs which events are recorded and where they are sent.
If a non-privileged account can modify these files, it could disable logging of critical events, redirect logs away from a central collector, or alter filters to hide activity, undermining the integrity and availability of the audit trail. Restricting access to root protects the logging configuration from unauthorized tampering and disclosure.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following commands to set ownership to root:root and remove group write, all access for other accounts, and all execute bits from the rsyslog configuration files, resulting in mode 0640 or more restrictive:
# chown root:root /etc/rsyslog.conf
# chmod u-x,g-wx,o-rwx /etc/rsyslog.conf
# find /etc/rsyslog.d/ -type f -name '*.conf' -exec chown root:root {} +
# find /etc/rsyslog.d/ -type f -name '*.conf' -exec chmod u-x,g-wx,o-rwx {} +

check.check-content:
Verify that the rsyslog configuration files are owned by root, group-owned by root, and mode 0640 or more restrictive.
1. Run the following command to list the main configuration file if it is not owned by root, not group-owned by root, or less restrictive than mode 0640:
# find /etc/rsyslog.conf -not -type l \( ! -user root -o ! -group root -o -
perm /0137 \) 2>/dev/null
Nothing should be returned.
2. Run the following command to list any .conf drop-in under /etc/rsyslog.d/ that is not owned by root, not group-owned by root, or less restrictive than mode 0640:
# find /etc/rsyslog.d/ -type f -name '*.conf' \( ! -user root -o ! -group
root -o -perm /0137 \) 2>/dev/null
Nothing should be returned.
Note: If rsyslog is not installed, /etc/rsyslog.conf and /etc/rsyslog.d/ may not exist; the commands return nothing and this recommendation is Not Applicable.

Rule.title: Ensure access to the /etc/rsyslog.d directory is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The /etc/rsyslog.d/ directory holds drop-in rsyslog configuration files ending in .conf. The directory should be owned by root, group-owned by root, and not writable by any account other than root so that unauthorized users cannot add, remove, or replace rsyslog configuration fragments.

Rationale:
Because rsyslog reads every .conf file in /etc/rsyslog.d/, an account able to write to this directory could introduce a new configuration fragment that disables logging, changes filters, or redirects log forwarding, without altering any existing file. Restricting write access to the directory to root prevents unauthorized modification of the effective logging configuration.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following commands to set ownership to root:root and remove group and other write from the directory:
# chown root:root /etc/rsyslog.d
# chmod g-w,o-w /etc/rsyslog.d

check.check-content:
Verify that the /etc/rsyslog.d/ directory is owned by root, group-owned by root, and mode 0755 or more restrictive (that is, not group- or world-writable).
Run the following command to list the directory if it is not owned by root, not group- owned by root, or less restrictive than mode 0755:
# find /etc/rsyslog.d/ -maxdepth 0 -type d \( ! -user root -o ! -group root -
o -perm /0022 \) 2>/dev/null
Nothing should be returned.
Note: If rsyslog is not installed, /etc/rsyslog.d/ may not exist; the command returns nothing and this recommendation is Not Applicable.

Rule.title: Ensure access to the rsyslog work directory is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>rsyslog's work directory, set by the global $WorkDirectory / global(workDirectory=...) directive and defaulting to /var/lib/rsyslog, stores disk-assisted queue spool files. These files can hold buffered log data written to disk when in-memory queues are exhausted or a forwarding action is retrying. The work directory should be owned by root, group- owned by root, and accessible only to root.

Rationale:
Spooled queue files under the rsyslog work directory can contain log records, potentially including sensitive event data, held on disk before delivery. If the work directory is readable or writable by non-privileged accounts, buffered log data could be disclosed, altered, or deleted before it reaches its destination. Restricting the work directory to root protects buffered log data at rest.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following commands to set ownership to root:root and remove all group and other access from the work directory (substitute a non-default $WorkDirectory path if configured):
# chown root:root /var/lib/rsyslog
# chmod go-rwx /var/lib/rsyslog

check.check-content:
Verify that the rsyslog work directory is owned by root, group-owned by root, and mode 0700 or more restrictive. The work directory is set by the $WorkDirectory / global(workDirectory=...) directive and defaults to /var/lib/rsyslog.
1. Run the following command to determine the configured work directory:
# grep -Psi -- '^[^#]*(WorkDirectory|workDirectory)\s*[= ]' /etc/rsyslog.conf
/etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf 2>/dev/null
If a line is returned, use the path it sets in the next command; if nothing is returned, the default /var/lib/rsyslog applies.
2. Run the following command to list the work directory if it is not owned by root, not group-owned by root, or less restrictive than mode 0700 (substitute the configured path if $WorkDirectory is set to a non-default location):
# find /var/lib/rsyslog -maxdepth 0 -type d \( ! -user root -o ! -group root
-o -perm /0077 \) 2>/dev/null
Nothing should be returned.
Note: If rsyslog is not installed, the work directory may not exist; the command returns nothing and this recommendation is Not Applicable.

Rule.title: Ensure rsyslog is not configured as a log server
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>rsyslog can be configured to receive log messages from remote hosts over the network by loading a remote-input module (imtcp, imudp, imptcp, or imrelp) and starting a listener, which makes the host act as a central log server.

Rationale:
A general-purpose host that is not intended to be a central log collector should not run a syslog listener. Accepting remote log messages opens a network-facing service that increases the attack surface and exposes the host to remote log injection or poisoning (which can corrupt the local log store) and to resource exhaustion from unsolicited traffic. Only hosts explicitly designated and hardened as log servers should receive remote logs.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Should any active log server configuration be found by the audit, edit the file(s) where those directives appear - /etc/rsyslog.conf, a drop-in under /etc/rsyslog.d/, or any non-standard file identified by the audit's configuration discovery - and remove or comment out the remote-input module load, input, and run directives for all of imtcp, imudp, imptcp, and imrelp. Ensure none of the following entries are present:
advanced format
module(load="imtcp")
module(load="imudp")
module(load="imptcp")
module(load="imrelp")
input(type="imtcp" port="514")
input(type="imudp" port="514")
input(type="imptcp" port="514")
input(type="imrelp" port="2514")
deprecated legacy format
$ModLoad imtcp
$ModLoad imudp
$ModLoad imptcp
$ModLoad imrelp
$InputTCPServerRun 514
$UDPServerRun 514
$InputPTCPServerRun 514
$InputRELPServerRun 2514
2. Run the following command to restart rsyslog:
# systemctl restart rsyslog

check.check-content:
Review the effective rsyslog configuration and verify the system is not configured to accept incoming logs from remote hosts. A log server may be configured with any of the input modules imtcp, imudp, imptcp, or imrelp. Run the following script (it assembles the effective configuration, including non-standard includes, then checks for remote- input modules in both the modern and legacy syntax):
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
a_conf=(/etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf)
while IFS= read -r l_inc; do
for l_f in $l_inc; do
[ -d "$l_f" ] && a_conf+=("$l_f"/*.conf) || a_conf+=("$l_f")
done
done < <(grep -Psoih --
'^\h*(?:\$IncludeConfig\h+|include\h*\(\h*file\h*=\h*"?)\K[^")\h]+'
"${a_conf[@]}" 2>/dev/null)
grep -Psi -- '^\h*module\(load="?(imtcp|imudp|imptcp|imrelp)"?\)'
"${a_conf[@]}" 2>/dev/null
grep -Psi -- '^\h*input\(type="?(imtcp|imudp|imptcp|imrelp)"?'
"${a_conf[@]}" 2>/dev/null
grep -Psi -- '^\h*\$ModLoad\h+(imtcp|imudp|imptcp|imrelp)\b'
"${a_conf[@]}" 2>/dev/null
grep -Psi --
'^\h*\$(InputTCPServerRun|UDPServerRun|InputPTCPServerRun|InputRELPServerRun)
\b' "${a_conf[@]}" 2>/dev/null
}
Nothing should be returned. If any output is returned, a remote-input module or network listener is configured and the system is acting as a log server, which does not meet this recommendation.

Rule.title: Ensure rsyslog logging rules are configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The /etc/rsyslog.conf file and the drop-in files ending in .conf under /etc/rsyslog.d/ specify rsyslog's logging rules - which classes of messages (by facility and severity) are recorded and which files they are written to.

Rationale:
Security-relevant events - such as authentication successes and failures, privilege escalation, and root activity - are recorded through rsyslog. If logging rules are not configured to capture and retain these events, the records needed for accountability, detection, and investigation may never be written.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Edit the following lines in the /etc/rsyslog.conf and /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf files as appropriate for your environment.
Note: The below configuration is shown for example purposes only. Due care should be given to how the organization wishes to store log data.
*.emerg :omusrmsg:*
auth,authpriv.* /var/log/secure
mail.* -/var/log/mail
mail.info -/var/log/mail.info
mail.warning -/var/log/mail.warn
mail.err /var/log/mail.err
cron.* /var/log/cron
*.=warning;*.=err -/var/log/warn
*.crit /var/log/warn
*.*;mail.none;news.none -/var/log/messages
local0,local1.* -/var/log/localmessages
local2,local3.* -/var/log/localmessages
local4,local5.* -/var/log/localmessages
local6,local7.* -/var/log/localmessages
2. Run the following command to restart rsyslog:
# systemctl restart rsyslog

check.check-content:
1. Run the following script to assemble the effective rsyslog configuration and review the active logging rules; verify appropriate logging is set per site policy:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
a_conf=(/etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf)
while IFS= read -r l_inc; do
for l_f in $l_inc; do
[ -d "$l_f" ] && a_conf+=("$l_f"/*.conf) || a_conf+=("$l_f")
done
done < <(grep -Psoih --
'^\h*(?:\$IncludeConfig\h+|include\h*\(\h*file\h*=\h*"?)\K[^")\h]+'
"${a_conf[@]}" 2>/dev/null)
grep -Ph -- '^\h*[^#[:space:]]' "${a_conf[@]}" 2>/dev/null
}
The active logging rules across the effective configuration are listed. Rules should route the security-relevant facilities (for example authpriv, auth, cron, mail) to log files under /var/log/ per site policy.
Example output:
module(load="imuxsock")
global(workDirectory="/var/lib/rsyslog")
include(file="/etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf" mode="optional")
*.info;mail.none;authpriv.none;cron.none /var/log/messages
authpriv.* /var/log/secure
mail.* -/var/log/maillog
cron.* /var/log/cron
*.emerg :omusrmsg:*
2. Run the following command to verify the expected log files exist and are being written to:
# ls -l /var/log/
Example output:
-rw-------. 1 root root 102400 Jul 31 10:15 messages
-rw-------. 1 root root 20480 Jul 31 10:15 secure
-rw-------. 1 root root 8192 Jul 31 10:14 cron
-rw-------. 1 root root 4096 Jul 31 10:10 maillog
Recent modification times on the security-relevant log files indicate rsyslog is actively writing to them.

Rule.title: Ensure rsyslog is configured to send logs to a remote log host
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>rsyslog can forward the log events it collects to a remote log host over the network (for example, with an omfwd action), sending a copy of local log data to a central collector for centralized log management.

Rationale:
Storing log data on a remote host protects log integrity from local attacks. If an attacker gains root access on the local system, they could tamper with or remove log data that is stored on the local system.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Edit the /etc/rsyslog.conf and /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf files and add a forwarding action (where loghost.example.com is the name of your central log host; the target directive may be a fully qualified domain name or an IP address):
*.* action(type="omfwd" target="loghost.example.com" port="514"
protocol="tcp"
action.resumeRetryCount="100"
queue.type="LinkedList" queue.size="1000")
2. Run the following command to restart rsyslog:
# systemctl restart rsyslog

check.check-content:
Run the following script to assemble the effective rsyslog configuration and verify logs are forwarded to a central log host. Both the basic and advanced configuration formats are accepted:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
a_conf=(/etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf)
while IFS= read -r l_inc; do
for l_f in $l_inc; do
[ -d "$l_f" ] && a_conf+=("$l_f"/*.conf) || a_conf+=("$l_f")
done
done < <(grep -Psoih --
'^\h*(?:\$IncludeConfig\h+|include\h*\(\h*file\h*=\h*"?)\K[^")\h]+'
"${a_conf[@]}" 2>/dev/null)
grep -Psi -- '^\h*[^#]\S*\h+@@\S+' "${a_conf[@]}" 2>/dev/null
grep -Psi -- '^\s*([^#]+\s+)?action\(([^#]+\s+)?\btarget="?[^#"]+"?\b'
"${a_conf[@]}" 2>/dev/null
}
A forwarding line naming the remote loghost should be returned - either a basic-format line or an advanced omfwd action.
Example output:
*.* @@loghost.example.com
*.* action(type="omfwd" target="loghost.example.com" port="514"
protocol="tcp")
