Note: @@ denotes a TCP connection; a single @ denotes UDP, which does not meet this recommendation.

Rule.title: Ensure a rsyslog TLS network stream driver is installed
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>rsyslog encrypts forwarded syslog traffic using a TLS network stream driver, a layer between rsyslog and the transport that provides confidentiality, integrity, and peer authentication for messages sent over the network using the syslog-transport-tls standard. Two interchangeable drivers are available and packaged separately: the GnuTLS driver gtls (package rsyslog-gnutls) and the OpenSSL driver ossl (package rsyslog-openssl). Either driver satisfies this recommendation; only the selected driver's package needs to be installed.
Installing a TLS network stream driver ensures the capability to forward logs over an encrypted, authenticated channel is available whenever remote forwarding is used.

Rationale:
Traditional syslog forwarding is a clear-text protocol, so anyone able to observe the network can read forwarded log data. A TLS network stream driver implements the SSL/TLS protocols that encrypt syslog communication in transit and authenticate the remote peer. The driver package must be installed before rsyslog can select a TLS driver, so installing rsyslog-gnutls or rsyslog-openssl is the prerequisite for any encrypted forwarding configuration.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Install a rsyslog TLS network stream driver. Only one driver package is required; the GnuTLS driver is the recommended default.
Run the following command to install the rsyslog-gnutls package:
# dnf install rsyslog-gnutls
Or, if the OpenSSL driver is preferred, run the following command to install the rsyslog-openssl package:
# dnf install rsyslog-openssl

check.check-content:
Verify that a rsyslog TLS network stream driver package is installed. Either the GnuTLS driver (rsyslog-gnutls) or the OpenSSL driver (rsyslog-openssl) satisfies this recommendation.
Run the following command to verify that either the rsyslog-gnutls or the rsyslog- openssl package is installed:
# rpm -q rsyslog-gnutls rsyslog-openssl
Verify at least one of the two driver packages is installed.
Example output:
rsyslog-gnutls-<version>
package rsyslog-openssl is not installed
It is normal for the unused driver to report that it is not installed.

Rule.title: Ensure rsyslog network forwarding uses TLS
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>When rsyslog forwards logs to a remote host, the omfwd output action can wrap the connection in TLS by selecting a TLS network stream driver (gtls or ossl), running that driver in TLS-only mode, and setting a peer authentication mode. The driver may be selected globally (DefaultNetstreamDriver) or per action (StreamDriver), using either the modern advanced (global(...) / action(...)) syntax or the legacy $-directive syntax. This recommendation applies only where rsyslog forwards to a remote host; hosts that do not forward syslog over the network may document it as Not Applicable.

Rationale:
If forwarding is not wrapped in TLS, syslog traffic crosses the network in clear text and is subject to interception, modification, or silent loss. Selecting a TLS stream driver and forcing TLS-only mode ensures the connection is encrypted, and setting an authentication mode ensures rsyslog will only deliver logs to a verified remote peer, defeating passive sniffing and man-in-the-middle attacks against the log stream.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Configure rsyslog to forward over TLS using a drop-in file, the recommended method for local rsyslog configuration, and ensure no plaintext forwarding action remains.
1. Run the following command to locate any existing forwarding actions for review:
# grep -PHns -- 'type="omfwd"|^\h*[^#]*@' /etc/rsyslog.conf
/etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf
2. In each file returned, remove or convert to TLS any forwarding action that is not already TLS-secured, so the only remaining forwarding path uses TLS.
3. Create a drop-in file such as /etc/rsyslog.d/60-forward-tls.conf with the TLS forwarding configuration. The example below uses the GnuTLS driver:
# Select the TLS driver and trust material globally
global(
DefaultNetstreamDriver="gtls"
DefaultNetstreamDriverCAFile="/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt"
)
# Forward all messages to the remote collector over TLS only
*.* action(type="omfwd"
target="loghost.example.com" port="6514" protocol="tcp"
StreamDriver="gtls"
StreamDriverMode="1"
StreamDriverAuthMode="x509/name"
StreamDriverPermittedPeers="loghost.example.com"
action.resumeRetryCount="100"
queue.type="LinkedList" queue.size="1000")
4. Run the following command to restart rsyslog:
# systemctl restart rsyslog
If the OpenSSL driver is preferred, substitute ossl for gtls in the DefaultNetstreamDriver and StreamDriver settings above.

check.check-content:
Verify that rsyslog forwards logs over TLS. A compliant forwarding action selects a TLS network stream driver ( gtls or ossl), runs it in TLS-only mode, sets a peer authentication mode, and targets the encrypted syslog-over-TLS port ( 6514). All four elements must be present on the same forwarding action. The checks accept either driver and both the modern advanced syntax ( global(...) / action(...)) and the legacy $ -directive syntax; legacy directives are deprecated and should be migrated to the advanced format.
1. Identify all active rsyslog configuration files. In addition to /etc/rsyslog.conf and the.conf drop-ins under /etc/rsyslog.d/, rsyslog may include further files via $IncludeConfig or include(). Run the following command and include any files it returns in the searches below (the bound automated check assembles this set recursively):
# grep -Psoih --
'^\h*(?:\$IncludeConfig\h+|include\h*\(\h*file\h*=\h*"?)\K[^")\h]+'
/etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf
On a system that uses only the standard configuration paths, nothing is returned.
2. Run the following command to verify a TLS network stream driver ( gtls or ossl) is selected:
# grep -Psi -- '^[^#]*(StreamDriver|DefaultNetstreamDriver)(\.Name)?\s*[=
]\s*"?(gtls|ossl)"?' /etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf
A line setting the driver to gtls or ossl should be returned (for example StreamDriver="gtls", or the legacy $DefaultNetstreamDriver gtls).
3. Run the following command to verify the driver runs in TLS-only mode (mode 1):
# grep -Psi --
'^[^#]*(StreamDriverMode\s*=\s*"?1"?|ActionSendStreamDriverMode\s+1)'
/etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf
A line setting the driver mode to 1 should be returned (for example StreamDriverMode="1", or the legacy $ActionSendStreamDriverMode 1).
4. Run the following command to verify a peer authentication mode is set:
# grep -Psi --
'^[^#]*(StreamDriverAuthMode\s*=\s*"?(x509/name|x509/certvalid|x509/fingerpri
nt|anon)"?|ActionSendStreamDriverAuthMode\s+(x509/name|x509/certvalid|x509/fi
ngerprint|anon))' /etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf
A line setting the authentication mode should be returned (for example StreamDriverAuthMode="x509/name", or the legacy $ActionSendStreamDriverAuthMode x509/name). x509/name is recommended because it validates the remote certificate chain and matches the peer identity; anon encrypts but does not authenticate the peer and should be avoided in production.
5. Run the following command to verify the forwarding action targets the encrypted syslog-over-TLS port ( 6514):
# grep -Psi -- '^[^#]*(port\s*=\s*"?6514"?|:6514)' /etc/rsyslog.conf
/etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf
A line targeting port 6514 should be returned (for example port="6514", or the legacy @@loghost:6514).
All four elements (steps 2-5) must be present on the same forwarding action.

Rule.title: Ensure rsyslog TLS CA certificate is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>When rsyslog forwards logs over TLS, it uses a Certificate Authority (CA) certificate to verify the remote collector's TLS certificate. The CA is specified with the global DefaultNetstreamDriverCAFile directive, or per action with StreamDriver.CAFile (rsyslog 8.2108.0 and later). For mutual authentication, the client also presents its own certificate and key (DefaultNetstreamDriverCertFile / DefaultNetstreamDriverKeyFile, or the per- action StreamDriver.CertFile / StreamDriver.KeyFile). This recommendation applies where rsyslog forwards over TLS.

Rationale:
A trusted CA certificate ensures rsyslog only connects to log servers whose TLS certificates are signed by a known, trusted authority. Without a properly configured CA, forwarding can proceed without verifying the server's identity, exposing the host to man- in-the-middle attacks that intercept, tamper with, or silently discard forwarded logs, resulting in undetected data leakage or loss of audit-trail integrity.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Configure rsyslog with the CA certificate that signs the remote log server's TLS certificate.
1. Add the global CA directive to the drop-in file that defines the TLS forwarding action (for example /etc/rsyslog.d/60-forward-tls.conf):
global(DefaultNetstreamDriverCAFile="/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt")
Set the path to the CA that signed the log server certificate: use the system trust bundle /etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt when the server certificate chains to a CA already in the system trust store, or a dedicated CA file (for example /etc/pki/rsyslog/ca.pem) for an internal certificate authority.
2. Run the following command to restart rsyslog:
# systemctl restart rsyslog
Note: On rsyslog 8.2108.0 and later the CA may instead be set per forwarding action with StreamDriver.CAFile="..." inside the action(type="omfwd" ...) block, preferred when different targets use different CA chains.
If a non-default CA path is used on a system with SELinux in enforcing mode, label the path so rsyslogd can read it, for example:
# semanage fcontext -a -t cert_t '/etc/pki/rsyslog(/.*)?'
# restorecon -Rv /etc/pki/rsyslog

check.check-content:
Verify that rsyslog is configured with a trusted CA certificate for TLS forwarding. The CA certificate may be set globally with DefaultNetstreamDriverCAFile or per forwarding action with StreamDriver.CAFile (rsyslog 8.2108.0 and later); either form satisfies this recommendation. Both the modern advanced syntax and the legacy $ -directive syntax are accepted; legacy directives are deprecated and should be migrated when possible.
1. Identify all active rsyslog configuration files. In addition to /etc/rsyslog.conf and the.conf drop-ins under /etc/rsyslog.d/, rsyslog may include further files via $IncludeConfig or include(). Run the following command and include any files it returns in the search below:
# grep -Psoih --
'^\h*(?:\$IncludeConfig\h+|include\h*\(\h*file\h*=\h*"?)\K[^")\h]+'
/etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf
On a system that uses only the standard configuration paths, nothing is returned.
2. Run the following command to verify a CA certificate file is configured:
# grep -Psi --
'^[^#]*(DefaultNetstreamDriverCAFile|StreamDriver\.CAFile)\s*[= ]'
/etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf
A line naming a CA certificate file should be returned (for example DefaultNetstreamDriverCAFile="/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt").
3. For each CA file configured in step 2, run the following command to confirm the file exists and is a readable certificate (substitute the path returned above):
# openssl x509 -in /etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt -noout -subject
A certificate subject line should be returned (for example subject=C = US, O = Example, CN = Example Logging CA). If the file is missing or unreadable, or openssl reports an error, the CA certificate is not correctly configured.
Confirm the CA originates from a known, trusted authority appropriate to the environment and local site policy - a public CA or an organization-managed internal enterprise CA. Avoid ad-hoc or untrusted self-signed certificates in production; the steps above confirm a CA file is configured and readable but do not establish that the issuing authority is trusted.

Rule.title: Ensure rsyslog TLS client certificate is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>In mutual (two-way) TLS, the rsyslog forwarding client presents its own X.509 certificate and private key so the receiving log server can authenticate it, in addition to the client verifying the server against a trusted CA. The client certificate and key are configured with the modern advanced parameters DefaultNetstreamDriverCertFile / DefaultNetstreamDriverKeyFile (or the per-action StreamDriver.CertFile / StreamDriver.KeyFile), or the equivalent legacy $DefaultNetstreamDriverCertFile / $DefaultNetstreamDriverKeyFile directives.

Rationale:
With one-way TLS the forwarding client verifies the receiver, but the receiver cannot verify the forwarder: any host that can reach the collector and present a certificate chaining to a trusted CA - or connect with an anonymous authentication mode - can establish a session and inject log records. Configuring a client certificate enables mutual authentication so the receiving log server can confirm the identity of each connecting forwarder, preventing unauthorized or spoofed hosts from injecting or poisoning the central log store.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Provision a client certificate and private key issued by a CA the receiving log server trusts, then configure rsyslog to present them.
1. Add the following to a drop-in such as /etc/rsyslog.d/60-forward-tls.conf:
global(
DefaultNetstreamDriver="gtls"
DefaultNetstreamDriverCAFile="/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt"
DefaultNetstreamDriverCertFile="/etc/pki/tls/certs/rsyslog-client.pem"
DefaultNetstreamDriverKeyFile="/etc/pki/tls/private/rsyslog-client.key"
)
2. Run the following command to restrict permissions on the private key:
# chmod 0600 /etc/pki/tls/private/rsyslog-client.key
3. Run the following command to restart rsyslog:
# systemctl restart rsyslog
On the receiving log server, require and authorize client certificates (for example StreamDriverAuthMode="x509/name" with an appropriate permittedPeer list) so only authenticated forwarders may connect.

check.check-content:
This recommendation applies only where rsyslog forwards logs over TLS.
Verify that rsyslog presents a client certificate and private key for mutual TLS authentication. The certificate and key may be set globally ( DefaultNetstreamDriverCertFile / DefaultNetstreamDriverKeyFile) or per forwarding action ( StreamDriver.CertFile / StreamDriver.KeyFile); either form satisfies this recommendation. Legacy $ -directive forms are also accepted but are deprecated and should be migrated to the advanced format.
1. Identify all active rsyslog configuration files. In addition to /etc/rsyslog.conf and the.conf drop-ins under /etc/rsyslog.d/, rsyslog may include further files via $IncludeConfig or include(). Run the following command and include any files it returns in the searches below:
# grep -Psoih --
'^\h*(?:\$IncludeConfig\h+|include\h*\(\h*file\h*=\h*"?)\K[^")\h]+'
/etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf
On a system that uses only the standard configuration paths, nothing is returned.
2. Run the following command to verify a client certificate file is configured:
# grep -Psi -- '(DefaultNetstreamDriverCertFile|StreamDriver\.CertFile)\h*[=
]' /etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf
A line naming a client certificate file should be returned (for example DefaultNetstreamDriverCertFile="/etc/pki/tls/certs/rsyslog- client.crt").
3. Run the following command to verify a client private key file is configured:
# grep -Psi -- '(DefaultNetstreamDriverKeyFile|StreamDriver\.KeyFile)\h*[= ]'
/etc/rsyslog.conf /etc/rsyslog.d/*.conf
A line naming a private key file should be returned (for example DefaultNetstreamDriverKeyFile="/etc/pki/tls/private/rsyslog- client.key").
4. For the certificate and key files configured in steps 2 and 3, run the following command to confirm each file exists and to check the private key's ownership and access (substitute the paths returned above):
# ls -l /etc/pki/tls/certs/rsyslog-client.crt /etc/pki/tls/private/rsyslog-
client.key
Both files should exist. The private key file should be owned by root and not readable by group or other (for example -rw------- 1 root root).
Confirm the client certificate is issued by a certificate authority the receiving log server trusts and matches the forwarding host's identity.

Rule.title: Ensure logrotate is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>logrotate manages the automatic rotation, compression, and removal of log files so they do not grow without bound. The log files produced by rsyslog are rotated according to /etc/logrotate.conf and the drop-in files under /etc/logrotate.d/ (for example /etc/logrotate.d/syslog).

Rationale:
Without log rotation, log files grow without bound and can consume all available space on their filesystem, disrupting logging itself and other services that share that filesystem.
Rotating and aging logs bounds disk use while retaining recent records for the period required by site policy.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit /etc/logrotate.conf (and any files under /etc/logrotate.d/) to rotate logs on a fixed schedule, retain a bounded number of rotations, compress old logs, and set a maximum age. Apply the following baseline in /etc/logrotate.conf:
# rotate log files weekly
weekly
# keep 13 weeks of backlogs
rotate 13
# remove rotated logs older than 90 days
maxage 90
# compress rotated logs
compress
# create new (empty) log files after rotating old ones
create
Note: Tune the weekly, rotate, and maxage values to your organization's log-retention policy; the values above are a recommended starting point.

check.check-content:
Run the following command to review the configured log rotation settings across the main configuration file and the drop-in files:
# grep -PH '^\h*(daily|weekly|monthly|rotate|maxage|compress|create)\b'
/etc/logrotate.conf /etc/logrotate.d/*
The output should show a rotation schedule (for example daily, weekly, or monthly), a bounded retention count ( rotate), and, where required by site policy, a maximum age ( maxage) and compression ( compress). Verify the settings meet the organization's log- retention policy.
Example output:
/etc/logrotate.conf:weekly
/etc/logrotate.conf:rotate 13
/etc/logrotate.conf:maxage 90
/etc/logrotate.conf:compress
/etc/logrotate.conf:create

Rule.title: Ensure access to all logfiles has been configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Log files contain information from many services on the local system, or in the event of a centralized log server, other systems' logs as well.
In general log files are found in /var/log/, although applications can be configured to store logs elsewhere. Should your application store logs in another location, apply the same audit to that location.

Rationale:
It is important that log files have the correct permissions to ensure that sensitive data is protected and that only the appropriate users / groups have access to them.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Log file access is most reliably enforced at the point of creation: if the mechanism that creates each log sets the correct mode and ownership, new and rotated logs are born compliant and the state does not drift back on the next rotation or reboot. Correct the creating mechanism first, then adjust any existing files.
1. Configure the log-creating mechanisms so new logs are created with restrictive access:
o For the general system and authentication logs written by rsyslog, set the file creation mode to 0640 or more restrictive (see the recommendation for configuring the rsyslog log file creation mode).
o systemd journal files are created mode 0640, group systemd-journal by systemd-journald; no change is required.
o For logs rotated by logrotate, use a create directive with the correct mode and ownership so rotated files retain the restrictive access (see the recommendation for configuring logrotate).
2. Correct existing files. For each file returned by the Audit, set its mode and ownership to match its class in the table. For a general system or authentication log that is more permissive than 0640, or not owned by root:root, run the following commands to restrict its access and set its ownership:
# chmod u-x,g-wx,o-rwx <file>
# chown root:root <file>
For the other classes, apply the corresponding values instead:
• Login accounting ( wtmp*, btmp*, lastlog*) - mode 0664 or more restrictive, group utmp.
• systemd journal ( *.journal, *.journal~) - group systemd-journal.
• Package-manager logs (files written by the system package manager, e.g.
/var/log/apt/, /var/log/dnf.*, /var/log/dnf5.log, /var/log/zypp/) - mode 0644 or more restrictive, group root or adm.
• Cloud or agent logs ( cloud-init.log*, localmessages*, waagent.log*) - mode 0644 or more restrictive.
• Service-account logs - keep that account as the owner and group; only remove world and any excess access. Do not force root ownership, as it can break the service that writes the log.
3. Re-run the Audit to confirm no files remain.
Note: Each class's ceiling matches the platform's default creation mode, so a file corrected to its class value stays compliant when the service or logrotate recreates it - provided the creating mechanism in step 1 is set correctly. Applying step 2 without step 1 may allow a sensitive log to be recreated world-readable on the next rotation.

check.check-content:
Log files under /var/log/ do not all share the same expected access: login- accounting, systemd journal, and package or cloud logs each have different owner, group, and mode requirements from the general system logs. The intent is to keep sensitive log data - the system and authentication logs - from being read or altered by unauthorized users, while accepting each platform's own default access for non- sensitive logs so that compliance stays stable across log rotation and reboot.
A file is compliant when its mode is the value shown (or more restrictive) and its owner and group are among those listed for its class:
Mode (or Log file(s) Owner Group more restrictive) General system logs - messages, syslog, root or secure*, auth.log, and any other /var/log root or adm 0640 syslog log not covered below root or Login accounting - wtmp*, btmp*, lastlog* root 0664 utmp root or systemd journal - *.journal, *.journal~ root systemd- 0640 journal Package-manager logs - files written by the system package manager: /var/log/apt/* (apt), /var/log/dnf.*, /var/log/dnf5.log, root root or adm 0644 /var/log/hawkey.log* (dnf/dnf5), /var/log/zypp/* and /var/log/zypper.log* (zypper), /var/log/yum.log* (legacy yum) Cloud or agent logs - cloud-init.log*, root or root or adm 0644 localmessages*, waagent.log* syslog that that Service-account logs - a log written by a account's account, dedicated service account (an account whose group, 0640 root, or login shell is not listed in /etc/shells) root, or syslog adm Run the following command to list every file under /var/log/ whose mode, owner, or group differs from the strictest baseline (mode 0640, owner root, group root); these are the files to compare against the table. The output columns are the file name, owner, group, and octal mode - matching the table order:
# find -L /var/log -type f \( -perm /0137 -o ! -user root -o ! -group root \)
-exec stat -Lc '%n %U %G %#a' {} +
For each file returned, find its class in the table and confirm its mode is the listed value (or more restrictive) and its owner and group are among those listed. Files that are not returned are already mode 0640 or more restrictive, owned by root, and group-owned by root, and need no further review.
Example output ( wtmp is returned because it is group utmp and mode 0664 - the expected access for the login-accounting class, so it is compliant; a general system log returned at 0644 would not be compliant, because it would be world-readable):
/var/log/wtmp root utmp 0664
Any returned file whose mode, owner, or group does not match its class does not meet this recommendation. Application logs stored outside /var/log/ should be held to the equivalent standard for their class.

Rule.title: Ensure auditd packages are installed
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>audit is the userspace component of the Linux Auditing System. It is responsible for writing audit records to disk.

Rationale:
The capturing of system events provides system administrators with information to allow them to determine if unauthorized access to their system is occurring.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to install audit and audit-libs:
# dnf install audit audit-libs

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that the audit and audit-libs packages are installed:
# rpm -q audit audit-libs
audit-<version>
audit-libs-<version>

Rule.title: Ensure auditing for processes that start prior to auditd is enabled
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The audit=1 kernel boot parameter enables the Linux Auditing System early in the boot process, before the auditd service starts.

Rationale:
Audit events need to be captured on processes that start up prior to auditd, so that potential malicious activity cannot go undetected.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to update the grub2 configuration with audit=1:
# grubby --update-kernel ALL --args 'audit=1'
Edit /etc/default/grub and add audit=1 to the GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX= line between the opening and closing double quotes:
Example:
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="quiet audit=1"
Note: audit=1 is a kernel boot parameter; the change takes effect on the next reboot.

check.check-content:
Both of the following must be true.
1. Run the following command to verify the audit=1 parameter is set in the running boot configuration:
# grubby --info=ALL | grep -Po '\baudit=1\b'
audit=1
audit=1 may be returned multiple times.
2. Run the following command to verify the audit=1 parameter is set in /etc/default/grub:
# grep -Psoi -- '^\h*GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="([^#\n\r]+\h+)?audit=1\b'
/etc/default/grub
Example output:
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="quiet audit=1"

Rule.title: Ensure audit_backlog_limit is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The audit_backlog_limit parameter determines how many audit records can be held in the audit backlog.

Rationale:
During boot if audit=1, then the backlog will hold 64 records. If more than 64 records are created during boot, audit records will be lost and potential malicious activity could go undetected.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to add audit_backlog_limit=<BACKLOG SIZE> to GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX:
# grubby --update-kernel ALL --args 'audit_backlog_limit=<BACKLOG SIZE>'
Example:
# grubby --update-kernel ALL --args 'audit_backlog_limit=8192'
Edit /etc/default/grub and add audit_backlog_limit=<BACKLOG SIZE> to the GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX= line between the opening and closing double quotes:
Example:
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="quiet audit_backlog_limit=8192"
Note: audit_backlog_limit is a kernel boot parameter; the change takes effect on the next reboot.

check.check-content:
Both of the following must be true.
1. Run the following command to verify the audit_backlog_limit= parameter is set to an appropriate size for your organization:
# grubby --info=ALL | grep -Po "\baudit_backlog_limit=\d+\b"
audit_backlog_limit=<BACKLOG SIZE>
It is recommended that this value be 8192 or larger.
2. Run the following command to verify the audit_backlog_limit= parameter is set in /etc/default/grub:
# grep -Psoi --
'^\h*GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="([^#\n\r]+\h+)?\baudit_backlog_limit=\d+\b'
/etc/default/grub
Example output:
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX="quiet audit_backlog_limit=8192"

Rule.title: Ensure auditd service is enabled and active
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The auditd service is the userspace daemon of the Linux Auditing System. When enabled and active it records system events to the audit log.

Rationale:
The capturing of system events provides system administrators with information to allow them to determine if unauthorized access to their system is occurring.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following commands to unmask, enable, and start auditd:
# systemctl unmask auditd
# systemctl enable auditd
# systemctl start auditd

check.check-content:
Both of the following must be true.
1. Run the following command to verify the auditd service is enabled:
# systemctl is-enabled auditd
enabled
2. Run the following command to verify the auditd service is active:
# systemctl is-active auditd
active

Rule.title: Ensure audit log storage size is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Configure the maximum size of the audit log file. Once the log reaches the maximum size, it will be rotated and a new log file will be started.

Rationale:
It is important that an appropriate size is determined for log files so that they do not impact the system and audit data is not lost.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Set the following parameter in /etc/audit/auditd.conf in accordance with site policy:
max_log_file = <MB>

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify the max_log_file parameter is configured in accordance with site policy:
# grep -Po -- '^\h*max_log_file\h*=\h*\d+\b' /etc/audit/auditd.conf
max_log_file = <MB>

Rule.title: Ensure audit logs are not automatically deleted
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The max_log_file_action setting determines how to handle the audit log file reaching the max file size. A value of keep_logs will rotate the logs but never delete old logs.

Rationale:
In high security contexts, the benefits of maintaining a long audit history exceed the cost of storing the audit history.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Set the following parameter in /etc/audit/auditd.conf:
max_log_file_action = keep_logs

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify the max_log_file_action parameter is set to keep_logs:
# grep -Pi -- '^\h*max_log_file_action\h*=\h*keep_logs\b'
/etc/audit/auditd.conf
max_log_file_action = keep_logs

Rule.title: Ensure system is disabled when audit logs are full
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The disk_full_action parameter sets the action auditd takes when the partition holding the audit log files has no free space. The disk_error_action parameter sets the action auditd takes when an error is detected on that partition.

Rationale:
In high security contexts, the risk of detecting unauthorized access or nonrepudiation exceeds the benefit of the system's availability.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Set one of the following parameters in /etc/audit/auditd.conf depending on your local security policies.
disk_full_action = <halt|single>
disk_error_action = <syslog|single|halt>
Example:
disk_full_action = halt
disk_error_action = halt

check.check-content:
Both of the following must be true.
1. Run the following command to verify disk_full_action is set to halt or single:
# grep -Pi -- '^\h*disk_full_action\h*=\h*(halt|single)\b'
/etc/audit/auditd.conf
disk_full_action = <halt|single>
2. Run the following command to verify disk_error_action is set to syslog, single, or halt:
# grep -Pi -- '^\h*disk_error_action\h*=\h*(syslog|single|halt)\b'
/etc/audit/auditd.conf
disk_error_action = <syslog|single|halt>

Rule.title: Ensure system warns when audit logs are low on space
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The space_left_action parameter sets the action auditd takes when free space on the partition holding the audit log files drops below the space_left threshold. The admin_space_left_action parameter sets the action auditd takes when free space drops below the lower admin_space_left threshold.

Rationale:
In high security contexts, the risk of detecting unauthorized access or nonrepudiation exceeds the benefit of the system's availability.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Set the space_left_action parameter in /etc/audit/auditd.conf to email, exec, single, or halt:
space_left_action = email
2. Set the admin_space_left_action parameter in /etc/audit/auditd.conf to single or halt:
admin_space_left_action = single
Note: A Mail Transfer Agent (MTA) must be installed and configured to use space_left_action = email.

check.check-content:
Both of the following must be true.
1. Run the following command to verify space_left_action is set to email, exec, single, or halt:
# grep -Pi -- '^\h*space_left_action\h*=\h*(email|exec|single|halt)\b'
/etc/audit/auditd.conf
space_left_action = email
2. Run the following command to verify admin_space_left_action is set to single or halt:
# grep -Pi -- '^\h*admin_space_left_action\h*=\h*(single|halt)\b'
/etc/audit/auditd.conf
admin_space_left_action = single

Rule.title: Ensure modification of the /etc/sudoers file is collected
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Monitor scope changes for system administrators. If the system has been properly configured to force system administrators to log in as themselves first and then use the sudo command to execute privileged commands, it is possible to monitor changes in scope. The file /etc/sudoers, or files in /etc/sudoers.d, will be written to when the file(s) or related attributes have changed. The audit records will be tagged with the identifier "scope".

Rationale:
Changes in the /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d files can indicate that an unauthorized change has been made to the scope of system administrator activity.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Add the audit rule(s) that monitor changes to /etc/sudoers and /etc/sudoers.d. The procedure adds each rule only for targets that exist, so augenrules --load does not error. Run:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
[ -e /etc/sudoers ] && printf '%s\n' "-a always,exit -S all -F
path=/etc/sudoers -F perm=wa -F key=scope"
[ -e /etc/sudoers.d ] && printf '%s\n' "-a always,exit -S all -F
dir=/etc/sudoers.d -F perm=wa -F key=scope"
} >> /etc/audit/rules.d/50-scope.rules
2. Merge and load the rules into active configuration:
# augenrules --load
3. Check if reboot is required:
# if [[ $(auditctl -s | grep "enabled") =~ "2" ]]; then printf "Reboot
required to load rules\n"; fi

check.check-content:
1. Run the following command to verify the rule(s) are present in a rules file:
# grep -Ps -- 'scope' /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules
Verify a watch rule covering each target below is present — in either the modern -F path= / -F dir= form shown (preferred) or the legacy -w <path> -p <perms> form;
both are a passing state:
-a always,exit -S all -F path=/etc/sudoers -F perm=wa -F key=scope
-a always,exit -S all -F dir=/etc/sudoers.d -F perm=wa -F key=scope
2. Run the following command to verify the rule(s) are loaded in the running configuration:
# auditctl -l | grep -Ps -- 'scope'
Verify the same watch rules are loaded (either form is accepted):
-a always,exit -S all -F path=/etc/sudoers -F perm=wa -F key=scope
-a always,exit -S all -F dir=/etc/sudoers.d -F perm=wa -F key=scope

Rule.title: Ensure actions as another user are always logged
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>sudo provides users with temporary elevated privileges to perform operations, either as the superuser or another user.

Rationale:
Creating an audit log of users with temporary elevated privileges and the operation(s) they performed is essential to reporting. Administrators will want to correlate the events written to the audit trail with the records written to sudo 's logfile to verify if unauthorized commands have been executed.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Add the audit rule(s) for the execve and execveat system calls. The procedure adds a rule for each audit ABI (b64/b32) the running kernel supports and skips any unsupported ABI or system call, so augenrules --load does not error.
Run:
for ARCH in b64 b32; do
CALLS=""; for C in execve execveat; do ausyscall "$ARCH" "$C" >/dev/null
2>&1 && CALLS="${CALLS:+$CALLS,}$C"; done
[ -n "$CALLS" ] && printf '%s\n' "-a always,exit -F arch=$ARCH -C
euid!=uid -F auid!=unset -S $CALLS -k user_emulation"
done >> /etc/audit/rules.d/50-user_emulation.rules
2. Merge and load the rules into active configuration:
# augenrules --load
3. Check if reboot is required:
# if [[ $(auditctl -s | grep "enabled") =~ "2" ]]; then printf "Reboot
required to load rules\n"; fi

check.check-content:
1. Run the following command to verify the rule(s) are present in a rules file:
# grep -Ps -- 'execve' /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules
Verify a rule equivalent to each line below is present:
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -C euid!=uid -F auid!=unset -S execve,execveat -k
user_emulation
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -C euid!=uid -F auid!=unset -S execve,execveat -k
user_emulation
2. Run the following command to verify the rule(s) are loaded in the running configuration:
# auditctl -l | grep -Ps -- 'execve'
Verify the same rules are loaded; auditctl -l displays them in the normalized form below:
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve,execveat -C uid!=euid -F auid!=-1 -F
key=user_emulation
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S execve,execveat -C uid!=euid -F auid!=-1 -F
key=user_emulation

Rule.title: Ensure events that modify the sudo log file are collected
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Monitor the sudo log file. If the system has been properly configured to disable the use of the su command and force all administrators to have to log in first and then use sudo to execute privileged commands, then all administrator commands will be logged to /var/log/sudo.log. Any time a command is executed, an audit event will be triggered as the /var/log/sudo.log file will be opened for write and the executed administration command will be written to the log.

Rationale:
Changes in /var/log/sudo.log indicate that an administrator has executed a command or the log file itself has been tampered with. Administrators will want to correlate the events written to the audit trail with the records written to /var/log/sudo.log to verify if unauthorized commands have been executed.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Edit the file /etc/sudoers or a file in /etc/sudoers.d/ with visudo -f <PATH TO FILE> and add the following line:
Defaults logfile="<PATH TO CUSTOM LOG FILE>"
Example:
Defaults logfile="/var/log/sudo.log"
2. Edit or create a file in the /etc/audit/rules.d/ directory, ending in.rules extension, with the relevant rules to monitor events that modify the sudo log file.
The rule is added only if the configured log file exists.
Example:
[ -e /var/log/sudo.log ] && printf '%s\n' "-a always,exit -S all -F
path=/var/log/sudo.log -F perm=wa -F key=sudo_log_file" >>
/etc/audit/rules.d/50-sudo.rules
3. Merge and load the rules into active configuration:
# augenrules --load
4. Check if reboot is required:
# if [[ $(auditctl -s | grep "enabled") =~ "2" ]]; then printf "Reboot
required to load rules\n"; fi

check.check-content:
1. Run the following command to verify that sudo has a custom log file configured:
# grep -rPsi
"^\\h*Defaults\\h+([^#]+,\\h*)?logfile\\h*=\\h*(\"|\')?\\H+(\"|\')?(,\\h*\\H+
\\h*)*\\h*(#.*)?$" /etc/sudoers*
Example output:
Defaults logfile="/var/log/sudo.log"
2. Run the following command to verify the rule is present in a rules file:
# grep -Ps -- 'sudo.log' /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules
Verify a watch rule covering the target below is present — in either the modern -F path= / -F dir= form shown (preferred) or the legacy -w <path> -p <perms> form;
both are a passing state:
-a always,exit -S all -F path=/var/log/sudo.log -F perm=wa -F
key=sudo_log_file
3. Run the following command to verify the rule is loaded in the running configuration:
# auditctl -l | grep -Ps -- 'sudo.log'
Verify the same watch rule is loaded (either form is accepted):
-a always,exit -S all -F path=/var/log/sudo.log -F perm=wa -F
key=sudo_log_file

Rule.title: Ensure events that modify date and time information are collected
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Capture events where the system date and/or time has been modified. The parameters in this section are set to determine if the;
• adjtimex - tune kernel clock
• settimeofday - set time using timeval and timezone structures
• clock_settime - allows for the setting of several internal clocks and timers system calls have been executed. Further, ensure to write an audit record to the configured audit log file upon exit, tagging the records with a unique identifier such as "time-change".

Rationale:
Unexpected changes in system date and/or time could be a sign of malicious activity on the system.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Add the audit rule(s) for the adjtimex, settimeofday, and clock_settime system calls and changes to /etc/localtime. The procedure adds a rule for each audit ABI (b64/b32) the running kernel supports, skips any unsupported ABI or system call, and adds the watch only when its target exists, so augenrules - -load does not error. Run:
for ARCH in b64 b32; do
CALLS=""; for C in adjtimex settimeofday; do ausyscall "$ARCH" "$C"
>/dev/null 2>&1 && CALLS="${CALLS:+$CALLS,}$C"; done
[ -n "$CALLS" ] && printf '%s\n' "-a always,exit -F arch=$ARCH -S $CALLS -
k time-change"
CALLS=""; for C in clock_settime; do ausyscall "$ARCH" "$C" >/dev/null
2>&1 && CALLS="${CALLS:+$CALLS,}$C"; done
[ -n "$CALLS" ] && printf '%s\n' "-a always,exit -F arch=$ARCH -S $CALLS -
F a0=0x0 -k time-change"
done >> /etc/audit/rules.d/50-time-change.rules
[ -e /etc/localtime ] && printf '%s\n' "-a always,exit -S all -F
path=/etc/localtime -F perm=wa -F key=time-change" >> /etc/audit/rules.d/50-
time-change.rules
2. Merge and load the rules into active configuration:
# augenrules --load
3. Check if reboot is required:
# if [[ $(auditctl -s | grep "enabled") =~ "2" ]]; then printf "Reboot
required to load rules\n"; fi

check.check-content:
1. Run the following command to verify the rule(s) are present in a rules file:
# grep -Ps -- '(adjtimex|settimeofday|clock_settime|/etc/localtime)'
/etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules
Verify a rule equivalent to each line below is present:
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S adjtimex,settimeofday -k time-change
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S adjtimex,settimeofday -k time-change
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S clock_settime -F a0=0x0 -k time-change
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S clock_settime -F a0=0x0 -k time-change
-a always,exit -S all -F path=/etc/localtime -F perm=wa -k time-change
The /etc/localtime watch (last line) may be written in either the modern -F path= form shown or the legacy -w /etc/localtime -p wa form; both are a passing state (the system-call rules above have no -w equivalent).
2. Run the following command to verify the rule(s) are loaded in the running configuration:
# auditctl -l | grep -Ps --
'(adjtimex|settimeofday|clock_settime|/etc/localtime)'
Verify the same rules are loaded; auditctl -l displays them in the normalized form below:
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S adjtimex,settimeofday -F key=time-change
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S adjtimex,settimeofday -F key=time-change
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S clock_settime -F a0=0x0 -F key=time-change
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S clock_settime -F a0=0x0 -F key=time-change
-a always,exit -S all -F path=/etc/localtime -F perm=wa -F key=time-change

Rule.title: Ensure events that modify sethostname and setdomainname are collected
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Record changes to network environment files or system calls. The below parameters monitors the following system calls, and write an audit event on system call exit:
• sethostname - set the systems host name
• setdomainname - set the systems domain name

Rationale:
Monitoring sethostname and setdomainname will identify potential unauthorized changes to host and domain name of a system. The changing of these names could potentially break security parameters that are set based on those names.</VulnDiscussion>

{
for ARCH in b64 b32; do
CALLS=""; for C in sethostname setdomainname; do ausyscall "$ARCH" "$C"
>/dev/null 2>&1 && CALLS="${CALLS:+$CALLS,}$C"; done
[ -n "$CALLS" ] && printf '%s\n' "-a always,exit -F arch=$ARCH -S
$CALLS -k system-locale"
done >> /etc/audit/rules.d/50-system_locale.rules
}
2. Merge and load the rules into active configuration:
# augenrules --load
3. Check if reboot is required:
# if [[ $(auditctl -s | grep "enabled") =~ "2" ]]; then printf "Reboot
required to load rules\n"; fi

Rule.title: Ensure use of privileged commands are collected
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Monitor privileged programs, those that have the setuid and/or setgid bit set on execution, to determine if unprivileged users are running these commands.

Rationale:
Execution of privileged commands by non-privileged users could be an indication of someone trying to gain unauthorized access to the system.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit or create a file in the /etc/audit/rules.d/ directory, ending in.rules extension, with the relevant rules to monitor the use of privileged commands.
Example script:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
UID_MIN=$(awk '/^\s*UID_MIN/{print $2}' /etc/login.defs)
AUDIT_RULE_FILE="/etc/audit/rules.d/50-privileged.rules"
# Emit a rule only for the audit ABIs the running kernel supports
ARCHES=""; for ARCH in b64 b32; do ausyscall "$ARCH" execve >/dev/null 2>&1
&& ARCHES="${ARCHES:+$ARCHES }$ARCH"; done
NEW_DATA=()
for PARTITION in $(findmnt -n -l -k -it $(awk '/nodev/ { print $2 }'
/proc/filesystems | paste -sd,) | grep -Pv "noexec|nosuid" | awk '{print
$1}'); do
while IFS= read -r FILE; do
for ARCH in $ARCHES; do
NEW_DATA+=("-a always,exit -F arch=$ARCH -S all -F path=${FILE} -F
perm=x -F auid>=${UID_MIN} -F auid!=unset -k privileged")
done
done < <(find "${PARTITION}" -xdev \( -path "*/containers/storage/*" -o -
path "*/containerd/*" -o -path "*/kubelet/*" -o -path "/snap/*" \) -prune -o
-perm /6000 -type f -print)
done
readarray &> /dev/null -t OLD_DATA < "${AUDIT_RULE_FILE}"
COMBINED_DATA=( "${OLD_DATA[@]}" "${NEW_DATA[@]}" )
printf '%s\n' "${COMBINED_DATA[@]}" | sort -u > "${AUDIT_RULE_FILE}"
}
Merge and load the rules into active configuration:
# augenrules --load
Check if reboot is required.
# if [[ $(auditctl -s | grep "enabled") =~ "2" ]]; then printf "Reboot
required to load rules\n"; fi
Special mount points If there are any special mount points that are not visible by default from just scanning /, change the PARTITION variable to the appropriate partition and re-run the remediation.
Excluded paths. noexec / nosuid mounts, and the ephemeral container/snap layer paths pruned above ( */containers/storage/*, */containerd/*, */kubelet/*, /snap/*), are intentionally out of scope: those setuid files live in versioned/overlay paths that churn and execute inside container namespaces, so a host -F path= rule cannot usefully audit them. The recommendation targets unprivileged use of host privileged commands.

check.check-content:
Privileged programs are those with the setuid and/or setgid bit set on execution. For each such program on a device-backed filesystem (excluding noexec / nosuid mounts and the ephemeral container/snap paths noted below), verify an auditd rule records its execution by unprivileged users, both on disk and in the running configuration.
On disk configuration Run the following script. Nothing should be returned (any output names a privileged program lacking a compliant on-disk rule):
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
UID_MIN="$(awk '/^\s*UID_MIN/{print $2}' /etc/login.defs)"
for PARTITION in $(findmnt -n -l -k -it $(awk '/nodev/ { print $2 }'
/proc/filesystems | paste -sd,) | grep -Pv "noexec|nosuid" | awk '{print
$1}'); do
while IFS= read -r FILE; do
ok=""
while IFS= read -r L; do
grep -Pq -- '-a\s+(always,exit|exit,always)' <<< "$L" \
&& grep -Pq -- '-F\s+perm=x' <<< "$L" \
&& grep -Pq -- "-F\s+auid>=${UID_MIN}" <<< "$L" \
&& grep -Pq -- '-F\s+auid!=(unset|-1|4294967295)' <<< "$L" &&
ok="Y"
done < <(grep -h -- "path=${FILE}" /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules
2>/dev/null)
[ -z "$ok" ] && printf 'MISSING or incomplete on-disk rule: %s\n'
"$FILE"
done < <(find "${PARTITION}" -xdev \( -path "*/containers/storage/*" -o
-path "*/containerd/*" -o -path "*/kubelet/*" -o -path "/snap/*" \) -prune -o
-perm /6000 -type f -print)
done
}
Running configuration Run the following script. Nothing should be returned (any output names a privileged program not covered by a loaded rule):
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
UID_MIN="$(awk '/^\s*UID_MIN/{print $2}' /etc/login.defs)"
RUNNING="$(auditctl -l)"
for PARTITION in $(findmnt -n -l -k -it $(awk '/nodev/ { print $2 }'
/proc/filesystems | paste -sd,) | grep -Pv "noexec|nosuid" | awk '{print
$1}'); do
while IFS= read -r FILE; do
ok=""
while IFS= read -r L; do
grep -Pq -- '-a\s+(always,exit|exit,always)' <<< "$L" \
&& grep -Pq -- '-F\s+perm=x' <<< "$L" \
&& grep -Pq -- "-F\s+auid>=${UID_MIN}" <<< "$L" \
&& grep -Pq -- '-F\s+auid!=(unset|-1|4294967295)' <<< "$L" &&
ok="Y"
done < <(printf '%s\n' "$RUNNING" | grep -- "path=${FILE}")
[ -z "$ok" ] && printf 'MISSING or incomplete loaded rule: %s\n'
"$FILE"
done < <(find "${PARTITION}" -xdev \( -path "*/containers/storage/*" -o
-path "*/containerd/*" -o -path "*/kubelet/*" -o -path "/snap/*" \) -prune -o
-perm /6000 -type f -print)
done
}
The running configuration normalizes some fields (for example -F auid!=unset is shown as -F auid!=-1, and -k key as -F key=key); the checks above accept these equivalent forms.
Excluded paths. noexec / nosuid mounts confer no execution or privilege and are out of scope. Ephemeral, runtime-managed container and snap layer paths ( */containers/storage/*, */containerd/*, */kubelet/*, /snap/*) are also excluded: their setuid files live in versioned/overlay paths that churn and execute inside container namespaces, so a host -F path= rule cannot usefully audit them. The control targets unprivileged use of host privileged commands.

Rule.title: Ensure unsuccessful file access attempts are collected
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Monitor for unsuccessful attempts to access files. The following parameters are associated with system calls that control files:
• creation - creat
• opening - open, openat
• truncation - truncate, ftruncate An audit log record will only be written if all of the following criteria is met for the user when trying to access a file:
• a non-privileged user ( auid>=UID_MIN)
• is not a Daemon event ( auid=4294967295/unset/-1)
• if the system call returned EACCES (permission denied) or EPERM (some other permanent error associated with the specific system call)

Rationale:
Failed attempts to open, create or truncate files could be an indication that an individual or process is trying to gain unauthorized access to the system.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Add the audit rule(s) for the creat, open, openat, truncate, and ftruncate system calls. The procedure adds a rule for each audit ABI (b64/b32) the running kernel supports and skips any unsupported ABI or system call, so augenrules - -load does not error. Run:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
UID_MIN="$(awk '/^[[:space:]]*UID_MIN/{print $2}' /etc/login.defs)"
for ARCH in b64 b32; do
CALLS=""; for C in creat open openat truncate ftruncate; do ausyscall
"$ARCH" "$C" >/dev/null 2>&1 && CALLS="${CALLS:+$CALLS,}$C"; done
[ -n "$CALLS" ] && printf '%s\n' "-a always,exit -F arch=$ARCH -S
$CALLS -F exit=-EACCES -F auid>=$UID_MIN -F auid!=unset -k access"
[ -n "$CALLS" ] && printf '%s\n' "-a always,exit -F arch=$ARCH -S
$CALLS -F exit=-EPERM -F auid>=$UID_MIN -F auid!=unset -k access"
done >> /etc/audit/rules.d/50-access.rules
}
2. Merge and load the rules into active configuration:
# augenrules --load
3. Check if reboot is required:
# if [[ $(auditctl -s | grep "enabled") =~ "2" ]]; then printf "Reboot
required to load rules\n"; fi

check.check-content:
1. Run the following command to verify the rule(s) are present in a rules file:
# grep -Ps -- '(EACCES|EPERM)' /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules
Verify a rule equivalent to each line below is present, one per audit ABI the kernel supports:
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S creat,open,openat,truncate,ftruncate -F exit=-
EACCES -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k access
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S creat,open,openat,truncate,ftruncate -F exit=-
EACCES -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k access
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S creat,open,openat,truncate,ftruncate -F exit=-
EPERM -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k access
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S creat,open,openat,truncate,ftruncate -F exit=-
EPERM -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=unset -k access
2. Run the following command to verify the rule(s) are loaded in the running configuration:
# auditctl -l | grep -Ps -- '(EACCES|EPERM)'
Verify the same rules are loaded; auditctl -l displays them in the normalized form below:
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S creat,open,openat,truncate,ftruncate -F exit=-
EACCES -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -F key=access
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S creat,open,openat,truncate,ftruncate -F exit=-
EACCES -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -F key=access
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S creat,open,openat,truncate,ftruncate -F exit=-
EPERM -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1 -F key=access
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S creat,open,openat,truncate,ftruncate -F exit=-

Rule.title: Ensure discretionary access control permission modification events chmod,fchmod,fchmodat are collected
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Monitor changes to file permissions, attributes, ownership and group. The parameters in this section track changes for system calls that affect file permissions and attributes.
The following commands and system calls effect the permissions, ownership and various attributes of files.
• chmod: changes the mode of the file
• fchmod: changes the mode of the file referred to by the open file descriptor
• fchmodat: change permissions of a file In all cases, an audit record will only be written for non-system user ids and will ignore Daemon events. All audit records will be tagged with the identifier "perm_mod."

Rationale:
Monitoring for changes in file attributes could alert a system administrator to activity that could indicate intruder activity or policy violation.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Add the audit rule(s) for the chmod, fchmod, and fchmodat system calls. The procedure adds a rule for each audit ABI (b64/b32) the running kernel supports and skips any unsupported ABI or system call, so augenrules --load does not error. Run:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
UID_MIN="$(awk '/^[[:space:]]*UID_MIN/{print $2}' /etc/login.defs)"
for ARCH in b64 b32; do
CALLS=""; for C in chmod fchmod fchmodat; do ausyscall "$ARCH" "$C"
>/dev/null 2>&1 && CALLS="${CALLS:+$CALLS,}$C"; done
[ -n "$CALLS" ] && printf '%s\n' "-a always,exit -F arch=$ARCH -S
$CALLS -F auid>=$UID_MIN -F auid!=unset -F key=perm_mod"
done >> /etc/audit/rules.d/50-perm_mod.rules
}
2. Merge and load the rules into active configuration:
# augenrules --load
3. Check if reboot is required:
# if [[ $(auditctl -s | grep "enabled") =~ "2" ]]; then printf "Reboot
required to load rules\n"; fi

1. Run the following command to verify the rule(s) are present in a rules file:
# grep -Ps -- 'chmod' /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules
Verify a rule equivalent to each line below is present:
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S chmod,fchmod,fchmodat -F auid>=1000 -F
auid!=unset -F key=perm_mod
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S chmod,fchmod,fchmodat -F auid>=1000 -F
auid!=unset -F key=perm_mod
2. Run the following command to verify the rule(s) are loaded in the running configuration:
# auditctl -l | grep -Ps -- 'chmod'
Verify the same rules are loaded; auditctl -l displays them in the normalized form below:
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S chmod,fchmod,fchmodat -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1
-F key=perm_mod
-a always,exit -F arch=b32 -S chmod,fchmod,fchmodat -F auid>=1000 -F auid!=-1
-F key=perm_mod

Rule.title: Ensure successful file system mounts are collected
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Monitor the use of the mount system call. The mount (and umount) system call controls the mounting and unmounting of file systems. The parameters below configure the system to create an audit record when the mount system call is used by a non- privileged user

Rationale:
It is highly unusual for a non privileged user to mount file systems to the system. While tracking mount commands gives the system administrator evidence that external media may have been mounted (based on a review of the source of the mount and confirming it's an external media type), it does not conclusively indicate that data was exported to the media. System administrators who wish to determine if data were exported, would also have to track successful open, creat and truncate system calls requiring write access to a file under the mount point of the external media file system. This could give a fair indication that a write occurred. The only way to truly prove it, would be to track successful writes to the external media. Tracking write system calls could quickly fill up the audit log and is not recommended. Recommendations on configuration options to track data export to media is beyond the scope of this document.</VulnDiscussion>

# grep -Ph -- '^\h*-e\h+2\b' /etc/audit/rules.d/*.rules | tail -1
-e 2
2. Run the following command to check whether the immutable flag is active in the running configuration:
# auditctl -s | grep 'enabled'
enabled 2
A running value of enabled 2 confirms the configuration is currently immutable. If step 1 returns -e 2 but this returns enabled 1, the immutable flag is configured on disk but not yet active in the running kernel; it takes effect when the audit rules are reloaded at the next reboot. This is expected immediately after applying the audit rules (immutability is finalized on reboot so that rule changes are not locked out mid-configuration) and is not, on its own, a finding.

Rule.title: Ensure the running and on disk configuration is the same
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The Audit system have both on disk and running configuration. It is possible for these configuration settings to differ.
Note: Due to the limitations of augenrules and auditctl, it is not absolutely guaranteed that loading the rule sets via augenrules --load will result in all rules being loaded or even that the user will be informed if there was a problem loading the rules.

Rationale:
Configuration differences between what is currently running and what is on disk could cause unexpected problems or may give a false impression of compliance requirements.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
If the rules are not aligned across all three areas (the *.rules files in /etc/audit/rules.d/, the merged /etc/audit/audit.rules, and the running kernel configuration), run the following command to merge and load all rules:
# augenrules --load
Check if reboot is required.
if [[ $(auditctl -s | grep "enabled") =~ "2" ]]; then echo "Reboot required
to load rules"; fi

check.check-content:
Merged rule sets Ensure that all rules in /etc/audit/rules.d have been merged into /etc/audit/audit.rules:
# augenrules --check
/usr/sbin/augenrules: No change
Should there be any drift, run augenrules --load to merge and load all rules.

Rule.title: Ensure the audit log file directory mode is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The audit log directory contains audit log files.

Rationale:
Audit information includes all information including: audit records, audit settings and audit reports. This information is needed to successfully audit system activity. This information must be protected from unauthorized modification or deletion. If this information were to be compromised, forensic analysis and discovery of the true source of potentially malicious system activity is impossible to achieve.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to configure the audit log directory to have a mode of "0750" or more restrictive:
# chmod g-w,o-rwx "$(dirname "$(awk -F= '/^\s*log_file\s*/{print $2}'
/etc/audit/auditd.conf | xargs)")"

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify the audit log file directory is mode 0750 or more restrictive:
# stat -Lc '%n %a' "$(dirname "$(awk -F= '/^\s*log_file\s*/{print $2}'
/etc/audit/auditd.conf | xargs)")"
Example output:
/var/log/audit 750
The mode should be 0750 or more restrictive (no write access for group and no access for other).

Rule.title: Ensure audit log files mode is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Audit log files contain information about the system and system activity.

Rationale:
Access to audit records can reveal system and configuration data to attackers, potentially compromising its confidentiality.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to remove more permissive mode than 0640 from audit log files:
# [ -f /etc/audit/auditd.conf ] && find "$(dirname $(awk -F "="
'/^\s*log_file/ {print $2}' /etc/audit/auditd.conf | xargs))" -type f -perm
/0137 -exec chmod u-x,g-wx,o-rwx {} +

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify all audit log files are mode 0640 or more restrictive:
# [ -f /etc/audit/auditd.conf ] && find "$(dirname "$(awk -F=
'/^\s*log_file\s*/{print $2}' /etc/audit/auditd.conf | xargs)")" -maxdepth 1
-type f -perm /0137
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure audit log files owner is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Audit log files contain information about the system and system activity.

Rationale:
Access to audit records can reveal system and configuration data to attackers, potentially compromising its confidentiality.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to configure the audit log files to be owned by the root user:
# [ -f /etc/audit/auditd.conf ] && find "$(dirname $(awk -F "="
'/^\s*log_file/ {print $2}' /etc/audit/auditd.conf | xargs))" -type f ! -user
root -exec chown root {} +

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify all audit log files are owned by the root user:
# [ -f /etc/audit/auditd.conf ] && find "$(dirname "$(awk -F=
'/^\s*log_file\s*/{print $2}' /etc/audit/auditd.conf | xargs)")" -maxdepth 1
-type f ! -user root
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure audit log files group owner is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Audit log files contain information about the system and system activity.

Rationale:
Access to audit records can reveal system and configuration data to attackers, potentially compromising its confidentiality.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Run the following command to configure the audit log files to be owned by adm group:
# find $(dirname $(awk -F"=" '/^\s*log_file\s*=\s*/ {print $2}'
/etc/audit/auditd.conf | xargs)) -type f \( ! -group adm -a ! -group root \)
-exec chgrp adm {} +
2. Run the following command to set the log_group parameter in the audit configuration file to log_group = adm:
# sed -ri 's/^\s*#?\s*log_group\s*=\s*\S+(\s*#.*)?.*$/log_group = adm\1/'
/etc/audit/auditd.conf
3. Run the following command to restart the audit daemon to reload the configuration file:
# service auditd restart
Note: If the audit log file directory is not configured ( log_file is unset in /etc/audit/auditd.conf), set a valid log_file location before applying the steps above.

check.check-content:
Both of the following must be true.
1. Run the following command to verify the log_group parameter is set to root or adm:
# grep -Po '^\s*log_group\s*=\s*\K\S+' /etc/audit/auditd.conf
The returned value should be root or adm.
2. Run the following command to verify all audit log files are group-owned by root or adm:
# [ -f /etc/audit/auditd.conf ] && find "$(dirname "$(awk -F=
'/^\s*log_file\s*/{print $2}' /etc/audit/auditd.conf | xargs)")" -maxdepth 1
-type f \( ! -group root -a ! -group adm \)
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure audit configuration files mode is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Audit configuration files control auditd and what events are audited.

Rationale:
Access to the audit configuration files could allow unauthorized personnel to prevent the auditing of critical events.
Misconfigured audit configuration files may prevent the auditing of critical events or impact the system's performance by overwhelming the audit log. Misconfiguration of the audit configuration files may also make it more difficult to establish and investigate events relating to an incident.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to remove more permissive mode than 0640 from the audit configuration files:
# find /etc/audit/ -type f \( -name '*.conf' -o -name '*.rules' \) -exec
chmod u-x,g-wx,o-rwx {} +

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify all audit configuration files are mode 0640 or more restrictive:
# find /etc/audit/ -type f \( -name '*.conf' -o -name '*.rules' \) -perm
/0137
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure audit configuration files owner is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Audit configuration files control auditd and what events are audited.

Rationale:
Access to the audit configuration files could allow unauthorized personnel to prevent the auditing of critical events.
Misconfigured audit configuration files may prevent the auditing of critical events or impact the system's performance by overwhelming the audit log. Misconfiguration of the audit configuration files may also make it more difficult to establish and investigate events relating to an incident.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to change ownership to root user:
# find /etc/audit/ -type f \( -name '*.conf' -o -name '*.rules' \) ! -user
root -exec chown root {} +

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify all audit configuration files are owned by the root user:
# find /etc/audit/ -type f \( -name '*.conf' -o -name '*.rules' \) ! -user
root
Nothing should be returned.

Run the following command to change group to root:
# find /etc/audit/ -type f \( -name '*.conf' -o -name '*.rules' \) ! -group
root -exec chgrp root {} +

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify all audit configuration files are group-owned by the root group:
# find /etc/audit/ -type f \( -name '*.conf' -o -name '*.rules' \) ! -group
root
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure audit tools mode is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Audit tools include, but are not limited to, vendor-provided and open source audit tools needed to successfully view and manipulate audit information system activity and records. Audit tools include custom queries and report generators.

Rationale:
Protecting audit information includes identifying and protecting the tools used to view and manipulate log data. Protecting audit tools is necessary to prevent unauthorized operation on audit information.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to remove more permissive mode from the audit tools:
# chmod go-w /sbin/auditctl /sbin/aureport /sbin/ausearch /sbin/autrace
/sbin/auditd /sbin/augenrules

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify all audit tools are mode 0755 or more restrictive:
# stat -Lc '%n %a' /sbin/auditctl /sbin/aureport /sbin/ausearch /sbin/autrace
/sbin/auditd /sbin/augenrules
Example output:
/sbin/auditctl 755
/sbin/aureport 755
/sbin/ausearch 755
/sbin/autrace 755
/sbin/auditd 755
/sbin/augenrules 755
Each audit tool should be mode 0755 or more restrictive (no write access for group or other).

Rule.title: Ensure audit tools owner is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Audit tools include, but are not limited to, vendor-provided and open source audit tools needed to successfully view and manipulate audit information system activity and records. Audit tools include custom queries and report generators.

Rationale:
Protecting audit information includes identifying and protecting the tools used to view and manipulate log data. Protecting audit tools is necessary to prevent unauthorized operation on audit information.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to change the owner of the audit tools to the root user:
# chown root /sbin/auditctl /sbin/aureport /sbin/ausearch /sbin/autrace
/sbin/auditd /sbin/augenrules

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify all audit tools are owned by the root user:
# stat -Lc "%n %U" /sbin/auditctl /sbin/aureport /sbin/ausearch /sbin/autrace
/sbin/auditd /sbin/augenrules | awk '$2 != "root" {print}'
Nothing should be returned.

Rule.title: Ensure audit tools group owner is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Audit tools include, but are not limited to, vendor-provided and open source audit tools needed to successfully view and manipulate audit information system activity and records. Audit tools include custom queries and report generators.

Rationale:
Protecting audit information includes identifying and protecting the tools used to view and manipulate log data. Protecting audit tools is necessary to prevent unauthorized operation on audit information.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to change group ownership to the group root:
# chgrp root /sbin/auditctl /sbin/aureport /sbin/ausearch /sbin/autrace
/sbin/auditd /sbin/augenrules

/sbin/auditd /sbin/augenrules | awk '$2 != "root" {print}'
