Rule.title: Ensure AIDE is installed
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment (AIDE) is a intrusion detection tool that uses predefined rules to check the integrity of files and directories in the Linux operating system. AIDE has its own database to check the integrity of files and directories.
aide takes a snapshot of files and directories including modification times, permissions, and file hashes which can then be used to compare against the current state of the filesystem to detect modifications to the system.

Rationale:
By monitoring the filesystem state compromised files can be detected to prevent or limit the exposure of accidental or malicious misconfigurations or modified binaries.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Run the following command to install aide:
# dnf install aide
2. Configure aide as appropriate for your environment. Consult the aide documentation for options.
3. Run the following command to Initialize aide:
# aide --init
4. Run the following command to create a baseline copy of the AIDE database:
# mv /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new.gz /var/lib/aide/aide.db.gz

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify the aide package is installed:
# rpm -q aide
aide-<version>

Rule.title: Ensure filesystem integrity is regularly checked
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Periodic checking of filesystem integrity detects unauthorized changes to files. AIDE (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment) compares the current state of the filesystem against a previously initialized baseline database; this recommendation ensures that comparison runs automatically on a regular schedule rather than only on demand.

Rationale:
Periodic file checking allows the system administrator to determine on a regular basis if critical files have been changed in an unauthorized fashion. Running the integrity check on a defined schedule -- rather than manually or ad hoc -- ensures changes are detected consistently and reduces the window in which unauthorized modifications can go unnoticed.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Configure a systemd timer to run a periodic AIDE integrity check.
1. Create the file /etc/systemd/system/aidecheck.service with the following content:
[Unit]
Description=Aide Check
[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/sbin/aide --check
2. Create the file /etc/systemd/system/aidecheck.timer with the following content:
[Unit]
Description=Aide check every day at 5AM
[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* 05:00:00
Persistent=true
Unit=aidecheck.service
[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
3. Run the following commands to set access on the unit files, reload systemd, and enable the timer:
# chown root:root /etc/systemd/system/aidecheck.service
/etc/systemd/system/aidecheck.timer
# chmod 0644 /etc/systemd/system/aidecheck.service
/etc/systemd/system/aidecheck.timer
# systemctl daemon-reload
# systemctl enable --now aidecheck.timer

check.check-content:
A periodic AIDE integrity check should be scheduled through cron or an enabled or active systemd timer. At least one of the following should return a matching entry.
1. Run the following command to list cron-scheduled AIDE checks:
# grep -rEi 'aide[[:space:]]+(--check|--update)' /var/spool/cron/
/etc/crontab /etc/cron.d /etc/cron.hourly /etc/cron.daily /etc/cron.weekly
/etc/cron.monthly 2>/dev/null
Example output:
/etc/cron.d/aidecheck:0 5 * * * root /usr/sbin/aide --check
2. Run the following command to list enabled or active systemd timers that run AIDE:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
for t in $(systemctl list-unit-files --type=timer --no-legend | awk
'{print $1}'); do
en="$(systemctl is-enabled "$t" 2>/dev/null)"; ac="$(systemctl is-
active "$t" 2>/dev/null)"
[ "$en" = "enabled" ] || [ "$ac" = "active" ] || continue
s="$(systemctl show -p Unit --value "$t")"; [ -z "$s" ] &&
s="${t%.timer}.service"
systemctl cat "$s" 2>/dev/null | grep -Eq
'ExecStart=.*aide[[:space:]]+(--check|--update)' && echo "$t -> $s"
done
}
Example output:
aidecheck.timer -> aidecheck.service
At least one of the two commands above should return a matching entry, confirming that a periodic AIDE integrity check is scheduled (via cron or a systemd timer).

Rule.title: Ensure cryptographic mechanisms are used to protect the integrity of audit tools
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Audit tools include the vendor-provided and open-source utilities used to view and manipulate audit records and settings (for example auditctl, auditd, ausearch, aureport, autrace, and augenrules, along with custom queries and report generators). This recommendation uses AIDE (Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment) to protect the integrity of those tools by recording cryptographic hashes and file attributes, so that modification or replacement of a tool can be detected.

Rationale:
Protecting the integrity of the tools used for auditing purposes is a critical step toward ensuring the integrity of audit information. Audit information includes all information (e.g., audit records, audit settings, and audit reports) needed to successfully audit information system activity.
Attackers may replace the audit tools or inject code into the existing tools with the purpose of providing the capability to hide or erase system activity from the audit logs.
Audit tools should be cryptographically signed in order to provide the capability to identify when the audit tools have been modified, manipulated, or replaced. An example is a checksum hash of the file or files.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. Run the following command to determine the absolute path to the non-symlinked version on the audit tools:
# readlink -f /sbin
The output will be either /usr/sbin - OR - /sbin. Ensure the correct path is used.
2. Edit /etc/aide.conf and add or update the following selection lines replacing <PATH> with the correct path returned in the command above:
# Audit Tools
<PATH>/auditctl p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512
<PATH>/auditd p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512
<PATH>/ausearch p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512
<PATH>/aureport p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512
<PATH>/autrace p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512
<PATH>/augenrules p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512
Example
# printf '\n%s' "# Audit Tools" "$(readlink -f /sbin/auditctl)
p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512" "$(readlink -f /sbin/auditd)
p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512" "$(readlink -f /sbin/ausearch)
p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512" "$(readlink -f /sbin/aureport)
p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512" "$(readlink -f /sbin/autrace)
p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512" "$(readlink -f /sbin/augenrules)
p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512" >> /etc/aide.conf
Note: - IF - /etc/aide.conf includes a @@x_include statement:
Example:
@@x_include /etc/aide.conf.d ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+$
• @@x_include FILE
• @@x_include DIRECTORY REGEX
o @x_include is identical to @@include, except that if a config file is executable it is run and the output is used as config.
o If the executable file exits with status greater than zero or writes to stderr aide stops with an error.
o For security reasons DIRECTORY and each executable config file must be owned by the current user and must not be group or world-writable.

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that AIDE is configured to monitor the integrity of the audit tools:
# grep -E '/(auditctl|auditd|ausearch|aureport|autrace|augenrules)\b'
/etc/aide.conf
Each of the six audit tools -- auditctl, auditd, ausearch, aureport, autrace, augenrules (at their absolute path, typically under /usr/sbin) -- should have a selection line applying at least the attributes p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512 (directly or via an equivalent rule group).
Example output:
/usr/sbin/auditctl p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512
/usr/sbin/auditd p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512
/usr/sbin/ausearch p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512
/usr/sbin/aureport p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512
/usr/sbin/autrace p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512
/usr/sbin/augenrules p+i+n+u+g+s+b+acl+xattrs+sha512
Note: If /etc/aide.conf uses an @@x_include statement, also check the included configuration files.

Rule.title: Ensure report_url is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The report_url directive in aide.conf names the destination(s) to which AIDE writes each integrity check's report. It accepts multiple destinations and supports a syslog:<facility> target - where <facility> is a syslog facility, such as one of LOG_LOCAL0 through LOG_LOCAL7 - that sends the report to the system log rather than, or in addition to, a local file. AIDE has no built-in mail transport; syslog is its native mechanism for directing the report to the system logging service.

Rationale:
A scheduled integrity check is only useful if its findings reach a monitored location.
When the report is written only to a local file - or to standard output that the scheduling job discards - an unauthorized addition, modification, or deletion of a critical system file or audit tool can be recorded where no one is watching, and on the same host an attacker may be able to alter or delete it. Writing the report to the system log routes integrity findings into the centrally collected, retained, and access-controlled log stream, so discrepancies are preserved off the checked file's local context and are available for review and alerting.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Edit /etc/aide.conf and add a report_url directive that writes the check report to the system log, using a syslog facility that the system logging service is configured to collect (the local-use facilities LOG_LOCAL0 through LOG_LOCAL7 are commonly used for this):
report_url=syslog:<facility>
Example:
report_url=syslog:LOG_LOCAL0
AIDE supports multiple report_url destinations, so an existing destination (such as report_url=file:/var/log/aide.log) may be kept alongside the syslog entry.
Ensure the system logging service is configured to collect and retain the selected facility (see the logging recommendations) so the report is captured in the central log stream.

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that AIDE writes its integrity-check report to the system log. Review the effective aide.conf, including any files pulled in by @@include or @@x_include directives:
# grep -P '^\h*report_url' /etc/aide.conf
A report_url directive sending the report to syslog should be returned, for example:
Example output:
report_url=syslog:LOG_LOCAL0
Additional report_url destinations (such as report_url=file:/var/log/aide.log) may also be present; at least one syslog: destination should be configured. If nothing is returned, or report_url resolves only to a non-logging destination, AIDE is not sending its report to the system log.

Group.title: 7.1 Configure system file and directory access

Rule.title: Ensure access to /etc/passwd is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The /etc/passwd file contains user account information that is used by many system utilities and therefore must be readable for these utilities to operate.

Rationale:
It is critical to ensure that the /etc/passwd file is protected from unauthorized write access. Although it is protected by default, the file permissions could be changed either inadvertently or through malicious actions.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following commands to remove excess permissions, set owner, and set group on /etc/passwd:
# chmod u-x,go-wx /etc/passwd
# chown root:root /etc/passwd

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that access to /etc/passwd is configured (mode 0644 or more restrictive, owned by root:root):
# stat -Lc 'Access: (%#a/%A) Uid: ( %u/ %U) Gid: ( %g/ %G)' /etc/passwd
The following should be returned:
Access: (0644/-rw-r--r--) Uid: (0/root) Gid: (0/root)

%g/ %G)' /etc/passwd-

Access: (0644/-rw-r--r--) Uid: (0/root) Gid: (0/root)

Run the following commands to remove excess permissions, set owner, and set group on /etc/group-:
# chmod u-x,go-wx /etc/group-
# chown root:root /etc/group-

Run the following command to verify that access to /etc/group- is configured.
/etc/group- is a backup written by account-management tools and may not exist:
# [ -e /etc/group- ] && stat -Lc 'Access: (%#a/%A) Uid: ( %u/ %U) Gid: ( %g/
%G)' /etc/group-
If the file exists, the following should be returned; - OR - if it does not exist, nothing is returned (the recommendation is not applicable):
Access: (0644/-rw-r--r--) Uid: (0/root) Gid: (0/root)

Group.title: 7.1 Configure system file and directory access

Rule.title: Ensure access to /etc/shadow is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The /etc/shadow file is used to store the information about user accounts that is critical to the security of those accounts, such as the hashed password and other security information.

Rationale:
If attackers can gain read access to the /etc/shadow file, they can easily run a password cracking program against the hashed password to break it. Other security information that is stored in the /etc/shadow file (such as expiration) could also be useful to subvert the user accounts.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following commands to set mode, owner, and group on /etc/shadow:
# chown root:root /etc/shadow
# chmod 0000 /etc/shadow

check.check-content:
Run the following command to verify that access to /etc/shadow is configured (mode 0000, owned by root:root):
# stat -Lc 'Access: (%#a/%A) Uid: ( %u/ %U) Gid: ( %g/ %G)' /etc/shadow
The following should be returned:
Access: (0000/----------) Uid: (0/root) Gid: (0/root)

Group.title: 7.1 Configure system file and directory access

Rule.title: Ensure access to /etc/shells is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>/etc/shells is a text file which contains the full pathnames of valid login shells. This file is consulted by chsh and available to be queried by other programs.

Rationale:
It is critical to ensure that the /etc/shells file is protected from unauthorized access.
Although it is protected by default, the file permissions could be changed either inadvertently or through malicious actions.</VulnDiscussion>

( %u/ %U) Gid: ( %g/ %G)' /etc/security/opasswd.old

Group.title: 7.1 Configure system file and directory access

Rule.title: Ensure world writable files and directories are secured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>World writable files are the least secure. Data in world-writable files can be modified and compromised by any user on the system. World writable files may also indicate an incorrectly written script or program that could potentially be the cause of a larger compromise to the system's integrity. See the chmod(2) man page for more information.
Setting the sticky bit on world writable directories prevents users from deleting or renaming files in that directory that are not owned by them.

Rationale:
Data in world-writable files can be modified and compromised by any user on the system. World writable files may also indicate an incorrectly written script or program that could potentially be the cause of a larger compromise to the system's integrity.
This feature prevents the ability to delete or rename files in world writable directories (such as /tmp) that are owned by another user.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
• World Writable Files:
o It is recommended that write access is removed from other with the command ( chmod o-w <filename>), but always consult relevant vendor documentation to avoid breaking any application dependencies on a given file.
• World Writable Directories:
o Set the sticky bit on all world writable directories with the command ( chmod a+t <directory_name>) Run the following script to:
• Remove other write permission from any world writable files
• Add the sticky bit to all world writable directories
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
l_smask='01000' a_file=() a_dir=()
a_path=(-path "*/containers/storage/*" -o -path "*/containerd/*" -o -path
"*/kubelet/*" -o -path "*/docker/*" -o -path "/sys/*" -o -path "/snap/*" -o -
path "/boot/efi/*")
l_exclude="nfs|proc|cifs|smb|vfat|iso9660|efivarfs|selinuxfs|ncpfs"
l_exclude2="\/run|\/tmp|\/var\/tmp"
while IFS= read -r l_mount; do
while IFS= read -r -d $'\0' l_file; do
l_mode="$(stat -Lc '%#a' "$l_file" 2>/dev/null)"
if [ -f "$l_file" ]; then # Remove excess permissions from WW files
printf '%s\n' "" " - File: \"$l_file\" is mode: \"$l_mode\"" \
" - removing write permission on \"$l_file\" from \"other\""
chmod o-w "$l_file"
fi
if [ -d "$l_file" ]; then # Add sticky bit
if [ ! $(( $l_mode & $l_smask )) -gt 0 ]; then
printf '%s\n' "" " - Directory: \"$l_file\" is mode:
\"$l_mode\"" \
" and doesn't have the sticky bit set" \
" - Adding the sticky bit"
chmod a+t "$l_file"
fi
fi
done < <(find "$l_mount" -mount -xdev \( "${a_path[@]}" \) \
-prune -o \( -type f -o -type d \) -perm -0002 -print0 2> /dev/null)
done < <(findmnt -Dkerno fstype,target | \
awk '($1 !~ /^[[:space:]]*('"$l_exclude"')/ && $2 !~
/^('"$l_exclude2"')(\/|$)/){print $2}')
}

check.check-content:
Run the following script to list any world-writable files and any world-writable directories that do not have the sticky bit set:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
a_path=(-path "*/containers/storage/*" -o -path "*/containerd/*" -o -path
"*/kubelet/*" -o -path "*/docker/*" -o -path "/sys/*" -o -path "/snap/*" -o -
path "/boot/efi/*")
while IFS= read -r l_mount; do
find "$l_mount" -mount -xdev \( "${a_path[@]}" \) -prune -o \
\( \( -type f -perm -0002 \) -o \( -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000
\) \) \
-printf '%y %p\n' 2>/dev/null
done < <(findmnt -Dkerno fstype,target | awk '($1 !~
/^[[:space:]]*(nfs|proc|cifs|smb|vfat|iso9660|efivarfs|selinuxfs|ncpfs)/ &&
$2 !~ /^(\/run|\/tmp|\/var\/tmp)(\/|$)/){print $2}')
}
Nothing should be returned (each result is tagged f = file or d = directory).
Note: on systems with many files/directories this may run for some time.

Group.title: 7.1 Configure system file and directory access

Rule.title: Ensure no files or directories without an owner and a group exist
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Administrators may delete users or groups from the system and neglect to remove all files and/or directories owned by those users or groups.

Rationale:
A new user or group who is assigned a deleted user's user ID or group ID may then end up "owning" a deleted user or group's files, and thus have more access on the system than was intended.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content: Remove or set ownership and group ownership of these files and/or directories to an active user on the system as appropriate.

check.check-content:
Run the following script to list any files or directories that have no owner or no group:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
a_path=(-path "*/containers/storage/*" -o -path "*/containerd/*" -o -path
"*/kubelet/*" -o -path "*/docker/*" -o -path "/sys/*" -o -path "/snap/*" -o -
path "/boot/efi/*")
while IFS= read -r l_mount; do
find "$l_mount" -mount -xdev \( "${a_path[@]}" \) -prune -o \
\( -type f -o -type d \) \( -nouser -o -nogroup \) -printf '%u %g
%p\n' 2>/dev/null
done < <(findmnt -Dkerno fstype,target | awk '($1 !~
/^[[:space:]]*(nfs|proc|cifs|smb|vfat|iso9660|efivarfs|selinuxfs|ncpfs)/ &&
$2 !~ /^(\/run|\/tmp|\/var\/tmp)(\/|$)/){print $2}')
}
Nothing should be returned. Each line is <owner> <group> <path>; a numeric owner or group indicates no matching user/group exists. Any path returned is unowned and/or ungrouped and should be investigated.
Note: on systems with many files/directories this may run for some time.

Group.title: 7.1 Configure system file and directory access

Rule.title: Ensure SUID and SGID files are reviewed
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The owner of a file can set the file's permissions to run with the owner's or group's permissions, even if the user running the program is not the owner or a member of the group. The most common reason for a SUID or SGID program is to enable users to perform functions (such as changing their password) that require root privileges.

Rationale:
There are valid reasons for SUID and SGID programs, but it is important to identify and review such programs to ensure they are legitimate. Review the files returned by the action in the audit section and check to see if system binaries have a different checksum than what from the package. This is an indication that the binary may have been replaced.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Ensure that no rogue SUID or SGID programs have been introduced into the system.
Review the files returned by the action in the Audit section and confirm the integrity of these binaries.

check.check-content:
Run the following script to list all SUID and SGID files on local filesystems:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
while IFS= read -r l_mount; do
find "$l_mount" -xdev -type f \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) -printf
'%M %p\n' 2>/dev/null
done < <(findmnt -Dkerno fstype,target,options | awk '($1 !~
/^[[:space:]]*(nfs|proc|smb|vfat|iso9660|efivarfs|selinuxfs)/ && $2 !~
/^\/run\/user\// && $3 !~ /noexec/ && $3 !~ /nosuid/){print $2}')
}
Each line is <mode> <path> - an s in the owner-execute position is SUID ( -rwsr-xr- x), an s in the group-execute position is SGID ( -rwxr-sr-x). Review each file returned and confirm it is an expected SUID/SGID program and that its integrity is intact - for example, verify the binary against its owning package with rpm -Vf <file>.
Investigate any unexpected entry.
Note: on systems with many files this may run for some time.

Rule.title: Ensure accounts in /etc/passwd use shadowed passwords
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Local accounts can use shadowed passwords. With shadowed passwords, the passwords are saved in shadow password file, /etc/shadow, encrypted by a salted one-way hash. Accounts with a shadowed password have an x in the second field in /etc/passwd.

Rationale:
The /etc/passwd file also contains information like user ID's and group ID's that are used by many system programs. Therefore, the /etc/passwd file must remain world readable. In spite of encoding the password with a randomly-generated one-way hash function, an attacker could still break the system if they got access to the /etc/passwd file. This can be mitigated by using shadowed passwords, thus moving the passwords in the /etc/passwd file to /etc/shadow. The /etc/shadow file is set so only root will be able to read and write. This helps mitigate the risk of an attacker gaining access to the encoded passwords with which to perform a dictionary attack.
Note: A user account with an empty second field in /etc/passwd allows the account to be logged into by providing only the username.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Run the following command to set accounts to use shadowed passwords and migrate passwords in /etc/passwd to /etc/shadow:
# pwconv

check.check-content:
Run the following command and verify that no output is returned:
# awk -F: '($2 != "x" ) { print "User: \"" $1 "\" is not set to shadowed
passwords "}' /etc/passwd

Rule.title: Ensure /etc/shadow password fields are not empty
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>An account with an empty password field means that anybody may log in as that user without providing a password.

Rationale:
All accounts must have passwords or be locked to prevent the account from being used by an unauthorized user.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
If any accounts in the /etc/shadow file do not have a password, run the following command to lock the account until it can be determined why it does not have a password:
# passwd -l <username>
Also, check to see if the account is logged in and investigate what it is being used for to determine if it needs to be forced off.

check.check-content:
Run the following command and verify that no output is returned:
# awk -F: '($2 == "" ) { print $1 " does not have a password "}' /etc/shadow

Rule.title: Ensure all groups in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Over time, system administration errors and changes can lead to groups being defined in /etc/passwd but not in /etc/group.

Rationale:
Groups defined in the /etc/passwd file but not in the /etc/group file pose a threat to system security since group permissions are not properly managed.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Based on the Audit Procedure output, for each local interactive user whose primary group ID (the fourth field of the user's /etc/passwd entry) has no matching group in /etc/group, follow local site policy and perform one of the following:
• If the group is legitimate and should exist, create it with the reported GID:
# groupadd -g <GID> <groupname>
• If the user should instead belong to an existing group, change the user's primary group to a valid one:
# usermod -g <groupname> <username>

check.check-content:
Run the following script to verify all GIDs in /etc/passwd exist in /etc/group:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
a_passwd_group_gid=("$(awk -F: '{print $4}' /etc/passwd | sort -u)")
a_group_gid=("$(awk -F: '{print $3}' /etc/group | sort -u)")
a_passwd_group_diff=("$(printf '%s\n' "${a_group_gid[@]}"
"${a_passwd_group_gid[@]}" | sort | uniq -u)")
while IFS= read -r l_gid; do
awk -F: '($4 == '"$l_gid"') {print " - User: \"" $1 "\" has GID: \""
$4 "\" which does not exist in /etc/group" }' /etc/passwd
done < <(printf '%s\n' "${a_passwd_group_gid[@]}"
"${a_passwd_group_diff[@]}" | sort | uniq -D | uniq)
unset a_passwd_group_gid; unset a_group_gid; unset a_passwd_group_diff
}
Nothing should be returned

Rule.title: Ensure no duplicate UIDs exist
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Although the useradd program will not let you create a duplicate User ID (UID), it is possible for an administrator to manually edit the /etc/passwd file and change the UID field.

Rationale:
Users must be assigned unique UIDs for accountability and to ensure appropriate access protections.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Based on the Audit Procedure output, for each UID shared by more than one account, keep the UID on the correct account and assign a new, unused UID to each of the other accounts:
# usermod -u <UID> <username>
usermod reassigns ownership of files in the account's home directory automatically.
Review any other files owned by the previously shared UID and reassign ownership to the correct account as appropriate.

Rule.title: Ensure no duplicate GIDs exist
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Although the groupadd program will not let you create a duplicate Group ID (GID), it is possible for an administrator to manually edit the /etc/group file and change the GID field.

Rationale:
User groups must be assigned unique GIDs for accountability and to ensure appropriate access protections.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Based on the Audit Procedure output, for each GID shared by more than one group, keep the GID on the correct group and assign a new, unused GID to each of the other groups:
# groupmod -g <GID> <groupname>
Review any files group-owned by the previously shared GID and reassign group ownership to the correct group as appropriate.

Rule.title: Ensure no duplicate user names exist
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Although the useradd program will not let you create a duplicate user name, it is possible for an administrator to manually edit the /etc/passwd file and change the username.

Rationale:
If a user is assigned a duplicate user name, it will create and have access to files with the first UID for that username in /etc/passwd. For example, if "test4" has a UID of 1000 and a subsequent "test4" entry has a UID of 2000, logging in as "test4" will use UID 1000. Effectively, the UID is shared, which is a security problem.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Based on the Audit Procedure output, for each duplicated user name, determine which entry is correct and make each user name unique. Use vipw to safely edit the user database and either remove the redundant entry or rename it to a unique user name:
# vipw
File ownerships will reflect the change automatically as long as each account has a unique UID.

Rule.title: Ensure no duplicate group names exist
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>Although the groupadd program will not let you create a duplicate group name, it is possible for an administrator to manually edit the /etc/group file and change the group name.

Rationale:
If a group is assigned a duplicate group name, it will create and have access to files with the first GID for that group in /etc/group. Effectively, the GID is shared, which is a security problem.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Based on the Audit Procedure output, for each duplicated group name, determine which entry is correct and make each group name unique. Use vigr to safely edit the group database and either remove the redundant entry or rename it to a unique group name:
# vigr
File group ownerships will reflect the change automatically as long as each group has a unique GID.

Rule.title: Ensure local interactive user home directories are configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>The user home directory is space defined for the particular user to set local environment variables and to store personal files. While the system administrator can establish secure permissions for users' home directories, the users can easily override these.
Users can be defined in /etc/passwd without a home directory or with a home directory that does not actually exist.

Rationale:
Since the user is accountable for files stored in the user home directory, the user must be the owner of the directory. Group or world-writable user home directories may enable malicious users to steal or modify other users' data or to gain another user's system privileges. If the user's home directory does not exist or is unassigned, the user will be placed in "/" and will not be able to write any files or have local environment variables set.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
1. If a local interactive user's home directory is undefined and/or does not exist, follow local site policy and perform one of the following:
• Lock the user account
• Remove the user from the system
• Create a directory for the user. If the home directory is undefined, set it to the absolute path of that directory:
# usermod --home <directory> <username>
2. For each existing home directory reported by the Audit Procedure, make changes in accordance with local site policy and apply the corresponding action:
• The directory is not owned by its user - set the owner:
# chown <user> <home_directory>
• The directory is more permissive than mode 0750 - remove the excess permissions:
# chmod g-w,o-rwx <home_directory>

check.check-content:
Run the following script to list local interactive user home directories that do not exist, are not owned by the user, or are mode more permissive than 750:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
l_valid_shells="^($( awk -F\/ '$NF != "nologin" {print}' /etc/shells | sed
-rn '/^\//{s,/,\\/,g;p}' | paste -s -d '|' - ))$"
l_mask='0027'; l_max="$( printf '%o' $(( 0777 & ~$l_mask )) )"
while IFS=" " read -r l_user l_home; do
if [ ! -d "$l_home" ]; then
printf '%s\n' " - User: \"$l_user\" home directory \"$l_home\" does
not exist"
else
while IFS=: read -r l_own l_mode; do
[ "$l_user" != "$l_own" ] && printf '%s\n' " - User: \"$l_user\"
home \"$l_home\" is owned by \"$l_own\" (should be owned by \"$l_user\")"
[ $(( $l_mode & $l_mask )) -gt 0 ] && printf '%s\n' " - User:
\"$l_user\" home \"$l_home\" is mode \"$l_mode\" (should be \"$l_max\" or
more restrictive)"
done <<< "$(stat -Lc '%U:%#a' "$l_home")"
fi
done <<< "$(awk -v pat="$l_valid_shells" -F: '$(NF) ~ pat { print $1 " "
$(NF-1) }' /etc/passwd)"
}
Nothing should be returned. On a system with many local interactive users this may take some time to run.

Rule.title: Ensure local interactive user dot files access is configured
Rule.description:
<VulnDiscussion>While the system administrator can establish secure permissions for users' "dot" files, the users can easily override these.
•.forward file specifies an email address to forward the user's mail to.
•.rhost file provides the "remote authentication" database for the rcp, rlogin, and rsh commands and the rcmd() function. These files bypass the standard password-based user authentication mechanism. They specify remote hosts and users that are considered trusted (i.e. are allowed to access the local system without supplying a password)
•.netrc file contains data for logging into a remote host or passing authentication to an API.
•.bash_history file keeps track of the user's commands.

Rationale:
User configuration files with excessive or incorrect access may enable malicious users to steal or modify other users' data or to gain another user's system privileges.</VulnDiscussion>

fixtext.+content:
Making global modifications to users' files without alerting the user community can result in unexpected outages and unhappy users. Establish a monitoring policy to report user dot-file permissions and ownership, and take action in accordance with local site policy.
For each file reported by the Audit Procedure, in the affected user's home directory, apply the corresponding action:
• A.forward or.rhosts file exists - review its contents and remove it:
# rm <file>
• The file is more permissive than allowed - remove the excess permissions (0600 or more restrictive for.netrc and.bash_history, 0644 or more restrictive for other dot files):
# chmod u-x,go-rwx <file> # .netrc and .bash_history
# chmod u-x,go-wx <file> # other dot files
• The file is not owned by its user - set the owner:
# chown <user> <file>
• The file is not group-owned by the user's primary group - set the group:
# chgrp <group> <file>

check.check-content:
Run the following script to list local interactive user dot files that are.forward /.rhost, or are not mode 0644 or more restrictive (0600 for.netrc /.bash_history), or are not owned by the user and their primary group:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
{
l_valid_shells="^($( awk -F\/ '$NF != "nologin" {print}' /etc/shells | sed
-rn '/^\//{s,/,\\/,g;p}' | paste -s -d '|' - ))$"
f_file_chk() {
l_max="$( printf '%o' $(( 0777 & ~$l_mask )) )"
[ $(( $l_mode & $l_mask )) -gt 0 ] && printf '%s\n' " - File:
\"$l_hdfile\" is mode \"$l_mode\" (should be \"$l_max\" or more restrictive)"
[[ ! "$l_owner" =~ ($l_user) ]] && printf '%s\n' " - File:
\"$l_hdfile\" is owned by \"$l_owner\" (should be owned by \"${l_user//|/ or
}\")"
[[ ! "$l_gowner" =~ ($l_group) ]] && printf '%s\n' " - File:
\"$l_hdfile\" is group owned by \"$l_gowner\" (should be group owned by
\"${l_group//|/ or }\")"
}
while IFS=: read -r l_user l_home; do
if [ -d "$l_home" ]; then
l_group="$(id -gn "$l_user" | xargs)"; l_group="${l_group// /|}"
while IFS= read -r -d $'\0' l_hdfile; do
while read -r l_mode l_owner l_gowner; do
case "$(basename "$l_hdfile")" in
.forward | .rhost ) printf '%s\n' " - File: \"$l_hdfile\"
exists (review and manually delete)" ;;
.netrc | .bash_history ) l_mask='0177'; f_file_chk ;;
* ) l_mask='0133'; f_file_chk ;;
esac
done <<< "$(stat -Lc '%#a %U %G' "$l_hdfile")"
done < <(find "$l_home" -xdev -type f -name '.*' -print0)
fi
done <<< "$(awk -v pat="$l_valid_shells" -F: '$(NF) ~ pat { print $1 " "
$(NF-1) }' /etc/passwd)"
}
Nothing should be returned. If a.netrc file is required and follows local site policy, it should be mode 0600 or more restrictive. On a system with many local interactive users this may take some time to run.
